docs.title: ObjectIO
docs.text:
S3-compatible object storage in Rust, built to not lose data. One storage core (erasure coding, failure-domain-aware placement, repair, metadata on Raft) with S3, data-lake catalogs and block volumes on top of it. Apache-2.0, every feature, no tiers. Source on GitHub.

docker run --rm -p 9000:9000 -v objectio-data:/var/lib/objectio \
  ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:latest objectio-aio --data /var/lib/objectio

That's a whole cluster in one process: meta, OSDs and the S3 gateway on port 9000. The quickstart has the binaries for Linux and macOS, and a 3-meta, 6-OSD cluster in Docker Compose; Kubernetes has the Helm chart.

docs.title: Where it stands
docs.text:
ObjectIO 0.1.0 is the first release, and an early one (release notes). S3 and the storage core are tested for production; the data lake APIs and block volumes are previews. Every feature and how far it has been proven is in features; what's next is in the roadmap.

Status S3 Passes 680 of 687 applicable ceph s3-tests; the other 7 are written down, none a bug. Versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle, multipart, checksums, SSE, bucket policies, IAM and STS APIs, tenants, replication between clusters, S3 Select, audit Storage core Erasure coding (Reed-Solomon with ISA-L, on x86_64 and arm64), placement groups across failure domains, recovery and repair by placement group, drain, backfill, balancer, small-object packing, scrub; raw disks with O_DIRECT and io_uring Meta Raft (openraft) on 3 or more nodes; any node serves; its own log, back within a second of a power cut Data lake (preview) Iceberg REST Catalog, Unity Catalog API and Delta Sharing are built; tests with real engines (Spark, Trino, pyiceberg) come next Block (preview) Volumes over NBD: thin provisioning, snapshots, clones, a write journal fsynced before the ack. Filesystem and database crash tests are the gate for production File NFS on the same core, later

docs.title: What "durable" means here
docs.text:
• An acknowledgement means the data is on stable storage. Every shard is fsynced, and its location record after it, before the PUT returns. Nothing trades this for speed.
  • No single copy decides. An object's shards are spread across failure domains (hosts by default; racks or zones if you declare them), and its metadata is kept with them on every OSD of its placement, written at a majority and read from a quorum, newest copy winning.
  • Every byte is checked twice. Each shard's checksum is recorded with the object when it's written and checked on every read and every repair, independently of the checksum the disk keeps.
  • Repair is continuous. A lost disk or host is rebuilt from the surviving shards onto the rest of the cluster, without an operator.

How it works has the detail.

docs.title: ObjectIO roadmap
docs.text:
What comes next, by release. What already exists, and how far each part has been proven, is in features.md; what each release shipped is in its notes (0.1.0). When a release is cut, its items move into its notes and leave this page, so this page only ever shows what is ahead.

Each item is one line: what will be true when it is done, which is also how it is tested. Moving an item between releases is an edit to this page, in a pull request like any other change. Each item links to its GitHub issue, and the ObjectIO project shows which are in progress.

Last reviewed: 2026-10-20, after an external production-readiness review of the release candidate.

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text:
1. S3: production-ready and bug-free. The product we ship first. No known bug stays open; every gap is either closed or written down as "not supported" with the reason.
  2. The storage engine core, worked on alongside S3: OSD, erasure coding, placement, meta, repair. Everything here is built once and reused by block and file; none of it is S3-specific.
  3. Data lake (Iceberg REST, Unity Catalog, Delta Sharing): next, and as important as S3 once S3 is in production.
  4. Block, then file, on the same core.

Rule for every domain: reliability first. An acknowledgement means the data is on stable storage; nothing trades durability for speed.

docs.title: ObjectIO features
docs.text:
Everything ObjectIO does today, by domain, and how far each part has been proven. A feature on this page exists; one that isn't here doesn't (what is planned is in the roadmap). How each feature works, with its wire format and settings, is in the feature reference and the guides.

Reading the columns

  • Status: ✅ shipped and covered by end-to-end tests; 🟡 shipped, but not yet proven for production (the gap is named); ✖ not supported, by decision (the reason is given).
  • Guide: where a user or operator reads how to use it.
  • Design: how it works inside.

docs.title: How far 0.1.0 has been proven
docs.text:
0.1.0 is the first release, and an early one. S3 and the storage core are tested for production; the data lake APIs, block volumes and file access are previews.

  • S3: ceph s3-tests, 680 of 687 applicable tests pass at the release candidate on Linux x86_64, 679 on Linux arm64; the rest are written down (6 known gaps, and tests caught by another running beside them, which pass alone). None is a bug.
  • The storage core: a 48-hour soak of 84 faults (power cuts, meta leader kills, network partitions, disks pulled and drives lost for good) under 7.02 M acknowledged operations and 1.50 TB written: no acknowledged object lost, no space leaked. The chaos suite on six machines: 81,436 acknowledged writes intact through every fault. Recorded disk writes replayed up to random power-cut points: nothing acknowledged lost.
  • Data lake, block, file: the data lake APIs and block volumes are built and unit- or end-to-end-tested, but not yet tested with real engines (Spark, Trino, pyiceberg) or under a filesystem and a database; file access is not built.

Adjacent releases upgrade one node at a time, under traffic, with every object readable after (upgrades). The admin API and the CLI may still change between 0.x releases; the release notes say when they do.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Feature Status Notes Guide Design Raw-disk OSD: O_DIRECT, 4 KiB blocks, a write-ahead log ✅ deployment storage engine Flush before acknowledge ✅ Each shard fsynced, then its location record; a drive's volatile cache flushed on every write; a failed location record fails the write production storage engine Crash consistency of the OSD ✅ The shard device's and state filesystem's writes recorded and replayed up to random power-cut points: every acknowledged write survives. Run in CI on every merge storage engine On-disk format checks ✅ Superblock feature words, protobuf records, strict logs and snapshots disk layout Superblock safety ✅ Two copies; a torn one mounts from the other; deletes no longer rewrite it disk layout An OSD's disks known by their ids ✅ Each disk's index recorded by the id in its superblock: disks found in any order or at other paths; an OSD missing one, or given one not its own, doesn't start; a blank disk replaces a missing one. Reads and scrub check each block is the shard its location names (object, stripe, length, CRC32C) production storage engine OSD metadata store (WAL, on-disk index, bounded cache) ✅ Memory flat with the object count; snapshots streamed, not cloned storage engine OSD back in seconds after a restart ✅ An OSD of 10 M shards serves 16.9 s after a power cut; its counts are rebuilt after it serves failure recovery OSD start io_uring shard I/O 🟡 The default in Linux release builds; a host that denies io_uring (docker's default seccomp profile) gets pread, with a warning. The data-path end-to-end tests run on it in CI (S3 calls, multipart, repair, restarts, packing, checksums, removed disks); the rest of the suite and the soak on pread Docker I/O levels Erasure coding: Reed-Solomon with ISA-L, on x86_64 and arm64 ✅ 4+2 by default. One code on every build, its parity checked against the reference code on both architectures, so amd64 and arm64 nodes mix in one cluster (not yet run as one). A pool takes only profiles with parity that every loss of m shards decodes Linux data protection Reads never serve a data shard rebuilt wrong ✅ Each data shard a read rebuilds is checked against its recorded checksum (or a spare parity shard) before it is served; a decode that doesn't check out is tried another way, then fails and reports the stripe for repair data protection LRC 🟡 Objects of any length, PUT or multipart, read back with a drive lost; repair built and tested. Survives every loss of its global parity count (LRC 6+2+2: any 2, 88% of 3); not yet through the full end-to-end suite or a soak CLI data protection Replica pools (2-way, 3-way) 🟡 Repair built and tested; not yet through the full end-to-end suite or a soak data protection End-to-end shard checksums, scrub ✅ Each shard's checksum kept with the object and checked on every read and repair, besides the OSD's own data protection Object metadata at quorum ✅ With one or two OSDs down (4+2), PUT, overwrite and DELETE go on; reads get the newest copy, never a deleted object object metadata quorum Small-object path ✅ A small object's shards travel with its metadata, one round trip; a small GET reads metadata from a read quorum performance small-object path Small-object packing (pack, reconcile, compact) ✅ packing Placement: CRUSH2, placement groups, copyset allocator ✅ feature reference topology Failure-domain topology (5 levels), locality-aware reads ✅ topologies topology Refusing placements the topology can't satisfy 🟡 A validation endpoint; enforcement on write is planned topology Storage pools (expand by adding a pool), balancer ✅ A pool's protection scheme is checked when it is made or changed: one the codecs can't keep (no parity, LRC groups of unequal size, no copies) is refused feature reference data protection Recovery by placement group ✅ Every pool has PGs whose acting set and epoch are committed before a write uses them; OSDs refuse writes from an older epoch; peering and a state machine per PG failure recovery PG recovery Repair after a disk or host is lost ✅ Rebuilt from the surviving shards onto the rest of the cluster, without an operator; parallel across PGs, sized from the drives failure recovery PG recovery Degraded objects recorded when written, repaired first ✅ A PUT acknowledged short of shards is recorded in the Raft commit that creates it degraded objects An OSD lost for good is re-protected ✅ A drive gone with its metadata, set out: every shard it held is rebuilt elsewhere failure recovery PG recovery Backfill ✅ A stripe with two shards on one OSD is re-spread once a distinct OSD can take one PG recovery Drain (planned removal of an OSD) ✅ failure recovery Full-disk behaviour ✅ Client writes stop at the full ratio (507 StorageFull); the rest is kept for repair; space returns after deletes production Meta: Raft (openraft), replicated state, snapshots, log compaction ✅ A node that was down longer than the kept log catches up from a snapshot meta HA meta Meta's own Raft log ✅ Sealed segments open from an index; a meta node listens within a second of a power cut, a torn last append cut off meta log Bucket listings that cost the same per page anywhere in the bucket ✅ The scan seeks to the continuation marker and past each common prefix: paging through 100,000 keys reads each row once meta Meta HA: any node serves, failover, node loss ✅ Leader killed, frozen and replaced under S3 traffic, in multi-process tests and on Kubernetes (3 metas through Helm) meta HA meta Meta reads confirmed by a quorum (read index) ✅ The leader answers only while a majority has confirmed it leads within the last second; one cut off from its followers answers UNAVAILABLE within about 3 s, in a multi-process test meta HA meta Rolling upgrade, format levels ✅ Meta, then OSDs, then gateways, under traffic; new formats gated until every node runs the new release; docs.title: How it works
docs.text: ObjectIO is three kinds of service around one storage core. This page follows an object through it: where it goes when it's written, how it's found and checked when it's read, and what happens when a disk or a host fails.

docs.title: The services
docs.text:
S3 / Iceberg / Unity Catalog / Delta Sharing / admin
                                │
                     ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                     │  Gateways (9000)    │  stateless: as many as you like
                     │  auth, erasure code │
                     └───┬─────────────┬───┘
            placement,   │             │   shards and object
            listings,    │             │   metadata, in parallel
            IAM          │             │
          ┌──────────────┴───┐   ┌─────┴──────────────────────────┐
          │ Meta (9100)      │   │ OSDs (9200), one per host      │
          │ Raft, 3+ nodes   │◀──│ raw disks: shards, and each    │
          │ one redb file    │   │ object's metadata copy         │
          │ each             │   │                                │
          └──────────────────┘   └────────────────────────────────┘
Service Holds Scales by Gateway Nothing: every request is served from meta and the OSDs. It speaks S3 (SigV4), the data-lake APIs and the admin API, and does the erasure coding Adding gateways behind a load balancer Meta Everything shared that isn't object bytes: buckets, IAM users and policies, tenants, pools and placement groups, bucket listings, catalog tables. Every write goes through Raft; any node answers, followers forward writes to the leader 3 or 5 nodes; a majority keeps it writable OSD Shards on raw block devices it owns outright, and a copy of the metadata of every object it holds a shard of One per host (or per disk set); add hosts

objectio-aio runs all of them in one process, for a laptop or an appliance; the wire protocol is the same. Between services, every gRPC hop can be mutual TLS.

docs.title: Placement
docs.text:
An object's key hashes (jump consistent hash) to one of a pool's placement groups. Each placement group is a fixed list of OSDs, one per shard, chosen so that no two share a failure domain: a host by default, or a rack, zone or region if you declare them. Meta records that list; the balancer moves whole placement groups, never single objects, so rebalancing costs the number of placement groups, not the number of objects.

A pool is an erasure code (4+2 or 8+4 Reed-Solomon, or replicas) over a set of OSDs. A cluster grows by adding OSDs to a pool or by adding a pool, never by splitting placement groups.

docs.title: Writing an object
docs.text:
With 4+2 erasure coding:

  1. The gateway authenticates the request and asks meta for the key's placement group.
  2. It splits the object into 4 data shards and computes 2 parity shards (with ISA-L, on x86_64 and arm64 alike), with a CRC32C of each.
  3. It writes the six shards to the six OSDs in parallel. Each OSD writes its shard to raw disk with O_DIRECT, flushes the drive's cache, then records and flushes the shard's location. The write needs 5 of the 6.
  4. It writes the object's metadata (size, ETag, version, stamp, where each shard is and its checksum) to every OSD of the placement. This needs a majority: 4 of 6.
  5. It records the key in the bucket's listing, in meta, through Raft.
  6. Only then does the client get its 200.

Objects up to 4 KiB skip the shards: they are kept whole inside their metadata, on every copy. Small objects written as separate stripes are later packed together in the background, so a million 8 KiB objects don't each take a stripe of their own.

A multipart upload writes each part this way and records the parts in one object at completion.

docs.title: Reading an object
docs.text:
1. The gateway reads the object's metadata from the OSDs of its placement and takes the copy with the highest stamp among a read quorum (3 of 6). Any 3 copies include one that took the last acknowledged write, so a copy that missed an overwrite or a delete is outvoted, never served.
  2. It reads 4 shards, preferring the nearest OSDs, and checks each against the checksum recorded in the metadata.
  3. If a shard is missing or doesn't match, it reads another and reconstructs: any 4 of the 6 rebuild the object. Each data shard it rebuilds is checked against its recorded checksum before it is served; one that doesn't match is rebuilt from other shards, or the read fails. The bad shard is reported for repair.

So with 4+2, any two OSDs can be down and every object still reads and every write still succeeds.

docs.title: Inside an OSD
docs.text:
• Raw disks. No filesystem: a superblock (kept twice), an allocation bitmap of 4 KiB blocks, and the shards. Each shard carries a header and footer with its own checksum. I/O is O_DIRECT, through io_uring on Linux.
  • Its metadata store. A write-ahead log, flushed before every acknowledgement, in front of an on-disk index with a bounded cache. The OSD's memory stays flat however many objects it holds.
  • Scrub. In the background, at a set rate, the OSD reads every shard it holds and checks it, so a shard that rots on disk is found even if nobody reads it.
  • It never formats a disk that holds data. A disk is formatted only if it's blank: a disk the OSD can't recognise is reported, not wiped.

docs.title: When something fails
docs.text:
Fault What happens A disk or an OSD fails Reads reconstruct from the remaining shards; writes go on at quorum. Repair rebuilds the missing shards from the survivors, checks each against its recorded checksum, and places it on another OSD in the same placement rules A host loses power The same. Every acknowledged write was flushed to stable storage, so it's there when the host returns; copies it missed are healed A shard rots on disk Scrub or a read finds the checksum mismatch; the shard is rebuilt from the others The meta leader fails The others elect a new leader in a few seconds; gateways retry. Writes resume, nothing acknowledged is lost Meta loses its majority Writes are refused with 503 (retry), never accepted and lost; they resume when the majority is back A network partition The side with the meta majority carries on; the cut-off side refuses writes. When the partition heals, the cut-off nodes catch up A gateway's clock drifts Writes are stamped with the gateway's clock and the newest stamp wins, so a gateway more than 500 ms off meta's clock refuses writes until it's back in step A disk fills Client writes stop at the full ratio (507); the space left is kept for repair You remove a disk or host Drain moves its shards off first, then it can go

Each of these is exercised by the chaos tests or the end-to-end suite on every pull request.

docs.title: Data lake and block on the same core
docs.text:
• The Iceberg REST Catalog and the Unity Catalog API keep their tables in meta and their data in buckets, so one deployment is the catalog and the storage. A Delta Sharing server shares tables from any tenant.
  • Block volumes (NBD) are 4 MiB chunks erasure-coded the same way, with a write journal flushed before each acknowledgement, and snapshots and clones that share stripes.

Features has the status of each, and the roadmap what's next.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository: how to propose a change, set up, test at the right level, and open a pull request. Security problems are reported privately (SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
Workflows live in the source tree:

  • make build / make test / make lint / make fmt — local workflows (see the repo Makefile).
  • docker compose run --rm build — sandboxed builds without a local Rust toolchain.
  • cargo test --package objectio-erasure — run a single crate's tests (erasure coding is ISA-L's on every build).

CONTRIBUTING.md covers the conventions (formatting, clippy, errors, commits, which tests a change needs). For coding agents working in a checkout, CLAUDE.md is the map of the code, and two skills in .claude/skills/ walk the work: objectio-contribute (issue to merge) and objectio-testing.

docs.title: Agent skills
docs.text:
ObjectIO ships skills for coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and others that read SKILL.md files). A skill tells the agent how a job is done on ObjectIO, in what order, and what not to do, so that "deploy this", "give this app its own bucket" or "why is this PG not clean" get the right commands the first time.

Skill For What it covers objectio-deploy operators Installing, sizing, upgrading, monitoring and troubleshooting: objectio-aio, the binaries, the Helm chart; the choices that are hard to change later; what is lost if objectio-admin operators Running a cluster with obioctl: tenants, users and keys, policies, roles and STS, buckets and provisioning, pools, placement groups, drain, upgrades, KMS, audit, replication objectio-sdk application developers Connecting S3 clients (addressing, region, SigV4), credentials (scoped keys, STS, environment), which S3 features exist and which are refused, the Python and Go SDKs, the data lake APIs

docs.title: Installing them
docs.text:
obioctl carries them, so they match the release you run:

obioctl skills list
obioctl skills install                         # every agent found under $HOME, and ~/.agents/skills
obioctl skills install --audience ops          # only the operators' skills (or dev)
obioctl skills install --agent claude          # one agent; repeatable
obioctl skills install --dir ./.claude/skills  # one project
obioctl skills install --force                 # replace older copies after upgrading obioctl

install needs no endpoint or credentials. It writes to each agent whose home directory exists (Claude Code ~/.claude/skills, Codex ~/.codex/skills, opencode ~/.config/opencode/skills, pi ~/.pi/agent/skills) and always to ~/.agents/skills. A copy that differs from the one carried is left alone unless --force is given.

In Claude Code, without obioctl, the repository is a plugin marketplace:

/plugin marketplace add object-io/objectio
/plugin install objectio-ops@objectio      # objectio-deploy, objectio-admin
/plugin install objectio-dev@objectio      # objectio-sdk

docs.title: Contributors
docs.text: For an agent working on ObjectIO's own code, the repository has two more skills in .claude/skills/, which Claude Code loads in a checkout: objectio-contribute (from the issue to the merge) and objectio-testing (unit, end-to-end, s3-tests, the upgrade test). The rules they follow are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: ObjectIO provides an S3-compatible REST API.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• S3 Operations - Supported S3 API operations
  • Iceberg REST Catalog - Iceberg namespace and table API
  • Authentication - AWS SigV4 and security
  • Identity and Access - IAM, OIDC providers, STS
  • Public Access - anonymous access, Block Public Access, request origin

docs.title: Using AWS CLI
docs.text:
# Configure endpoint
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your-access-key
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your-secret-key

# Create bucket
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket

# Upload object
aws s3 cp file.txt s3://my-bucket/

# List objects
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/

# Download object
aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/file.txt ./downloaded.txt

# Delete object
aws s3 rm s3://my-bucket/file.txt

docs.title: Using Python (boto3)
docs.text:
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client(
    's3',
    endpoint_url='http://localhost:9000',
    aws_access_key_id='your-access-key',
    aws_secret_access_key='your-secret-key',
)

# Create bucket
s3.create_bucket(Bucket='my-bucket')

# Upload object
s3.put_object(Bucket='my-bucket', Key='hello.txt', Body=b'Hello World')

# Download object
response = s3.get_object(Bucket='my-bucket', Key='hello.txt')
data = response['Body'].read()

# List objects
response = s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket='my-bucket')
for obj in response.get('Contents', []):
    print(obj['Key'])

docs.text:
# List buckets (no auth)
curl http://localhost:9000/

# Create bucket (no auth mode)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:9000/my-bucket

# Upload object
curl -X PUT -d "Hello World" http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/hello.txt

# Download object
curl http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/hello.txt

docs.title: ObjectIO — Feature Reference
docs.text:
What ObjectIO does today, and how. This page describes what is built. Every feature's status is in features.md, what is planned in the roadmap, and what each release added in its notes (0.1.0).

ObjectIO is a unified software-defined storage (SDS) platform: several storage paradigms on a single erasure-coded backend.

Paradigm Protocol Use Case Object Storage S3 API Unstructured data, backups, media, ML datasets Data Lakehouse Iceberg REST Catalog + Unity Catalog + Delta Sharing Analytics warehouses, three-level governance, Spark/Trino/Databricks-SDK queries, cross-org data sharing Block Storage gRPC + NBD Databases, VMs, thin-provisioned volumes with snapshots

All share the same underlying erasure-coded storage layer, IAM, multi-tenancy, and web console. File access (NFS) is planned on the same layer.

docs.title: Core S3 API
docs.text:
• Bucket operations: CreateBucket, DeleteBucket, HeadBucket, ListBuckets
  • Object operations: PutObject, GetObject, HeadObject, DeleteObject, DeleteObjects (batch)
  • Multipart upload: InitiateMultipartUpload, UploadPart, CompleteMultipartUpload, AbortMultipartUpload, ListParts, ListMultipartUploads
  • Range requests: HTTP Range header support (bytes=0-99, suffix ranges, open-ended ranges)
  • Copy object: Server-side copy via x-amz-copy-source header (metadata-only fast path when on same OSD)
  • S3 Select: SelectObjectContent on CSV, JSON and Parquet objects (GZIP/BZIP2 for CSV and JSON), CSV or JSON output
  • User metadata: x-amz-meta-* headers stored and returned
  • S3 error responses: Standard XML error format with S3 error codes

docs.title: Bucket Versioning
docs.text:
• PUT/GET /{bucket}?versioning — Enable, suspend, or query versioning state
  • Version-aware PUT: Generates UUID version ID when versioning enabled, returns x-amz-version-id header
  • Version-aware DELETE: Creates delete markers (new version with is_delete_marker=true) when no ?versionId specified
  • Version-specific DELETE: Permanently deletes a specific version via ?versionId=
  • ListObjectVersions: GET /{bucket}?versions returns all versions including delete markers
  • Dual-key OSD storage: Current version at m:{bucket}\0{key}, version history at v:{bucket}\0{key}\0{version_id}

docs.title: Object Locking (WORM)
docs.text:
• PUT/GET /{bucket}?object-lock — Configure object lock with default retention
  • Retention modes: GOVERNANCE (bypassable with header) and COMPLIANCE (immutable until expiry)
  • PUT/GET /{bucket}/{key}?retention — Per-object retention (mode + retain-until-date)
  • PUT/GET /{bucket}/{key}?legal-hold — Per-object legal hold (ON/OFF)
  • Delete enforcement: Objects under retention or legal hold cannot be deleted (403 AccessDenied)
  • Governance bypass: x-amz-bypass-governance-retention: true header allows deletion
  • Lock at creation: x-amz-bucket-object-lock-enabled: true on CreateBucket; or later, PutObjectLockConfiguration on a bucket with versioning enabled (otherwise 409 InvalidBucketState), as S3 allows. Versioning can't be suspended afterwards

docs.title: CORS and browser uploads
docs.text:
• CORS (?cors): preflights answered without credentials, headers on matching requests and their errors. S3 API § CORS
  • POST Object: S3 HTML form uploads (generate_presigned_post), SigV4 policy signatures, every policy condition, authorized as the signer and written as a PUT. S3 API § POST Object
  • GET response-* overrides (e.g. response-content-disposition on a presigned link), and objects keep Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Expires.

docs.title: Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
• PUT/GET/DELETE /{bucket}?lifecycle — S3's lifecycle configuration, checked as S3 checks it and read back as written. See S3 API § Lifecycle.
  • Expiration by Days or Date: unversioned buckets delete; versioned ones add a delete marker, as a DELETE would.
  • NoncurrentVersionExpiration (NoncurrentDays, NewerNoncurrentVersions): old versions expire by how long they've been noncurrent, keeping the newest N.
  • ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker: removes a delete marker only when it's the key's only version — never one with versions behind it.
  • AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload.
  • Filters: prefix, tags, object size, and <And>.
  • Safe by construction: every action goes through the S3 delete path, so Object Lock is honoured, the listing is kept and space reclaimed; every action is an audit event by lifecycle:<rule id>.
  • One scanner: gateways take a lease in meta, so one scans at a time (--lifecycle-interval-secs, default hourly).
  • Not supported: transitions (one storage class) — refused with InvalidStorageClass.

docs.title: Bucket Policies
docs.text:
• PUT/GET/DELETE /{bucket}?policy — IAM-style JSON bucket policies
  • Policy evaluation: Allow/Deny/ImplicitDeny decisions
  • ARN-based resources: arn:obio:s3:::{bucket} and arn:obio:s3:::{bucket}/{key}
  • Condition keys: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption, s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id, aws:SecureTransport — populated from PUT/GET/DELETE request headers, evaluated at request time

docs.title: Server-Side Encryption (SSE)
docs.text:
All three AWS S3 encryption modes are supported (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C). Encryption always happens before the erasure-coding stage so OSD shards only ever see ciphertext. Objects written without SSE remain plaintext; enabling SSE on a bucket does not retroactively encrypt existing objects. Ciphertext correctness is verified end-to-end in tests — grep for any plaintext marker on OSD shards returns zero matches when SSE is enabled.

  • PUT/GET/DELETE /{bucket}?encryption — Bucket default encryption configuration, AWS-compatible XML (ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration)
  • Per-request precedence: explicit x-amz-server-side-encryption* request header > bucket default > plaintext
  • ETag semantics: MD5 of plaintext for SSE-S3 / SSE-KMS (AWS-compatible). SSE-C uses the AWS multipart ETag format for multipart uploads
  • Response headers: x-amz-server-side-encryption, x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id, x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm, x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key-md5

docs.title: SSE-S3 (AES256)
docs.text:
• AES-256-CTR with a fresh per-object Data Encryption Key (DEK)
  • DEK wrapped with the gateway's service master key via AES-256-GCM and stored in ObjectMeta.encrypted_dek
  • Service master key loaded from OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY env var (base64 32 bytes); helm chart auto-generates one on first install and preserves it across helm upgrade
  • Range GETs and multipart uploads fully supported — each part/stripe uses its own IV so stripes decrypt independently

docs.title: SSE-KMS (aws:kms)
docs.text:
• Per-object DEK wrapped by a named KMS key (Key Encryption Key, KEK)
  • Local KMS provider: self-contained backend — KEK material is itself wrapped by the service master key before it reaches meta, so meta stores only encrypted blobs
  • Envelope encryption: client specifies KMS key via x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id (full ARN or short id)
  • Encryption context: optional x-amz-server-side-encryption-context (base64 JSON) bound to the DEK wrap as AEAD associated data; decrypt fails if context differs
  • Multipart support: MPU picks the key at CreateMultipartUpload time; per-part stripe IVs

docs.title: SSE-C (customer-provided keys)
docs.text:
• Three headers: x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-algorithm: AES256, -customer-key (base64 32 bytes), -customer-key-md5 (base64 MD5 of the key)
  • Key material is never persisted — object metadata stores only the algorithm marker + IV
  • MD5 binding verified on every PUT/GET/HEAD; wrong MD5 → InvalidArgument 400
  • Hard-blocked on warehouse buckets (iceberg-* and the configured warehouse bucket): query engines can't provide the customer key on every read, so writes are rejected at PUT rather than silently producing unreadable objects
  • Multipart upload: supported end-to-end. CreateMultipartUpload stores the customer-key MD5 in the MPU state; every UploadPart must resupply the same key, validated MD5-against-MD5 before encryption; CompleteMultipartUpload produces a standard AWS multipart ETag. The key itself never touches meta.

docs.title: KMS Administration (/_admin/kms/*)
docs.text:
AIStor-compatible KMS action model. Resource ARNs use arn:obio:kms:::{key_id}; the wildcard arn:obio:kms:::* matches all keys.

Endpoint Action Description GET /_admin/kms/status kms:Status Backend state (enabled, local, master-key configured) GET /_admin/kms/version kms:Version Service version + protocol GET /_admin/kms/api kms:API Supported endpoints POST /_admin/kms/keys kms:CreateKey Create a new KMS key GET /_admin/kms/keys kms:ListKeys List KMS keys GET /_admin/kms/keys/{key_id} kms:KeyStatus Get a specific key DELETE /_admin/kms/keys/{key_id} kms:DeleteKey Delete + drop cached KEK
  • Policy gating: every endpoint evaluates the caller's attached named IAM policies against (action, resource). The built-in admin user and console sessions bypass policy evaluation.
  • Dual auth on admin endpoints: SigV4 (for API clients) or console session cookie (for web UI). Cookie requests pass through a pre-router layer that validates SigV4 only when an Authorization header is present.

docs.title: KMS Backend Selection
docs.text:
The gateway's KMS backend picks how SSE-KMS wrap/unwrap is performed.

Two configuration sources, meta wins: 1. Meta kms/config (console-writable) — the persisted config. Hot-swappable at runtime via PUT /_admin/kms/config with no gateway restart. 2. --kms-backend CLI flag + env vars — fallback used at first boot when meta has no entry. Useful for IaC-pinned deployments.

Backends: - local — self-contained. Each KMS key's master material is generated on the gateway, wrapped by the service master key, and persisted via meta. Admin endpoints under /_admin/kms/keys manage the key lifecycle. Most appropriate for on-prem deployments that don't have an external KMS. - vault — HashiCorp Vault's Transit secrets engine. Needs addr + token + transit_path (defaults to transit). The gateway calls transit/datakey/plaintext/{key} to generate per-object DEKs and transit/decrypt/{key} on GET. Per-object encryption context is canonicalized and base64-passed as Vault's context so decrypt fails on context mismatch (AEAD binding at the Vault layer). On external backends the /_admin/kms/keys endpoints return NotImplemented — manage keys directly in Vault. - disabled — SSE-KMS off; SSE-S3 still works if a service master key is set.

Runtime config API (all under /_admin/kms/*; gated by kms:Status/CreateKey/DeleteKey/KeyStatus): - GET /_admin/kms/config — current persisted backend (Vault token redacted; only token_set: true exposed). - PUT /_admin/kms/config — persist + hot-swap. Body is {backend, addr?, transit_path?, token?}. An empty token on update keeps the previously-stored one so admins can edit addr/path without re-entering secrets. - DELETE /_admin/kms/config — remove the persisted entry; next boot falls back to CLI/env. - POST /_admin/kms/test — run a throwaway generate_data_key + decrypt round-trip against the active backend. Returns {ok: bool, error: string|null} so the console can render a green/red indicator on the Save form.

Console: top-level Encryption page (admin-only) shows master-key status (read-only), backend selector (Disabled / Local / Vault), Vault addr + transit path + token-paste fields (token shown as •••••••• when already stored), Save & Apply button, and a Test-connection form.

Safety note: switching backends does not retroactively re-encrypt existing objects. Objects wrapped by the old backend stay readable only while that backend is still reachable; use CopyObject (phase 2f) to migrate them.

docs.title: CopyObject with encryption transitions
docs.text:
• Fast path (no data movement): when source and destination share the same SSE algorithm (and same KMS key id for SSE-KMS), CopyObject does a metadata-only copy — shards are shared between source and dest until either is deleted.
  • Slow path (decrypt → re-encrypt): when SSE settings differ (plaintext → SSE-S3, SSE-S3 → SSE-KMS, SSE-KMS → plaintext, SSE-KMS with different key, or explicit override via request headers), the gateway reads the source through its normal decrypt path, then re-PUTs through the normal encrypt path so the destination bucket's default — or the copy request's x-amz-server-side-encryption* headers — controls the new encryption.
  • SSE-C on copy: not yet supported; returns NotImplemented 501 when either side is SSE-C (needs the AWS-specific x-amz-copy-source-server-side-encryption-customer-* header set).

A re-encrypting CopyObject buffers the object in memory, as a single-part PUT does.

docs.title: Reed-Solomon (MDS)
docs.text:
• Standard Maximum Distance Separable codes
  • Configurable k (data) + m (parity) shards
  • Any k shards can reconstruct the data
  • Presets: 3+2, 4+2, 8+4

docs.title: LRC (Locally Repairable Codes)
docs.text:
• Local parity groups for faster single-shard recovery
  • Three parameters: k (data) + local parity + global parity
  • Presets: 6+2+1, 10+2+2

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
• Simple N-way replication (no erasure coding)
  • Configurable replica count (2-way, 3-way)

docs.title: Bucket replication
docs.text:
• Asynchronous replication of every new version to a bucket on another ObjectIO cluster, configured by the bucket's owner with S3's PutBucketReplication, naming a target (/_admin/replication/targets) of the bucket's own tenant, which that tenant's admin manages.
  • Replicas keep the source's version id and ETag; delete markers replicate if a rule asks; version deletes never do; replicas aren't replicated on.
  • Reliable by construction: the replication mark is written with the version, a scanner finds anything the immediate send missed, and the target stores a repeated send once.
  • Existing objects reach a target through a resync (/_admin/replication/resync, obioctl replication resync), which survives restarts and shows its progress.
  • A per-target bandwidth limit, the cluster's, shared by every gateway's sends.
  • x-amz-replication-status, backlog and lag metrics. Guide: operations-guide/administration/replication.md.

docs.title: Small-object packing
docs.text:
• Small objects (above the 4 KiB inline cut-off, up to 64 KiB) are moved into packs: one erasure-coded stripe of about 1 MiB holding many objects. An 8 KiB object then takes about 1.6× its size on disk instead of 3× at 4+2.
  • Off by default. --pack-interval-secs N turns the packer on (aio and gateway); --pack-min-age-secs (default 3600) leaves recently written objects alone. One gateway packs at a time (a lease in meta).
  • Nothing changes for clients: an object reads, ranges, copies, locks and deletes the same packed or not. A pack is freed when its last object goes.
  • Crash-safe: a pack is recorded before it's written and sealed before any object points at it, and each pass reconciles what a packer that died left half done. Repair and drain handle packs from their record.
  • Compaction: a pack less than half live (its objects mostly deleted or overwritten) has its survivors moved into a new pack, and its space comes back. Packs shared by a copy are left alone.
  • Metrics: objectio_packs_written_total, objectio_pack_objects_total, objectio_pack_bytes_saved_total, objectio_pack_reconciled_total{action}, objectio_pack_compactions_total, objectio_pack_compacted_objects_total.

docs.title: Storage Pools
docs.text:
• Independent erasure coding and placement per pool
  • Failure domain configuration: OSD, node, rack, datacenter
  • OSD tags for hardware-class targeting (e.g., nvme, ssd)
  • Per-pool storage quotas
  • Protection presets with automatic feasibility check (greyed out if insufficient nodes)
  • Console shows efficiency %, min nodes, fault tolerance for each configuration
  • Buckets in pools: a bucket is created in a pool (x-objectio-pool on S3 CreateBucket, pool on the admin API, or the tenant's default_pool); tenants are limited to their allowed_pools; a pool in use can't be deleted. Pools currently select erasure coding and placement groups, not specific disks (OSD tags are planned).

docs.title: 2a. Placement Engine (CRUSH + Placement Groups)
docs.text: Two-hop placement: object_id → pg_id → [osd_1..k+m]. Replaces per-object CRUSH with a fixed set of placement groups (PGs), each PG mapped to a specific (k+m)-tuple of OSDs. Modelled on Ceph's PG model + Cidon/Stutsman copyset diversity.

docs.title: Every pool has placement groups
docs.text: Every pool, the default one too, pre-allocates its PGs when it is made. Writes hash object key → PG via jump-consistent hash; PG → OSDs is an explicit Meta lookup, committed with an epoch before any write uses it.

docs.title: Object → PG routing
docs.text:
• Algorithm: Lamping & Veach jump consistent hash (Google 2014). O(log N) multiplications per call (~100 ns).
  • Minimal remap property: growing pg_count by one only moves old/new of keys, and every moving key lands on the new PG. Mostly academic today — resize isn't live — but the property is preserved for future PG-split support.
  • Key = xxh64(bucket/key).

docs.title: PG → OSD assignment (copyset allocator)
docs.text:
• Cidon/Stutsman copyset pattern: precompute a pool of valid (k+m)-tuples of OSDs that respect the pool's failure-domain level. PGs are sampled from this pool — dramatically reduces the number of distinct copysets and the correlated-data-loss probability when multiple OSDs fail simultaneously.
  • Failure-domain aware: every copyset spans distinct FD values (host, rack, datacenter, zone, region, etc. as configured on the pool).
  • Scatter width knob (balancer/scatter_width) — Cidon/Stutsman recommend ~10. Lower = fewer distinct copysets, lower loss probability, fewer choices for the balancer. Default 10.
  • Deterministic: seeded by topology version × pool hash so the copyset pool is reproducible across Meta replicas and restarts.

docs.title: Placement Groups (PlacementGroup proto)
docs.text:
• One Raft-replicated row per PG: (pool, pg_id, osd_ids, version, updated_at, migrating_to_osd_ids).
  • CAS-versioned — the balancer bumps version on every move.
  • Cached in-memory on every Meta replica via the apply-listener; hot reads don't hit redb.
  • Listed via GET /_admin/pools/{name}/placement-groups (paginated).

docs.title: Balancer (descheduler pattern)
docs.text:
Leader-only background task. Evaluates every PG on each tick and commits moves via MultiCas when a PG is overloaded or underloaded.

Hysteresis gates (prevents thrash):

  • Overload: trigger a move when any OSD in the PG holds ≥ overload_multiplier × target PGs. Default 1.20 (20% above fair share).
  • Underload (optional): also trigger when any OSD in the cluster holds ≤ underload_multiplier × target PGs. Default 0.70 (30% below fair share); set to 0 to disable.
  • Improvement factor: candidate copyset's total load must be ≤ improvement_factor × current. Default 0.90 (≥10% improvement required to commit).

Concurrency cap: max(3, osds/3) moves per pool per tick by default. Bounds background churn. Override via balancer/per_tick_cap.

Greenfield mode: ObjectIO today has no live data migration. Balancer commits osd_ids directly — orphan shards on OSDs that dropped out of a PG are collected by the terminal-loss GC in the drain observer. If production data lands, the migrating_to_osd_ids field on PlacementGroup becomes the migration signal and the migrator task (not yet implemented) consumes it before committing the transition.

docs.title: Hot-reloadable tuning (via /_admin/config/balancer/*)
docs.text:
Key Default Effect balancer/sweep_interval_seconds 60 Tick cadence (clamped 5–3600) balancer/overload_multiplier 1.20 Overload trigger threshold balancer/underload_multiplier 0.0 Underload trigger (0 = off) balancer/improvement_factor 0.90 Min improvement to commit balancer/scatter_width 10 Copyset-pool diversity balancer/per_tick_cap 0 (auto) Moves per pool per tick balancer/paused false Halt all commits

Each knob re-reads on every tick — no restart required. Ticks themselves are skipped when the sweep interval changes so the clock stays monotonic.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
A pool made without a pg_count (the default pool too) gets one sized from the OSDs in service when it is made:

pg_count = 100 × OSDs in service / copies per PG,
           rounded up to a power of 2, from 256 to 4096

The 100 is config pg/members_per_osd. The reason is rebuild speed: a lost drive's PGs are rebuilt onto as many drives as it held PG members, so with too few PGs a large cluster rebuilds barely faster than a small one.

Cluster shape pg_count made 9 OSDs, 2+1 EC 512 24 OSDs, 4+2 EC 512 100 OSDs, 4+2 EC 2048 1,000 OSDs, 8+4 EC 4096 (the ceiling; give 8192 explicitly)

A count given when the pool is made is kept. Cost: ~200 bytes per PG row; pg_count=4096 is ~1 MB of Meta state per pool, and each PG is peered, scrubbed and recovered on its own. Hard cap is 65,536 per pool.

docs.title: Scaling without PG split
docs.text:
pg_count is fixed at pool creation (v1 non-goal: growable pg_count). Three escape hatches cover the scale range without bolting on split:

  1. Size for target. Pick pg_count for the cluster you expect to reach, not the one you start at — cost is trivial.
  2. New pool per expansion (MinIO "server pool" pattern). When a pool's PG count becomes tight, create a new pool with more PGs and point new bucket creations at it. Existing buckets keep working on the old pool untouched. Zero-downtime because pool selection is per-bucket, recorded in BucketMeta at create time.
  3. Multiple pools per tier from day 1. nvme-1, nvme-2, … Buckets round-robin or least-full across siblings. Failure isolation + admin-op blast-radius containment come for free.

Iceberg workloads effectively never need PG split — the catalog indirection makes "move data to a new pool" a metadata-only flip rather than a full copy. Long-lived bucket-scoped workloads where the bucket name is the permanent client API are the only case where split is cheaper than migration; not a v1 concern.

docs.title: Console visualization
docs.text:
/cluster/pools/{name} drill-down shows: - Stat cards (pg_count, k+m, target PGs/OSD, active OSDs). - Per-OSD PG-membership bar chart — red/amber coloring for overloaded/underloaded OSDs, target marker line. - PG × OSD matrix — scrollable grid, blue cell = OSD is a member, amber = migrating-to. Click a column to filter to one OSD's PGs; click a row to pin a single PG.

All backed by GET /_admin/pools/{name}/placement-groups + GET /_admin/nodes — no new data plane, just a read view.

docs.title: Live status
docs.text:
GET /_admin/rebalance-status returns a unified view (legacy drift-rebalance fields + new PG counters): - pgs_moved_total — cumulative PG moves since process start - pg_candidates_last_tick — PGs flagged for a move in the last tick - pgs_scanned_last_tick — total PGs evaluated per tick - paused — merged signal of rebalance/paused OR balancer/paused

The console's Topology banner and the new Cluster → Balancing tab both consume this.

docs.title: 3. Data Lakehouse (Iceberg Tables + Delta Sharing)
docs.text:
Create analytics warehouses, manage Iceberg tables, query with Spark/Trino, and share data across organizations via the Delta Sharing protocol.

The Iceberg Tables and Table Sharing sections below describe the full data lakehouse capabilities.

docs.title: Tenant Management
docs.text:
• Create/List/Update/Delete tenants via /_admin/tenants API and console
  • Per-tenant configuration: Default pool, allowed pools, OIDC provider, admin users
  • Tenant quotas: Storage bytes, max buckets, max objects
  • Tenant labels: Arbitrary key-value metadata

docs.title: Tenant-Scoped Resources
docs.text:
• Users: Created with tenant field, ARN includes tenant (arn:objectio:iam::{tenant}:user/{name})
  • Access keys: Inherit tenant from user
  • Buckets: Created with tenant scope, ListBuckets filtered by tenant
  • Warehouses: Tenant-scoped Iceberg warehouses
  • Shares: Tenant-scoped table shares

docs.title: Tenant Isolation
docs.text:
• Auth middleware: AuthResult carries tenant from access key → user → tenant chain
  • Console session: Session token includes tenant, admin pages hidden for tenant users
  • API filtering: All list operations filter by authenticated user's tenant
  • System admin: Users with empty tenant see all resources across tenants

docs.title: Tenant Admin Role
docs.text:
• TenantConfig.admin_users: List of user IDs (or ARNs) who can admin the tenant without being system admins
  • POST /_admin/tenants/{name}/admins — grant tenant-admin
  • DELETE /_admin/tenants/{name}/admins/{user} — revoke
  • Three-tier access model: System admin (tenant=""), tenant admin (in admin_users for their tenant), regular user
  • Scope: tenant admins can create/delete users + access keys + buckets + warehouses + shares within their own tenant; they cannot touch pools, tenants, nodes, system config, KMS backend, or other tenants
  • Console: dedicated "Manage admins" panel on each tenant row; picker lists that tenant's users + free-form user-id/ARN input
  • CLI: obioctl tenant admin add|remove|list <tenant> <user> — see CLI

docs.title: 5. IAM (Identity & Access Management)
docs.text: Full reference: Identity and Access and Public Access.

docs.title: Users & Access Keys
docs.text:
• Create/List/Get/Update/Delete users with display name, email, tenant
  • Suspend a user (PUT /_admin/users/{id} {"status": "suspended"}) or deactivate a key (PUT /_admin/access-keys/{id} {"status": "inactive"}) — refused within 15 s on every gateway, nothing deleted
  • Scoped keys: confined to s3://bucket/prefix/, read-only or read-write; refused on the admin API
  • Key format: AKIA* (permanent) or ASIA* (temporary)
  • Admin user: Auto-created on first meta service startup with credentials logged

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• AWS SigV4 for requests and presigned URLs. SigV2 is refused with 400 InvalidRequest, as S3 refuses it on buckets created since June 2020; with boto3 use botocore.config.Config(signature_version="s3v4").
  • Anonymous requests: served only what a bucket policy grants to everyone, with public access blocked by default
  • OIDC: the operator's provider and each tenant's own (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, Google, any compliant issuer); groups from any claim, dotted paths included
  • STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity: an OIDC token for a role's temporary keys, AWS-wire-compatible; a tenant's roles trust only that tenant's provider, system roles only the operator's
  • Vended credentials for Iceberg / Unity clients, confined to a table's location
  • Console session cookies with 24-hour TTL
  • Sessions, temporary credentials and listing tokens are signed with keys derived from a cluster secret held in meta's Raft log

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
• Tenant boundary: checked before any policy; no policy can grant across it
  • Bucket policies (PUT /{bucket}?policy) and IAM policies attached to users, groups and roles — per tenant, with a shared system catalogue (readonly, readwrite, writeonly)
  • Groups with members; roles with trust policies
  • Evaluation: explicit Deny wins; then any Allow; then the bucket's owner; else deny. No policy means owner-only.
  • Conditions: every IAM operator with IfExists, ForAnyValue:/ForAllValues: and Null; unknown operators refused at save. Keys include aws:SourceIp, aws:SourceVpce (named gateway endpoint), aws:SecureTransport, aws:username, s3:prefix, s3:ExistingObjectTag/*, the SSE request headers, obio:CredentialType
  • AWS policies work as written: arn:aws: ARNs and {"AWS": …} principals; NotPrincipal on Deny
  • Block Public Access at bucket, tenant and cluster level; new buckets start blocked
  • ACLs: bucket owner enforced — they grant nothing
  • Action namespaces: s3:*, iceberg:*, kms:*, sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
  • Admin access: the built-in admin user bypasses policy evaluation; console sessions are treated as admin for admin endpoints.

docs.title: Management SDKs
docs.text: • Go (github.com/object-io/objectio-go-sdk) and Python (objectio-sdk) clients for the whole admin API, standard library only — see SDKs

docs.title: Warehouse Management
docs.text:
• POST/GET/DELETE /_admin/warehouses — Create, list, delete warehouses
  • Backing bucket: Each warehouse automatically creates an S3 bucket (iceberg-{name})
  • Tenant-scoped: Warehouses isolated per tenant
  • Warehouse-scoped namespaces: Each warehouse has its own namespace/table hierarchy

docs.title: Iceberg REST Catalog API
docs.text:
• GET /iceberg/v1/config — Catalog configuration (warehouse location)
  • Namespace CRUD: Create, load, drop, list, update properties, check existence
  • Table CRUD: Create, load, commit (CAS), drop, list, rename, check existence
  • Multi-level namespaces: Dot-separated hierarchy (e.g., db.schema)
  • Namespace policies: IAM-style access control per namespace
  • Table policies: Per-table access control
  • Data filters: Column/row-level security per principal

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• SigV4: Same access key / secret key as S3 (industry standard)
  • OIDC/OAuth2: Bearer token authentication via external provider
  • Console session cookie: For web console access
  • Unified auth middleware: Tries SigV4 → OIDC → session cookie → unauthenticated

docs.title: Vended Credentials (STS)
docs.text:
• LoadTable response: Includes temporary S3 credentials in config field
  • Credential format: ASIA* access key + secret + HMAC-signed session token
  • 1-hour TTL: Fresh credentials generated per LoadTable call
  • Path-style access: s3.path-style-access=true for ObjectIO compatibility
  • External endpoint: Configured via --external-endpoint for public access

docs.title: Client Compatibility
docs.text:
• Catalog URI http://<gateway>/iceberg (clients add /v1), warehouse = a warehouse's name
  • PyIceberg: SigV4 signing (rest.sigv4-enabled=true); the code repo's examples/pyiceberg runs against objectio-aio
  • Spark, Trino: the REST catalog clients, with SigV4 or OAuth2
  • No query engine is tested against the catalog in CI yet (objectio#8)

docs.title: 3b. Unity Catalog (REST API)
docs.text: Databricks-shape governance plane for catalogs / schemas / tables / functions / volumes / models / model-versions, mounted at /api/2.1/unity-catalog/*. Coexists with the Iceberg REST Catalog — they share the same auth bridge, the same BucketPolicy/PolicyEvaluator backbone, and the same admin gate.

docs.title: Three-level entity model
docs.text:
• Catalog — top of the namespace; auto-provisions an unity-{name} backing bucket
  • Schema — addressed as {catalog}.{schema}
  • Table / Function / Volume / Model — addressed as {catalog}.{schema}.{name}
  • Model version — addressed as {catalog}.{schema}.{model}/versions/{n}

docs.title: Policy model
docs.text:
• IAM-style JSON — same BucketPolicy shape as S3 / Iceberg; unity: action prefix and arn:obio:unity:::{catalog}[/{schema}[/{table}]] resource ARNs
  • Three-level walk — catalog → schema → table; deny at any level wins
  • Grantable actions — unity:Get*, unity:Create*, unity:Delete* for every entity, plus unity:SetTableSecurity for row-filter / column-mask binding (grantable to non-admin via Unity policy — does not require admin)
  • Per-entity policy editor — PUT /api/2.1/unity-catalog/{catalogs|schemas|tables}/{name}/policy, GET to read, empty body clears

docs.title: Row filters & column masks
docs.text:
• PUT /api/2.1/unity-catalog/tables/{full_name}/security — binds a SQL UDF as a row filter and/or per-column masks
  • Validation — row-filter UDF must return BOOLEAN; mask functions must exist in the same catalog.schema; rejects unknown function references at config time
  • Engine-side enforcement — engines (Spark/Trino) read the binding from GET /tables/{full_name} and inject WHERE function(input_cols) / mask_function(col, …) at query compile time. Unity itself does not execute UDFs

docs.title: UDF context built-ins
docs.text:
• GET /api/2.1/unity-catalog/me returns {user_name, user_id, user_arn, groups, group_arns, tenant, is_admin} — the canonical principal context engines use to populate the SQL built-ins that row-filter and column-mask UDFs reference:
Built-in Source field current_user() user_name is_member(g) groups contains g is_account_group_member(g) groups contains g

docs.title: Default deny direct-S3 on backing buckets
docs.text:
• Auto-attached at catalog create — bucket policy on unity-{catalog} denies any access where obio:CredentialType != STS
  • Forces vended-credential flow — permanent IAM keys can't bypass row filters / column masks by going around Unity to the backing bucket
  • obio:CredentialType policy variable — surfaced from AuthMode (set to STS in the STS auth path, Permanent in SigV4/OIDC, Anonymous in --no-auth); usable in any bucket policy via StringNotEquals / StringEquals conditions

docs.title: Vended credentials (STS)
docs.text:
• POST /…/temporary-table-credentials — mint scoped 1-hour STS session for table data access
  • POST /…/temporary-volume-credentials — same for governed volumes
  • Admin-gated — recipients of the vended creds appear to the gateway as obio:CredentialType: STS and pass the default-deny policy

docs.title: OIDC group bridging
docs.text:
• Name-based mapping — Keycloak / OIDC group claim "data-team" maps to local IAM group "data-team" by exact name match
  • Dual stitching — every authenticated request gets BOTH the IAM group ARN (for policies that name the IAM ARN directly) AND the IAM group_id (so list_attached_policies(group_id=…) returns the right set), so a single IAM policy attached to the IAM group governs SigV4 and OIDC users uniformly

docs.title: Console UI
docs.text:
• Unity Catalog page — three-pane catalog → schema → entity navigation; Tables / Functions / Volumes / Models tabs per schema; full CRUD modals
  • Shield button — opens the PolicyEditor modal scoped to the entity
  • Filter button — opens the TableSecurityEditor modal (function dropdown filtered to same-schema UDFs, multi-mask rows); the icon turns green when a row filter or column mask is active on the row
  • Policy templates — Policies page generator now ships Unity-shape templates (unity-readonly, unity-data-engineer, unity-ml-engineer, unity-security-officer, unity-deny-delete) and an S3-shape s3-deny-non-sts template that mirrors the Unity backing-bucket default

docs.title: Client compatibility
docs.text:
• Databricks SDK — Unity REST API is wire-compatible with Databricks Unity Catalog (/api/2.1/unity-catalog/* paths, snake_case JSON)
  • PySpark with Unity connector — bind warehouse via standard config; SigV4 or OIDC for auth
  • Trino Unity connector — same

docs.title: Share Management
docs.text:
• Create/List/Delete shares via admin API and console
  • Tenant-scoped shares: Filtered by authenticated user's tenant

docs.title: Table Types
docs.text:
• Delta Lake: Share Delta tables by S3 bucket + path (table_type: "delta")
  • Iceberg UniForm: Share Iceberg tables via Delta Sharing protocol (table_type: "uniform")
  • Mixed sharing: Both Delta and Iceberg tables in the same share

docs.title: Recipient & Token Management
docs.text:
• Create recipients: Name + list of accessible shares
  • Bearer tokens: One-time display, SHA-256 hashed for storage
  • profile.share: Standard Delta Sharing credential file format
  • Token authentication: Recipients authenticate via Authorization: Bearer <token>

docs.title: Protocol Endpoints
docs.text:
• GET /delta-sharing/v1/shares — List accessible shares
  • GET /delta-sharing/v1/shares/{share}/schemas — List schemas in share
  • GET /delta-sharing/v1/shares/{share}/schemas/{schema}/tables — List tables
  • GET .../tables/{table}/version — Current table version (snapshot ID)
  • GET .../tables/{table}/metadata — Table metadata (NDJSON format)
  • POST .../tables/{table}/query — Query table data (returns presigned S3 URLs)

docs.title: Data Access
docs.text:
• Presigned URLs: Server generates SigV4 presigned URLs for Parquet data files
  • 1-hour expiry: Presigned URLs valid for 1 hour
  • No S3 credentials needed: Recipients access data via presigned URLs only

docs.title: 6. File Storage (NFS / POSIX)
docs.text: File protocols (NFS, SMB) are not built yet; they are roadmap track E. What exists today is file-like access through S3:

docs.title: Current File-Like Access (via S3)
docs.text:
• Object Browser (Console): Navigate bucket → folder → file hierarchy
  • Presigned URLs: Time-limited download/upload URLs for direct file access
  • Folder semantics: Delimiter-based folder listing (?delimiter=/)
  • Range reads: HTTP Range header for partial file reads
  • Multipart upload: Large file upload in parts (up to 10,000 parts)

docs.title: gRPC Block Service
docs.text:
• Thin provisioning: Storage allocated only on write
  • 4 MB chunks: Logical block addresses mapped to erasure-coded chunks on OSDs
  • 512-byte LBA: Standard sector size
  • Snapshots: Copy-on-write snapshots and writable clones
  • Write journal: Crash-consistent writes via write-ahead journal
  • Write cache: Coalesces small writes before flushing to chunks

docs.title: QoS (Quality of Service)
docs.text: • A volume carries QoS settings (IOPS and bandwidth limits, priority), and the objectio-block crate has a token-bucket limiter, but the block gateway does not enforce them yet.

docs.title: Protocol Support
docs.text:
• gRPC BlockService: Native block I/O over gRPC (port 9300)
  • NBD (Network Block Device): Linux kernel NBD attachment (port 10809)

docs.title: Block Gateway
docs.text:
• Stateless, horizontally scalable
  • Accepts block I/O, buffers in write cache, erasure-encodes 4 MB chunks, flushes to OSDs
  • Bridges block storage volumes to the erasure-coded object layer

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• Login page: Access key + secret key authentication
  • Session management: HMAC-signed HttpOnly cookies, 24-hour TTL
  • Tenant-aware: Sidebar adapts based on user's tenant (admin pages hidden for tenant users)
  • Logout: Clears session cookie

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page Description Dashboard Cluster health, stats (buckets, users, namespaces, S3 requests), services status Buckets Create/delete buckets, versioning/lock/lifecycle badges, tenant column Bucket Detail Tabs: Versioning toggle, Object Lock config, Lifecycle rule editor Object Browser Navigate buckets → folders → files, breadcrumb path, folder/file counts Cluster Unified view of cluster infrastructure via four tabs (all admin-only). Legacy /topology, /drives, /pools URLs redirect here.   → Topology Interactive, collapsible diagram of region → zone → datacenter → rack → host → OSDs with color-coded level pills. Per-pool placement satisfiability strip. Rebalance banner merges legacy drift + PG-balancer counters.   → Nodes & Drives K8s node grouping → OSD pods → disks, CPU/RAM/OS info, usage bars, Add Host via host-provider.   → Storage Pools Protection presets, EC config (RS/LRC/Replication), failure domain, PG count selector on create, PGs column on list. Click PG count → placement drill-down.   → Balancing Live balancer status card (Pause/Resume), 7 hot-reloadable tuning knobs (overload/underload/improvement thresholds, scatter width, per-tick cap, sweep interval, pause). Pool Placement (/cluster/pools/:name) Per-pool PG visualization: stat cards, per-OSD PG-membership bars with overload/underload coloring and target line, PG × OSD matrix grid with click-to-filter. Tenants Tenant CRUD, quotas, OIDC provider, pool assignment Users & Keys Create users with tenant selector, auto-create access keys, credential display Identity OIDC provider configuration (Azure, Keycloak, Okta, Google, generic) Tables Warehouse → Namespace → Table hierarchy, table metadata viewer Table Sharing Share/table/recipient CRUD, UniForm type support, token + profile.share generation Monitoring Live Prometheus metrics, charts (line, area, bar), 5s polling Encryption SSE master-key status, KMS backend selector (Disabled / Local / Vault), hot-swap + Test button

docs.title: UI Design
docs.text:
• Compact 13px base font (Inter)
  • Tailwind CSS styling
  • Loading bar animations
  • Hover-reveal actions (delete buttons)
  • Sticky table headers
  • Status badges with colored dots

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Gateway (stateless, horizontally scalable): S3 API, Iceberg REST Catalog, Delta Sharing, Admin API, Console
  • Meta (openraft 0.9 cluster): Bucket/object metadata, placement (CRUSH 2.0), IAM, tenant config. One code path; deployment picks single-voter (replicas=1) or HA quorum (replicas=3+).
  • OSD (one per disk): Erasure-coded shard storage with Direct I/O, WAL
  • Block Gateway (optional): Block storage over gRPC + NBD

docs.title: Meta HA (openraft 0.9)
docs.text:
• Real consensus, not a placeholder: RaftStorage implemented over redb (log + vote + state in raft_logs, raft_vote, raft_state tables); RaftNetwork over tonic gRPC on the existing meta port, JSON-encoded envelopes
  • Cluster size is a deployment choice: meta.replicas=1 boots a single-voter cluster (no election drama, same operational behavior as pre-Raft meta); meta.replicas=3+ gets true quorum, leader election, log replication. Same binary, same code path
  • Bootstrap automated via helm: a Job created with each install and upgrade calls /init on meta-0 unless the cluster exists, adds the pods that aren't voters as learners through the leader, and promotes the voter set; with every pod a voter it changes nothing
  • Admin API at :9102 per meta pod:
  • POST /init — bootstrap a single-voter cluster (idempotent)
  • POST /add-learner {node_id, addr} — onboard a peer non-voting
  • POST /change-membership {voters} — promote the voter set
  • GET /status — leader id, term, voters, learners, last_log_index, last_applied
  • GET /health — 200 while this node's Raft runs, 503 once it has stopped (the chart's liveness probe)
  • GET /ready — 200 while this node is a member with a leader known, 503 with the reason otherwise (the chart's readiness probe)
  • Every meta write goes through Raft: config, buckets, IAM, tenants, OSD registrations, KMS keys, multipart uploads; replicas apply them in order
  • Any meta node serves any client: a follower forwards each gRPC call to the leader (x-objectio-forwarded); clients take a comma-separated --meta-endpoint list, balanced over health-probed nodes, with a 5 s call timeout, so a dead or frozen meta is routed around
  • Snapshots: the whole state machine, built from the tables on demand and installed in full on a lagging or new node
  • Tested: multi-process e2e (tests/e2e/tests/meta_ha.rs) kills, freezes and replaces metas under S3 traffic

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• Kubernetes (Helm): Production-grade Helm chart with StatefulSets, PVCs, Ingress
  • Docker Compose: Local development cluster (3 meta + 6 OSD + 1 gateway)
  • Single binary: All-in-one Docker image with per-service entrypoints

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Prometheus metrics: Exported at /metrics on each service
  • Per-operation counters: objectio_s3_requests_total, objectio_iceberg_requests_total
  • Per-operation latency: Duration histograms
  • OSD status: Disk capacity, shard counts, SMART health
  • Node info: K8s node name (downward API), OS version, CPU, RAM, ObjectIO version

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: Service API Port Metrics Port Gateway 9000 9000 /metrics Meta 9100 9101 OSD 9200 9201 Block Gateway 9300 (gRPC) / 10809 (NBD) —

docs.title: Storage Engine
docs.text:
• 4 MiB chunk/stripe size: Fundamental EC unit
  • 4 KiB block size: Internal allocation unit; a shard takes a run of whole blocks, with a header and footer carrying its checksum
  • O_DIRECT / F_NOCACHE: Bypass OS page cache; io_uring on Linux release builds
  • Flush before acknowledge: a shard is fsynced, then its location, before the write returns
  • Metadata store: a write-ahead log in front of an on-disk index with a bounded cache (--meta-cache-mib), so an OSD's memory doesn't grow with its object count
  • Shard checksums: each shard's CRC32C is recorded with the object and checked on every read and repair; a background scrub reads every shard at a set rate
  • CRUSH 2.0 placement: Consistent hashing with failure domain awareness

docs.title: Cluster Topology & Locality
docs.text:
• 5-level failure domain model on OsdNode and FailureDomainInfo: region → zone → datacenter → rack → host. Additive proto change, back-compat with 3-level deployments (empty zone/host = "inherit from enclosing")
  • TopologyDistance metric (objectio-placement::distance): ranks two peers as SameHost < SameRack < SameDatacenter < SameZone < SameRegion < Remote < Unknown. Total order — safe to use as a sort key. Empty-on-both-sides at a level counts as matching so deployments that only use some levels aren't penalized
  • Placement feasibility validation: Crush2::validate_placement_feasibility(level, required_count) returns InsufficientDomainSpread { required_level, required_count, available_count } when a pool cannot spread across the configured level. Surfaced via GET /_admin/placement/validate?pool=NAME
  • Gateway self-positioning: --topology-region/zone/datacenter/rack/host CLI flags (or OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_* env vars). Stored on AppState.self_topology; visible via GET /_admin/cluster-info
  • Locality-aware EC reads: get_object ranks all candidate shard positions by distance(gateway, shard_host), fetches the k closest first. Parity reconstruction only triggers when nearer shards are unhealthy. No protocol change — same ReadShard RPCs, different ordering
  • GET /_admin/topology — aggregated region→zone→datacenter→rack→host→OSDs tree + per-level distinct counts
  • GET /_admin/cluster-info — gateway's self-position + every OSD's computed distance + is_local flag
  • Prometheus metric: objectio_read_locality_bytes_total{locality="same-rack"|"same-zone"|"same-datacenter"|"same-region"|"remote"|"unknown"} — bytes fetched from OSDs partitioned by topology distance. Multi-DC deployments use this to prove cross-DC bandwidth is being collapsed
  • CLI: obioctl cluster topology (full tree) and cluster validate-placement <pool> (exits non-zero when a pool is unsatisfiable)

docs.title: Stable OSD identity
docs.text:
• OSD registration retry: register_with_meta backs off exponentially (2s → 30s cap) until it succeeds. Stops OSDs from silently staying out of the cluster after a meta-first rolling restart
  • Address-based dedupe: re-registration at an existing address with a different node_id evicts the stale entry from both osd_nodes and the CRUSH topology. One-shot dedupe on meta startup also cleans ghosts left by older binaries

docs.title: Management SDKs
docs.text:
Go and Python clients for ObjectIO's management API: everything under /_admin/*, plus STS.

install source Go go get github.com/object-io/objectio-go-sdk objectio-go-sdk Python pip install objectio-sdk (import objectio) objectio-python-sdk

Both are developed in the main repository under sdk/ and mirrored to their own repos on every merge. Both are standard library only: no dependencies to vendor into an operator or a CSI driver. Method names match: Go CreatePolicy is Python create_policy.

They don't do S3 data operations. Use the S3 SDK you already have (boto3, aws-sdk-go-v2, rclone, mountpoint-s3), pointed at the same endpoint with a credential these mint or obtain.

docs.title: What they cover
docs.text:
• Tenants and tenant admins.
  • Users and access keys, including suspend and reactivate, and keys confined to a bucket or prefix.
  • IAM policies, groups and roles, attached to users, groups or roles.
  • Identity providers: the operator's and each tenant's own OIDC provider.
  • STS: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from a client that needs no keys.
  • Block Public Access at bucket, tenant and cluster level, and a bucket's policy status.
  • Buckets, bucket policies and dedup.
  • One-call provisioning: a bucket plus a key confined to it, with rotation and teardown.
  • Cluster operations: pools, nodes, OSD state, rebalance, usage, metrics.
  • KMS keys, Iceberg warehouses, and cluster config.

The concepts are explained in Identity and Access and Public Access.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
from objectio import Client
admin = Client.from_env()          # OBJECTIO_ENDPOINT, OBJECTIO_ACCESS_KEY(_FILE), OBJECTIO_SECRET_KEY(_FILE)

admin, err := objectio.NewFromEnv()

The AWS variable names (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, …) work as fallbacks. In Kubernetes, prefer the _FILE forms with a mounted Secret. The credential must be unscoped: a key confined to a bucket is refused on the management API.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
A tenant with its own identity provider, and a role its CI assumes with no stored credential:

from objectio import Client, tenant_oidc_provider_name

acme = Client.from_env()           # acme's tenant admin
acme.put_oidc_provider(tenant_oidc_provider_name("acme"), {
    "issuer_url": "https://keycloak.acme.example/realms/acme",
    "client_id": "objectio", "claim_name": "groups"})
acme.create_policy("data-rw", {"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:*",
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-data", "arn:aws:s3:::acme-data/*"]}]})
role = acme.create_role("ci", trust_policy)          # see Identity and Access
acme.attach_policy("data-rw", role_name="ci")

# In CI
creds = Client(endpoint=E).assume_role_with_web_identity(role.arn, token, "build-42")
s3 = boto3.client("s3", **creds.boto3_kwargs(E))

Suspend someone now, decide later:

_, err := admin.SuspendUser(ctx, userID)      // every key refused; nothing deleted
_, err = admin.ActivateUser(ctx, userID)

A bucket and a key confined to it, for an app:

ba = admin.provision_bucket("app-1", provisioner_user_id=prov_id)
s3 = boto3.client("s3", **ba.boto3_kwargs(E))

Block public access for a whole tenant:

_, err := acme.PutPublicAccessBlock(ctx, "", objectio.BlockAll, nil)

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Both surface the HTTP status and, for S3 and STS errors, the error code (AccessDenied, NoSuchBucket, InvalidIdentityToken, …). Use them to make calls idempotent:

try:
    admin.create_bucket("app-1")
except APIError as e:
    if not e.already_exists:
        raise

if err := admin.CreateBucket(ctx, "app-1", ""); err != nil && !objectio.IsAlreadyExists(err) {
    return err
}

The full reference, with every method, is in each SDK's README.

docs.title: Chaos: faults on a multi-host cluster
docs.text:
ObjectIO is tested under faults on a small cluster of separate machines (deploy/chaos/ in the code repo): six VMs on one lab host. Three run meta, all six run an OSD on its own block device, and two run a gateway. Six writers keep PUTting through both gateways throughout. Each fault is followed by a check:

  • every write that was acknowledged reads back intact: the new ones plus a sample of 2,000 after each fault, and all of them at the end;
  • writes resume, and fail only with 503 (retry) or a client timeout, never another error;
  • at the end, repair restores full redundancy: once it is quiet, any of the listed pairs of OSDs can be stopped and every object still reads.

docs.title: Latest: 2026-10-18: passes
docs.text:
The code of the 0.1.0 release candidate; 4+2 erasure coding; the VMs run release builds. A fault that destroys a drive waits first for every placement group to be Clean.

Fault What Longest pause in acknowledged writes Meta leader killed SIGKILL of the meta leader 2.2 s OSD host powered off one VM off for 60 s 5.0 s Meta leader's host powered off a meta VM off for 60 s 4.9 s Partition the meta leader's VM off the network for 60 s 13.2 s Disk pull an OSD's disk removed for 60 s, then replaced as documented 1.4 s Drive lost an OSD's drive and its metadata gone, the OSD back new on a blank drive, the old one evacuated 1.0 s
  • Acknowledged objects: 81,436. All read back after every fault and at the end.
  • Failed writes: 503s and client timeouts only.
  • Repair: every placement group was Clean 151 s after the partition healed (before the disk pull) and 482 s after the new disk was set in (before the drive loss). The lost drive's OSD was evacuated in 1,129 s, 72,738 shards onto the new one.
  • Redundancy: repair was quiet a minute after the last fault. Then any two OSDs (chaos-1+2, 3+4, 5+6) could be stopped with every sampled object readable.

The partition's pause is longer than on 2026-10-04 (5.4 s), within the 60 s the suite allows, and the same in both runs on this build. Its failed writes were client timeouts and 503s saying an election was under way; where the rest of the time goes isn't measured yet.

The run before it, on the same build, lost 247 objects. The faults then followed each other once every service was up, not once repair was done, and the drive loss (added to the suite with the soak) came 44 s after the disk pull. Repair was still rebuilding what chaos-3's OSD had missed while it was off (with six OSDs and 4+2, every placement group has a shard on every OSD), and every object lost had its shards on chaos-3, chaos-5 and chaos-4 gone: three of a 4+2 stripe, beyond what the code survives. The suite now makes disk-pull and drive-lost wait for every placement group to be Clean first.

docs.title: 2026-10-04: passes
docs.text: A development build (with backfill and the last two fixes in the table below), the first five faults: the longest pauses 2.2 s (meta leader killed), 5.2 s (OSD host off), 5.3 s (meta leader's host off), 5.4 s (partition), 0.3 s (disk pull); 16,597 acknowledged objects, all read back; repair quiet 16 minutes after the last fault.

docs.title: What the runs found
docs.text:
It took 15 runs to get here. Each run stops at the first broken invariant, so every fix uncovered the next problem. These are the problems the runs found and the fixes for them:

Found Fix A follower meta never learned an OSD's admin state, so after a leader change an OSD set back in reverted to out The admin state reaches every meta node A gateway kept using connections to a host that had vanished: writes stalled for up to 48 s Fail-fast per OSD address, HTTP/2 keepalive, stale channels redialled Acknowledged writes lost to an OSD power cut Compacting the OSD's metadata log no longer drops records, and syncs reach the live file An OSD on a replacement disk took 5 minutes to start The old disk's shard records are dropped in batches Objects written while an OSD was down kept two shards on one OSD A down OSD keeps its positions An update (tagging, a pack switch) racing a PUT could outrank it, so the acknowledged PUT was lost An update is ordered after its object, never above a newer one A connection cut mid-answer became a 500 It is a 503 Objects written while an OSD was out kept two shards on one OSD Backfill A gateway failed fast OSDs it had just seen restart It probes them until they answer The redundancy check stopped OSDs while repair was still working It waits for repair to be quiet A request dropped by its client hid a dead connection, so a partition held one gateway's writes for 60 s A slow call checks its OSD, and a dead OSD stays failed fast while it is gone A healed partition deposed the leader: the cut-off meta had raised its term A meta node campaigns only while it can reach a majority

docs.title: The soak
docs.text:
