docs.title: Bucket Logging
docs.text: S3 server access logging: every request on a bucket, as a line of AWS's access-log format, delivered as objects into a target bucket. Use it where a tool expects S3 access logs (Athena, log shippers). For a complete, real-time record of every request in the cluster, use the audit stream: bucket logging is per bucket, batched, and only for its owner's eyes.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
1. Create the target bucket in the source bucket's tenant (or, for the operator, a bucket in the system tenant).
  2. Let the logging service write there, with a bucket policy on the target:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "S3ServerAccessLogsPolicy",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "logging.s3.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "s3:PutObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::access-logs/web/*",
    "Condition": {
      "ArnLike": {"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:s3:::web-assets"},
      "StringEquals": {"aws:SourceAccount": "<owner user id of web-assets>"}
    }
  }]
}

aws:SourceAccount is the source bucket's owner, its user id (what GET ?acl shows as the owner's ID). Wildcards work as in S3 (arn:aws:s3:::*, "*"). A grant to everyone ("Principal": "*") is not consent: the service must be named. 3. As the source bucket's owner:

aws s3api put-bucket-logging --bucket web-assets --bucket-logging-status '{
  "LoggingEnabled": {"TargetBucket": "access-logs", "TargetPrefix": "web/"}}'
aws s3api get-bucket-logging --bucket web-assets

For date-partitioned keys add "TargetObjectKeyFormat": {"PartitionedPrefix": {"PartitionDateSource": "EventTime"}} (or DeliveryTime).

Turn it off with an empty status: aws s3api put-bucket-logging --bucket web-assets --bucket-logging-status '{}'.

Refusal Why 403 AccessDenied (only the bucket owner…) Only the bucket's owner (or the system admin) configures logging, whatever policies grant 403 AccessDenied (Logging bucket … policy …) The target's policy doesn't let the logging service put objects under the prefix for this bucket and owner 400 InvalidTargetBucketForLogging The target doesn't exist, or is in another tenant 400 InvalidArgument The target is the source, logs itself, or the prefix is over 512 bytes 400 MalformedXML No TargetBucket, or a PartitionDateSource other than EventTime/DeliveryTime 400 InvalidRequest (no spool) This gateway runs without a spool (below)

docs.title: What arrives
docs.text:
One object per batch, named in UTC:

  • web/2026-10-05-07-08-09-3F2A9C1B7D4E6F80 (simple prefix), or
  • web/<owner>/<region>/web-assets/2026/10/05/2026-10-05-07-08-09-3F2A9C1B7D4E6F80 (partitioned).

Each line is AWS's format (LogFormat):

<owner> web-assets [05/Oct/2026:07:08:01 +0000] 10.0.0.7 arn:objectio:iam::acme:user/etl 6F1C0D3A9B2E4F7C8D1A2B3C4D5E6F70 REST.GET.OBJECT img/logo.png "GET /web-assets/img/logo.png HTTP/1.1" 200 - 5120 5120 12 9 "-" "aws-cli/2.17" - - SigV4 - AuthHeader s3.example.com - - -

The request ID is the x-amz-request-id the client got, and the id of the same request in the audit stream. Operations are named as S3 names them: REST.PUT.OBJECT, REST.GET.BUCKET, REST.COPY.OBJECT (and REST.COPY.OBJECT_GET in the source bucket's log), REST.POST.UPLOADS, REST.PUT.PART, REST.POST.UPLOAD, REST.POST.MULTI_OBJECT_DELETE plus a BATCH.DELETE.OBJECT line per key deleted. Refused requests are logged too, with their status and error code. Host id, cipher suite, TLS version, access point and "ACL required" are -.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Records are kept on the gateway's disk before delivery, so a gateway that is killed or restarted loses none, and a request never waits for its log. A log object is written once its first record is --bucket-log-roll-secs old (default 300 s), or it holds --bucket-log-max-records (50 000) records or 16 MiB, and on shutdown. Delivery is at least once: after a crash a batch may be written twice (under two names); dedupe on the request id.

Before each object is written the target's consent is checked again: if the target is gone, in another tenant, or its policy no longer allows the logging service, those records are dropped (and counted). A target that fails otherwise (a full cluster, meta unavailable) is retried with backoff; records wait in the spool meanwhile.

A configuration change reaches other gateways within 10 seconds.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Gateway flag (env) Default --bucket-log-spool (OBJECTIO_BUCKET_LOG_SPOOL) <--audit-spool>/bucket-logging Where records wait. A local directory that survives restarts. aio: <data>/bucket-log-spool --bucket-log-spool-max-bytes (OBJECTIO_BUCKET_LOG_SPOOL_MAX_BYTES) 1 GiB (Helm: 512 MiB, gateway.audit.spool.bucketLogMaxBytes) Past it, new records are dropped and counted --bucket-log-roll-secs (OBJECTIO_BUCKET_LOG_ROLL_SECS) 300 How long a log object collects records --bucket-log-max-records (OBJECTIO_BUCKET_LOG_MAX_RECORDS) 50 000 A log object is written once it holds this many

With Helm the spool is in the audit spool's volume (gateway.audit.spool.enabled, on by default). A gateway with neither --bucket-log-spool nor --audit-spool refuses PutBucketLogging and drops the records of buckets logged through other gateways.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Metric objectio_bucket_logging_records_total Records delivered objectio_bucket_logging_dropped_total{reason} Not delivered: refused (the target no longer consents), target-refused (a 4xx writing it), spool-full, no-spool, lookup-failed (a bucket's configuration couldn't be read), unreadable objectio_bucket_logging_delivery_failures_total Writes retried

Alert on dropped_total{reason=~"spool-full|no-spool|lookup-failed"} rising: those are records lost to the cluster, not refused by a target.

docs.title: Differences from S3 and RGW
docs.text:
• A target must be in the source's tenant (or the system's): no cross-tenant (cross-account) logging.
  • RGW's extensions are not supported: LoggingType (Journal), ObjectRollTime, RecordsBatchSize, POST ?logging, key filters, tenant:bucket targets.
  • What the gateway does on its own (lifecycle expiry, replication) is not logged.
  • The region in partitioned keys is the gateway's --region.

docs.title: CLI (obioctl)
docs.text:
obioctl manages a cluster through the gateway's admin API, signed with SigV4 like the SDKs. Every command goes through the same authentication, tenant scoping, validation, Block Public Access and audit as any other caller. It never talks to meta directly, so meta's ports can stay closed to everything but the cluster.

Bucket lifecycle, CORS and bucket-level public access block are S3 calls, signed the same way. sts assume-role-with-web-identity needs no key. volume and snapshot talk to the block gateway (--block-endpoint, default http://localhost:9300).

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
obioctl configure                 # prompts for endpoint, key and secret
obioctl --profile acme configure --endpoint https://s3.example.com \
  --access-key AKIA… --secret-key … --non-interactive
obioctl configure --list          # secrets masked

Profiles live in ~/.objectio/config (mode 0600). Settings are resolved in this order: 1. flags (--endpoint, --access-key/--secret-key, --region); 2. --profile; 3. the environment, as the SDKs read it: OBJECTIO_ENDPOINT, OBJECTIO_ACCESS_KEY(_FILE), OBJECTIO_SECRET_KEY(_FILE), with the AWS_* names as fallbacks; 4. the OBJECTIO_PROFILE or default profile.

The key must be unscoped: a key confined to a bucket is refused on the admin API. The system admin and tenant admins use the same CLI; without --tenant, a command acts in the caller's own tenant.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Tables by default. -o json prints the API's JSON for scripting:

obioctl -o json user create alice | jq -r .user_id

On error the exit code is non-zero and stderr carries the server's message. A secret is printed only when it's created.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
group commands tenant list, show, create, update, delete, admin list\|add\|remove user list, show, create, update, suspend, activate, delete key list, create [--scope s3://b/p/ --read-only], activate, deactivate, delete policy list, show, create --file, update, delete, attach, detach, attached group list, show, create, delete, add-user, remove-user role list, show, create --trust-file, update, delete oidc list, show, put --file, delete, tenant-name sts assume-role-with-web-identity --role-arn --token[-file] [--env] public-access-block get, put, delete (tenant/cluster); bucket get\|put\|delete\|policy-status audit get, put --file, delete replication target list\|set\|delete, resync start\|status\|cancel (replication) bucket list, show, create [--pool], delete, set-owner, set-quota [--bytes] [--objects], policy …, dedup …, lifecycle …, cors … provision bucket B --user U (bucket + scoped key), rotate-key, deprovision cluster info, topology, usage, drain-status, validate-placement, rebalance status\|pause\|resume upgrade status, finalize (upgrades) node list, show osd set-state ID in\|out\|draining pool list, show, create, update, delete, placement-groups pg list [--pool] [--state], get <pg_id>, scrub <pg_id> kms status, keys list\|create\|show warehouse list (system admin), create, delete config list, get, set, delete metrics query, query-range (PromQL, through the gateway to the Prometheus named by its --prometheus-url; refused without one) volume list, create, show, resize, delete, attach [--read-only], detach, attachments snapshot list, create, show, delete, clone skills list, install (agent skills for coding agents)

obioctl <group> --help lists each command's options. The source tree has the full command → API route map in bin/cli/README.md.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Onboard a tenant, as the system admin:

obioctl tenant create acme --display-name "Acme" --quota-bytes 2T --default-pool standard
ADMIN=$(obioctl -o json user create acme-admin --tenant acme | jq -r .user_id)
obioctl tenant admin add acme "$ADMIN"
obioctl key create "$ADMIN"          # hand this to acme's admin

As acme's admin:

obioctl user create alice
obioctl policy create read-logs --file read-logs.json
obioctl policy attach read-logs --user <alice-id>
obioctl public-access-block put --all
obioctl bucket create logs
obioctl bucket lifecycle put logs --file lifecycle.xml

Make pools, one per protection scheme (--ec-type 0 is Reed-Solomon, 1 LRC, 2 replication):

obioctl pool create standard --ec-type 0 --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2 --failure-domain host
obioctl pool create wide --ec-type 1 --ec-k 6 --ec-local-parity 2 --ec-global-parity 2
obioctl pool create copies --ec-type 2 --replication-count 3

A scheme the codecs can't keep is refused, with what is wrong with it, and no pool is made: Reed-Solomon with no parity (--ec-m 0; one unprotected copy is --ec-type 2 --replication-count 1) or a profile some loss of m shards wouldn't decode; LRC whose data shards don't split into its local groups evenly, or with no local or global parity; replication of 0 copies; more than 255 shards. An LRC pool survives every loss of its global parity count, more by where they fall. The rules are in data protection.

Take an OSD out of service:

obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining
obioctl cluster drain-status

Temporary credentials from a CI job's OIDC token:

eval "$(obioctl sts assume-role-with-web-identity \
  --role-arn arn:obio:iam::acme:role/ci --token-file "$TOKEN_FILE" --env)"

docs.title: Gateway-side grep — searching objects without downloading
docs.text:
When an agent (or a fleet of 100 clients) needs to search inside object contents, the naive approach is GET the object and grep client-side. For a 10 GB log file and 100 agents that's 1 TB of egress for one search — unacceptable.

ObjectIO ships two grep endpoints that run the scan on the gateway and stream only matching records (with their byte offsets) back to the caller. Built for log / text / markdown / JSONL workloads where line-level regex is the right tool; use the Iceberg catalog for structured tabular queries.

docs.title: Single-object grep
docs.text:
POST /{bucket}/{key}?grep
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "pattern":          "ERROR.*timeout",
  "literal":          false,
  "case_insensitive": false,
  "max_matches":      100,
  "content_max_bytes": 2048,
  "invert":           false,
  "engine":           "regex"   // optional — "regex" | "pcre2" | "hyperscan"
}

Response is application/x-ndjson — one JSON event per newline:

{"type":"start","file_size":271,"etag":"\"abc123\"","pattern":"ERROR.*timeout"}
{"type":"match","line_number":3,"offset":80,"line_length":57,"match_offset":100,"match_length":13,"content":"2026-04-22 10:00:03 ERROR timeout connecting to host=db1"}
{"type":"match","line_number":5,"offset":179,"line_length":57,"match_offset":199,"match_length":13,"content":"2026-04-22 10:00:05 ERROR timeout connecting to host=db2"}
{"type":"end","matches":2,"bytes_scanned":271,"truncated":false,"elapsed_ms":1}

Every match frame gives the agent everything needed to find or fetch the source context:

Field Purpose line_number 1-indexed line in the source object offset Byte offset of the line start in the source file — use with Range: bytes=offset- line_length Bytes the line occupies (including the trailing newline if present) match_offset Byte offset of the matched substring itself match_length Length of the matched substring in bytes content The matched line, truncated to content_max_bytes (default 8 KiB) truncated true if the content field was clipped — agent can use offset + line_length to Range-fetch the full line

docs.title: Multi-object (prefix) grep
docs.text:
POST /{bucket}?grep
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "pattern":                "panic",
  "prefix":                 "2026-04/",
  "continuation_token":     "",        // paginate from a prior scan's next_continuation_token
  "max_keys":               100,
  "max_matches":            500,
  "max_matches_per_object": 20,
  "literal":                false,
  "case_insensitive":       false,
  "content_max_bytes":      2048,
  "invert":                 false
}

Response is the same NDJSON shape, with per-key brackets:

{"type":"start","file_size":0,"etag":"","pattern":"panic"}
{"type":"object","bucket":"logs","key":"2026-04/app-20.log","file_size":151,"etag":"\"c19ddee6…\""}
{"type":"match","bucket":"logs","key":"2026-04/app-20.log","line_number":3,"offset":93,...}
{"type":"match","bucket":"logs","key":"2026-04/app-20.log","line_number":7,"offset":410,...}
{"type":"object_end","bucket":"logs","key":"2026-04/app-20.log","matches_in_object":2,"per_object_truncated":false}
{"type":"object","bucket":"logs","key":"2026-04/app-21.log","file_size":151,"etag":"..."}
...
{"type":"end","matches":6,"bytes_scanned":453,"truncated":false,"elapsed_ms":5,"objects_scanned":3}

Every match now carries bucket and key so agents can cross-reference.

docs.title: Agent pattern: grep then Range-fetch
docs.text:
The canonical LLM workflow: small matches go straight into context; larger fetches happen only when the agent decides they're needed.

# Step 1 — grep
hits = tool.grep_object(
    bucket="logs", key="app.log",
    pattern="ERROR.*user=alice", max_matches=50)

# Step 2 — optional: fetch surrounding context around interesting match
m = hits[3]
chunk = tool.get_object(
    "logs", "app.log",
    range_header=f"bytes={m['offset']-4096}-"
                 f"{m['offset']+m['line_length']+4096}")

# Or: fetch the whole file if small
if hits.file_size < 1_000_000:
    full = tool.get_object("logs", "app.log")

docs.title: MCP tool stub
docs.text:
Drop into any agent runtime that understands MCP-style tool schemas (Claude Code, OpenAI function calling, Anthropic MCP):

{
  "name": "grep_object",
  "description": "Search inside an object using a regex. Returns matching lines with byte offsets so the agent can fetch surrounding context via Range reads.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["bucket", "key", "pattern"],
    "properties": {
      "bucket":           {"type": "string"},
      "key":              {"type": "string"},
      "pattern":          {"type": "string", "description": "Regex or literal. Set literal=true to disable regex interpretation."},
      "literal":          {"type": "boolean", "default": false},
      "case_insensitive": {"type": "boolean", "default": false},
      "max_matches":      {"type": "integer", "default": 100},
      "content_max_bytes":{"type": "integer", "default": 2048},
      "invert":           {"type": "boolean", "default": false}
    }
  }
}

And for prefix grep:

{
  "name": "grep_prefix",
  "description": "Search every object under a key prefix. Returns matches tagged by bucket+key so the agent knows which file each hit came from.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["bucket", "pattern"],
    "properties": {
      "bucket":                  {"type": "string"},
      "pattern":                 {"type": "string"},
      "prefix":                  {"type": "string", "default": ""},
      "continuation_token":      {"type": "string", "default": "", "description": "Pass back the prior response's next_continuation_token to resume a paginated scan."},
      "max_keys":                {"type": "integer", "default": 100},
      "max_matches":             {"type": "integer", "default": 500},
      "max_matches_per_object":  {"type": "integer", "default": 20},
      "literal":                 {"type": "boolean", "default": false},
      "case_insensitive":        {"type": "boolean", "default": false}
    }
  }
}

Both tools inherit normal S3 auth — the agent must sign with SigV4 credentials that have s3:GetObject on the target keys, same as any other read.

docs.title: Pattern engines
docs.text:
By default the scanner uses the pure-Rust regex crate — RE2-based, linear-time, no catastrophic backtracking. It handles nearly every pattern an agent will throw at it. When you need features the default can't express, pass "engine": "<name>" in the request body:

Engine Compiled into Adds regex (default) always — pcre2 Linux release binaries (--features grep-pcre2) backrefs (\1), lookaround ((?=foo), (?<!bar)), atomic groups, recursion, named captures hyperscan Linux x86_64 release binaries (--features grep-hyperscan) Intel SIMD-accelerated matching for high-throughput scanning over large streams

Selecting an engine that wasn't compiled into your gateway binary returns 400 BadRequest with a clear message:

HTTP 400: pattern compile failed: engine 'pcre2' is not compiled into
this gateway; rebuild with `--features pcre2` or select another engine

macOS release binaries ship with regex only. Linux arm64 ships with regex + pcre2. Linux amd64 ships with all three.

Example — duplicate-word detection (needs a backref, so regex can't do it; pcre2 can):

body = {"pattern": r"(\w+) \1", "engine": "pcre2"}
# → matches "hello hello", "foo foo", ...

docs.title: What this is and isn't
docs.text:
Good fit:

  • Plain text (.txt) logs and exports
  • Markdown documents (.md)
  • JSONL (one JSON object per line)
  • Source code files where regex grep is already the right tool
  • Any workload where "find matching lines without downloading the full file" is the ask

Not the right tool — use these instead:

Workload Use SQL over a table / filter a column Iceberg REST Catalog + DuckDB / Spark / Trino Column pruning on Parquet without a catalog DuckDB over S3 with httpfs, client-side Full-text search with relevance / BM25 Quickwit (S3-backed index, lightweight) or OpenSearch alongside the gateway Code search with symbol awareness Sourcegraph / Zoekt mirror Pretty-printed JSON with structural path ($.users[?(@.name=="alice")]) Pipe the raw object through jq client-side; grep can't give you structural semantics

docs.title: Limits and follow-ups
docs.text:
• Object body is collected into memory before scanning — fine up to a few GiB, hard cap at 16 GiB. Streaming off the EC read path is a planned follow-up that lifts the cap entirely.
  • . in regex doesn't cross line boundaries — line-based grep by design; multiline patterns aren't supported in v1.
  • Pretty-printed or single-line JSON has weaker match locality because there's no line structure. Use content_max_bytes and Range-fetch the offset to recover context.
  • Per-request timeout follows the gateway's HTTP timeout (60s default). Patterns that require scanning very large prefixes should page by adjusting max_keys across requests.
  • Pagination is supported via continuation tokens. When a prefix scan hits max_keys, the end frame includes next_continuation_token. Pass it back in the next request's continuation_token to resume. A response without next_continuation_token signals that the prefix is exhausted.
ct = ""
while True:
    resp = grep_prefix(bucket="logs", pattern="panic",
                       prefix="2026-04/", max_keys=100,
                       continuation_token=ct)
    # ... process matches ...
    ct = resp.end.get("next_continuation_token") or ""
    if not ct:
        break

docs.title: Example — from the command line
docs.text:
curl using SigV4 via awscurl / aws s3api helpers:

export OBJ=http://localhost:9000
python3 - <<'EOF'
import boto3, json, os
from botocore.awsrequest import AWSRequest
import botocore.auth
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen
creds = boto3.Session().get_credentials()
body = json.dumps({"pattern": "ERROR.*timeout", "max_matches": 20}).encode()
r = AWSRequest(method="POST", url=f"{os.environ['OBJ']}/logs/app.log?grep",
               data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
botocore.auth.SigV4Auth(creds, "s3", "us-east-1").add_auth(r)
with urlopen(Request(r.url, data=body, headers=dict(r.headers), method="POST")) as resp:
    for line in resp: print(line.decode().rstrip())
EOF

docs.title: Identity and Access
docs.text:
Who can do what in an ObjectIO cluster: tenants and their admins, users and access keys, IAM policies, groups and roles, identity providers, and temporary credentials from an OIDC token (STS).

Everything here is reachable two ways: the admin API under /_admin/*, and the AWS IAM and STS APIs (aws iam, aws sts, boto3, Terraform's AWS provider). Both are signed with SigV4 like any S3 request and work on the same records: a user created with aws iam create-user is the user GET /_admin/users lists. The management SDKs wrap the admin API for Go and Python.

docs.title: Scopes: the system and tenants
docs.text:
Every identity object lives in one scope.

  • The system scope belongs to the operator. Its admin (the credential meta prints on first boot) manages the whole cluster.
  • A tenant is a hard boundary. Its users, groups, roles, policies and buckets are its own. No policy can grant a tenant's identity access to another tenant's bucket: the check happens before any policy is read.

A tenant admin is a user of the tenant listed in its admin_users. A tenant admin manages everything in the tenant and nothing outside it.

# As the system admin
POST /_admin/tenants                    {"name": "acme", "display_name": "Acme", "enabled": true}
POST /_admin/users                      {"display_name": "acme-admin", "tenant": "acme"}
POST /_admin/tenants/acme/admins        {"user_id": "<user_id>"}
POST /_admin/users/<user_id>/access-keys {}

From then on the tenant admin works with its own key. Each call below acts in the caller's own tenant. The system admin can name a tenant with ?tenant= (or "tenant" in a body); a tenant admin can't name another tenant.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text:
A tenant can have quotas on bytes, objects and buckets, and a bucket can have quotas on bytes and objects. 0 means unlimited. Bytes and objects count every version stored, current and noncurrent; a tenant's usage is the sum of its buckets'.

obioctl tenant create acme --quota-bytes 2T --quota-objects 10000000
obioctl bucket set-quota photos --bytes 500G --objects 1000000
# or: PUT /_admin/buckets/{bucket}/quota  {"quota_bytes": N, "quota_objects": N}

A system admin sets tenant quotas. A bucket's quota can be set by a system admin or by its tenant's admin. The bucket quota is checked when a bucket is created.

A write that would pass a byte or object quota is refused with 403 QuotaExceeded: a PUT, a copy, a browser upload, an upload part, or a multipart completion. It is refused before any of its bytes are stored.

  • Usage comes from the usage report, which the OSDs feed. While any quota is set, each gateway refreshes the report every 5 s.
  • A delete makes room once the next report shows it.
  • Within one gateway, enforcement is exact, up to the writes already in flight when the limit is crossed.
  • With several gateways, each also allows what the others admitted within one report interval, so usage can pass a quota by that much. This is the same trade-off Ceph RGW and MinIO make. The design is in architecture/design/s3/quotas.md.

Refusals are counted in objectio_s3_quota_refusals_total{scope}.

docs.title: Users and access keys
docs.text:
GET /_admin/users users in scope POST /_admin/users {"display_name", "email"?, "tenant"?} create GET /_admin/users/{user_id} one user PUT /_admin/users/{user_id} {"status"?, "display_name"?, "email"?} update; status is active or suspended DELETE /_admin/users/{user_id} delete GET /_admin/users/{user_id}/access-keys the user's keys POST /_admin/users/{user_id}/access-keys {"scope"?, "operation"?} new key; a scope like s3://bucket/prefix/ confines it PUT /_admin/access-keys/{id} {"status": "active" \| "inactive"} turn a key off or back on DELETE /_admin/access-keys/{id} delete a key

Suspend rather than delete when you need to cut someone off now and decide later. A suspended user's keys are all refused, and deactivating a key refuses just that key. Nothing is deleted, and reactivating restores access. Gateways cache credentials for at most 15 seconds, so the change takes effect everywhere within that time.

A scoped key (one with a scope) can only reach that bucket or prefix, and is refused on the admin API entirely. A credential handed to a workload therefore can't mint itself a wider one.

User names are case-insensitive (Alice and alice are one user) and unique across the cluster, not only within a tenant. A user has a path (/, or /team/), which is part of its ARN: arn:objectio:iam::acme:user/team/alice. Renaming a user or moving it to another path changes its ARN; a tenant's admin_users entry that names it by ARN must then be updated (one naming its user id needn't).

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
IAM policies are AWS-format JSON documents: Effect, Action, Resource, Condition. They are attached to users, groups or roles. A bucket policy is attached to a bucket instead and set with S3's PUT /{bucket}?policy. The two are evaluated together:

  1. An explicit Deny anywhere wins.
  2. An Allow in an attached policy or the bucket policy grants access.
  3. With no Allow, the bucket's owner is allowed and everyone else is denied.

No policy means owner-only, not open.

GET /_admin/policies the tenant's own policies, plus the shared catalogue POST /_admin/policies {"name", "policy", "tenant"?, "shared"?} create GET /_admin/policies/{name} one policy PUT /_admin/policies/{name} {"policy"} replace the document DELETE /_admin/policies/{name} delete POST /_admin/policies/attach {"policy_name", "user_id" \| "group_id" \| "role_name"} attach POST /_admin/policies/detach detach, same body GET /_admin/policies/attached?user_id=\|group_id=\|role_name= what's attached

Policies are per tenant: acme's auditors and globex's auditors are different documents. The system admin can mark a system policy "shared": true so that every tenant can attach it but none can change it.

The built-in readonly, readwrite and writeonly policies are shared. consoleAdmin (admin:*) is the operator's alone.

AWS managed policies. AmazonS3FullAccess, AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, IAMFullAccess and IAMReadOnlyAccess are built in, the same in every cluster, and can't be changed or deleted. Attach one by its AWS ARN through the IAM API (arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess), or as aws:AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess through the admin API.

Inline policies belong to one user, group or role, by name, and go when it goes. They are managed through the IAM API (PutUserPolicy, PutGroupPolicy, PutRolePolicy, …) and evaluated with the attached ones: a Deny in any of them wins.

s3:* grants S3 actions only. (It used to match every action, which would have let an S3 grant make IAM calls once those existed.) Action names are case-insensitive.

Deleting a role or a group, through either API, also deletes its inline policies and its attachments: a role created later under the same name starts with none. Deleting a user takes its inline policies, attachments and group memberships with it.

Attaching and detaching take effect immediately on the gateway that made the change, and within 15 seconds on the others.

Policies support every IAM condition operator, plus IfExists, ForAnyValue:/ForAllValues: and Null. A document using an unknown operator is refused when you save it rather than being silently ignored. Policies written for AWS work unchanged: arn:aws: ARNs and {"AWS": ...} principals mean the same as arn:obio: and {"OBIO": ...}. See condition keys.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
GET /_admin/groups groups in scope POST /_admin/groups {"group_name", "tenant"?} create GET /_admin/groups/{group_id} one group, with its members DELETE /_admin/groups/{group_id} delete POST /_admin/groups/{group_id}/members {"user_id"} add a member of the group's own tenant DELETE /_admin/groups/{group_id}/members/{user_id} remove

A user gets the policies attached to every group it belongs to.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
A role is a set of policies that someone can take on for a while, rather than an identity of its own. Who may take it on is decided by its trust policy. A role is assumed with an OIDC token through STS, or by a user or another role's session with AssumeRole.

GET /_admin/roles roles in scope POST /_admin/roles {"name", "trust_policy", "description"?, "max_session_seconds"?} create GET /_admin/roles/{name} the role and its attached policies PUT /_admin/roles/{name} {"trust_policy"?, "description"?, "max_session_seconds"?} update DELETE /_admin/roles/{name} delete

A role's ARN names its scope: arn:obio:iam::acme:role/ci for tenant acme, arn:obio:iam::objectio:role/oncall for the system.

docs.title: Identity providers (OIDC)
docs.text:
The operator and each tenant can have their own OpenID Connect provider: Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, Google, Dex, or any other compliant issuer.

  • The operator's provider signs in system administrators. It is set with the gateway's --oidc-* flags, or stored with "system_admin": true.
  • A tenant's provider signs in that tenant's users. It's stored under the name t-<tenant>, which a tenant admin can create for itself. That also binds it to the tenant.
PUT /_admin/config/identity/openid/t-acme
{"issuer_url": "https://keycloak.acme.example/realms/acme",
 "client_id": "objectio", "client_secret": "…",
 "claim_name": "groups", "scopes": "openid profile email"}

claim_name can be a dotted path, such as realm_access.roles for Keycloak realm roles.

Only the system admin can set system_admin, or edit or delete a provider that has it. Otherwise a tenant admin could point the operator's sign-in at their own IdP.

docs.title: Temporary credentials from an OIDC token (STS)
docs.text:
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity trades an OIDC token for a role's temporary S3 keys. It's the AWS STS call, so AWS SDKs and tools speak it as is. Point them at the gateway's S3 endpoint:

import boto3

sts = boto3.client("sts", endpoint_url="https://s3.example.com", region_name="us-east-1")
r = sts.assume_role_with_web_identity(
    RoleArn="arn:obio:iam::acme:role/ci",
    RoleSessionName="build-42",
    WebIdentityToken=open("/var/run/secrets/token").read(),
    DurationSeconds=3600,
)
c = r["Credentials"]
s3 = boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="https://s3.example.com",
                  aws_access_key_id=c["AccessKeyId"],
                  aws_secret_access_key=c["SecretAccessKey"],
                  aws_session_token=c["SessionToken"])

Which provider can vouch for which role:

role accepted tokens system role (arn:obio:iam::objectio:role/…) the operator's providers only tenant role (arn:obio:iam::acme:role/…) that tenant's provider only. For a multi-tenant provider such as Entra organizations, only tokens from the upstream organisation registered to the tenant

A token from the wrong provider is refused with InvalidIdentityToken, however its claims read.

The trust policy then decides. Claims are condition keys named after the issuer (without https://): <issuer>:sub, <issuer>:aud, <issuer>:email, <issuer>:groups and any other claim. As in AWS, a trust policy has no Resource.

{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {"Federated": "https://keycloak.acme.example/realms/acme"},
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {"keycloak.acme.example/realms/acme:aud": "objectio"},
    "ForAnyValue:StringEquals": {"keycloak.acme.example/realms/acme:groups": "ci"}
  }
}]}

What the credentials can do: what the role's attached policies allow, inside the role's tenant. Detaching a policy affects sessions already issued. A system role is not a system admin.

How long they last: DurationSeconds is between 900 and the role's max_session_seconds. The default is 3600 and the maximum 12 hours.

Errors: AccessDenied (trust policy, or no such role: the two are answered the same, so role names can't be probed), InvalidIdentityToken, ExpiredTokenException, ValidationError.

docs.title: The AWS IAM and STS APIs
docs.text:
The gateway answers the AWS IAM and STS query APIs on its S3 endpoint: POST / with a form body (or GET /?Action=…), signed with SigV4 for the service iam or sts in any region. Point the client at the S3 endpoint:

aws --endpoint-url https://s3.example.com iam create-user --user-name alice --path /team/
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.example.com iam create-access-key --user-name alice
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.example.com iam attach-user-policy --user-name alice \
    --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess
aws --endpoint-url https://s3.example.com sts get-caller-identity

iam = boto3.client("iam", endpoint_url="https://s3.example.com", region_name="us-east-1")
sts = boto3.client("sts", endpoint_url="https://s3.example.com", region_name="us-east-1")

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text:
A tenant is an IAM account; its account id is the tenant's name. The system scope is the account with the empty id. A call acts in the caller's own account: a user of acme creates users in acme, and nothing of another tenant exists for it (NoSuchEntity).

Who may make which call:

Caller May the system admin any call, in the system account a tenant admin any call, in its tenant: it is the account's root any other user, or a role's session what its own policies allow (iam:CreateUser on arn:aws:iam::acme:user/team/*, …) a key scoped to a bucket, the data-lake APIs' vended credentials none

GetUser (with no user name) and GetCallerIdentity name the system admin and tenant admins arn:aws:iam::<account>:root.

docs.title: ARNs
docs.text:
The IAM API shows ARNs as AWS does. Policies may use either spelling.

IAM API stored (admin API) user arn:aws:iam::acme:user/team/alice arn:objectio:iam::acme:user/team/alice system user arn:aws:iam:::user/ops arn:objectio:iam::user/ops group arn:aws:iam::acme:group/devs arn:obio:iam::acme:group/devs role arn:aws:iam::acme:role/apps/ci arn:obio:iam::acme:role/apps/ci policy arn:aws:iam::acme:policy/readers acme/readers a shared system policy arn:aws:iam:::policy/readonly readonly AWS managed policy arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/IAMReadOnlyAccess aws:IAMReadOnlyAccess a role's session arn:aws:sts::acme:assumed-role/ci/build-42 arn:obio:sts::acme:assumed-role/ci/build-42

In policies, arn:aws:, arn:obio: and arn:objectio: ARNs are the same ARN, and an empty account and objectio both name the system scope.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Area Actions Users CreateUser, GetUser, ListUsers, UpdateUser (rename, move), DeleteUser Access keys CreateAccessKey, ListAccessKeys, UpdateAccessKey, DeleteAccessKey Groups CreateGroup, GetGroup, ListGroups, UpdateGroup (rename, move), DeleteGroup, AddUserToGroup, RemoveUserFromGroup, ListGroupsForUser Managed policies CreatePolicy, GetPolicy, GetPolicyVersion, ListPolicyVersions, ListPolicies, DeletePolicy Attachments Attach/Detach/ListAttached UserPolicies, GroupPolicies, RolePolicies Inline policies Put/Get/List/Delete UserPolicy, GroupPolicy, RolePolicy Roles CreateRole, GetRole, ListRoles, UpdateRole, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, DeleteRole Account GetAccountSummary, ListOpenIDConnectProviders STS GetCallerIdentity, GetSessionToken, AssumeRole (and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, unsigned)

Lists page with Marker and MaxItems and filter with PathPrefix; they sort by name, ignoring case.

As in IAM: names are case-insensitive; deleting a user with access keys or policies, a group with members or policies, or a role with policies is a DeleteConflict; inline policies are at most 2048 (user), 5120 (group) or 10240 (role) characters, managed ones 6144, whitespace aside.

docs.title: STS
docs.text:
• AssumeRole: the role's trust policy decides, with the caller as principal (its ARN, and for a user its id too: …:user/<user_id>). Within a tenant that is enough. A caller from another tenant must be named by the trust policy (a grant to * stays in the role's tenant) and its own policies must allow sts:AssumeRole on the role, as IAM's cross-account rule has it; a trust policy naming an account's root (arn:aws:iam::acme:root) lets in that account's users whose own policies allow it. The session acts as the role: its policies (attached and inline), its tenant. 15 minutes to the role's MaxSessionDuration (default 1 hour); a role's session assuming another gets at most 1 hour. Session policies (Policy, PolicyArns) are refused.
  • GetSessionToken: a user's own access key gets temporary keys that act as the user (its policies, groups, tenant), for 15 minutes to 36 hours (default 12). Requests with them carry sts:authentication = true for policy conditions. Suspending the user stops them within 15 seconds.
  • GetCallerIdentity: who the credentials are: user, root, or <RoleId>:<session> for a role's session.

The credentials work against S3 at once, on every gateway.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• OIDC provider management (CreateOpenIDConnectProvider, …): identity providers are configured through the admin API; ListOpenIDConnectProviders lists those the account trusts.
  • Policy versions beyond one: a policy has one version, v1 (CreatePolicyVersion isn't supported; change a policy through the admin API's PUT /_admin/policies/{name}).
  • Login profiles, MFA, signing certificates, SSH keys, service-specific credentials, tags, permission boundaries, instance profiles, GetFederationToken, SimulatePrincipalPolicy.
  • IAM quotas: none are enforced. GetAccountSummary reports the counts, and AWS's default quotas for clients that read them.
  • DeletePolicy detaches the policy everywhere rather than refusing while it is attached.
  • ListBuckets is never refused for lack of a grant: it lists the buckets the caller owns (AWS refuses a user no policy allows s3:ListAllMyBuckets). An explicit Deny of s3:ListAllMyBuckets refuses it.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Paths, descriptions of policies, group renames and inline policies are format level 3 (roles and policies created before it get ids derived from their ARN and creation time). On a cluster upgraded from level 2 they are refused (400 InvalidInput, "finalize the upgrade first") until obioctl upgrade finalize; the rest of the IAM API works before that.

docs.title: Session and token signing
docs.text: Temporary credentials, console sessions and listing continuation tokens are signed with keys derived from a cluster secret. Meta creates the secret once and replicates it through Raft, so every gateway shares it: a session issued by one gateway is honoured by all of them, and nothing about it can be forged from outside. The secret is never exposed by any API.

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text: Buckets are bucket owner enforced, the S3 default since 2023. The bucket owner owns every object, ACLs grant nothing, and access is decided by policies only. ACL reads answer with the owner's FULL_CONTROL. An ACL write that says only that is accepted; any other ACL write is refused with AccessControlListNotSupported. No ACL can make data public: see Public access for how that's done deliberately.

docs.title: Iceberg REST Catalog API
docs.text: ObjectIO includes an Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API, enabling query engines like Spark, Trino, and Flink to discover and manage Iceberg tables.

docs.title: Base URL
docs.text:
All Iceberg endpoints are served under /iceberg/v1/. Clients are given the catalog URI without /v1 and add it themselves:

http://gateway:9000/iceberg

Every catalog lives in a warehouse, named by the client's warehouse setting.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Iceberg endpoints use the same SigV4 authentication as S3. When --no-auth is set, all Iceberg endpoints are accessible without credentials.

docs.title: Warehouses
docs.text:
A warehouse is a catalog with its own namespaces and tables, and a bucket, iceberg-<name>, made with it for its data. Warehouses are managed on the admin API (obioctl warehouse …):

Call Who GET /_admin/warehouses system admin {"warehouses": [{"name", "bucket", "location", "tenant", "created_at", "properties"}]} POST /_admin/warehouses system admin, or the tenant's admin Body {"name": "...", "tenant": "...", "properties": {...}}; tenant defaults to the caller's. Answers the new warehouse; 400 if it or its bucket exists DELETE /_admin/warehouses/{name} system admin, or its tenant's admin 
obioctl warehouse create analytics      # also creates bucket iceberg-analytics
obioctl warehouse list

docs.title: GetConfig
docs.text:
Get catalog configuration for a warehouse (the warehouse parameter is required).

GET /iceberg/v1/config?warehouse=analytics

Response:

{
  "defaults": {
    "warehouse": "s3://iceberg-analytics"
  },
  "overrides": {
    "prefix": "ws/analytics"
  }
}

The client then sends every call under /iceberg/v1/ws/analytics/….

docs.title: ListNamespaces
docs.text:
List all namespaces, optionally filtered by parent.

GET /iceberg/v1/namespaces
GET /iceberg/v1/namespaces?parent=parent_ns

Response:

{
  "namespaces": [
    ["analytics"],
    ["production"]
  ]
}

docs.title: CreateNamespace
docs.text:
Create a new namespace.

POST /iceberg/v1/namespaces

Request Body:

{
  "namespace": ["analytics"],
  "properties": {
    "owner": "alice",
    "description": "Analytics data"
  }
}

Response:

{
  "namespace": ["analytics"],
  "properties": {
    "owner": "alice",
    "description": "Analytics data"
  }
}

docs.title: LoadNamespace
docs.text:
Get namespace details.

GET /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}

Response:

{
  "namespace": ["analytics"],
  "properties": {
    "owner": "alice"
  }
}

docs.title: NamespaceExists
docs.text:
Check if a namespace exists.

HEAD /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}

Response: 204 No Content (exists) or 404 Not Found

docs.title: DropNamespace
docs.text:
Delete a namespace. Must be empty (no tables).

DELETE /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: UpdateNamespaceProperties
docs.text:
Update namespace properties.

POST /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/properties

Request Body:

{
  "updates": {
    "description": "Updated description"
  },
  "removals": ["old_property"]
}

Response:

{
  "updated": ["description"],
  "removed": ["old_property"],
  "missing": []
}

docs.title: ListTables
docs.text:
List tables in a namespace.

GET /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables

Response:

{
  "identifiers": [
    {
      "namespace": ["analytics"],
      "name": "events"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: CreateTable
docs.text:
Create a new table.

POST /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables

Request Body:

{
  "name": "events",
  "schema": {
    "type": "struct",
    "fields": [
      {"id": 1, "name": "id", "type": "long", "required": true},
      {"id": 2, "name": "data", "type": "string", "required": false}
    ]
  },
  "properties": {}
}

Response:

{
  "metadata": {
    "format-version": 2,
    "table-uuid": "...",
    "location": "s3://objectio-warehouse/analytics/events",
    "schema": { ... }
  },
  "metadata-location": "s3://objectio-warehouse/analytics/events/metadata/v1.metadata.json"
}

docs.title: LoadTable
docs.text:
Get table metadata.

GET /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}

Response: Same format as CreateTable response.

docs.title: TableExists
docs.text:
Check if a table exists.

HEAD /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}

Response: 204 No Content (exists) or 404 Not Found

docs.title: UpdateTable
docs.text:
Update table metadata (schema evolution, property changes).

POST /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}

docs.title: DropTable
docs.text:
Delete a table.

DELETE /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: RenameTable
docs.text:
Rename a table (optionally across namespaces).

POST /iceberg/v1/tables/rename

Request Body:

{
  "source": {
    "namespace": ["analytics"],
    "name": "events"
  },
  "destination": {
    "namespace": ["analytics"],
    "name": "events_v2"
  }
}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: Namespace Policy
docs.text:
Set a policy on a namespace (admin only).

PUT /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/policy

Request Body:

{
  "policy": "{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\",\"Principal\":{\"OBIO\":[\"arn:objectio:iam::user/alice\"]},\"Action\":[\"iceberg:*\"],\"Resource\":[\"arn:obio:iceberg:::analytics/*\"]}]}"
}

docs.title: Table Policy
docs.text:
Set a policy on a table (admin only).

PUT /iceberg/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/policy

Request Body: Same format as namespace policy.

docs.title: Policy Evaluation
docs.text: Policies follow the same semantics as S3 bucket policies: - Explicit Deny always wins - Explicit Allow grants access - Implicit Deny (no matching statement) allows access (owner has implicit access) - No policy allows access

docs.title: Iceberg Actions
docs.text: Action Description iceberg:ListNamespaces List namespaces iceberg:CreateNamespace Create a namespace iceberg:LoadNamespace Load namespace details iceberg:DropNamespace Delete a namespace iceberg:UpdateNamespaceProperties Update namespace properties iceberg:ListTables List tables in a namespace iceberg:CreateTable Create a table iceberg:LoadTable Load table metadata iceberg:UpdateTable Update table metadata iceberg:DropTable Delete a table iceberg:RenameTable Rename a table

docs.title: Resource ARNs
docs.text:
• Namespace: arn:obio:iceberg:::{namespace}
  • Table: arn:obio:iceberg:::{namespace}/{table}

docs.title: Client Configuration
docs.text: The URI is .../iceberg: Iceberg's REST clients add /v1 themselves, so .../iceberg/v1 makes them call /iceberg/v1/v1/…. The warehouse is a warehouse's name, not an s3:// location. The pyiceberg example in the code repo (examples/pyiceberg) signs with SigV4 (rest.sigv4-enabled, rest.signing-name s3) and runs against objectio-aio; no query engine is tested against the catalog in CI yet (objectio#8), so treat the Spark and Trino settings below as a starting point.

docs.title: PyIceberg
docs.text:
from pyiceberg.catalog.rest import RestCatalog

catalog = RestCatalog(
    name="objectio",
    uri="http://gateway:9000/iceberg",
    warehouse="analytics",
    **{
        "rest.sigv4-enabled": "true",
        "rest.signing-name": "s3",
        "rest.signing-region": "us-east-1",
        "s3.endpoint": "http://gateway:9000",
        "s3.path-style-access": "true",
        "s3.access-key-id": "...",
        "s3.secret-access-key": "...",
    },
)

docs.title: Apache Spark
docs.text:
spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.objectio", "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog") \
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.objectio.type", "rest") \
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.objectio.uri", "http://gateway:9000/iceberg") \
    .config("spark.sql.catalog.objectio.warehouse", "analytics") \
    .getOrCreate()

# Use the catalog
spark.sql("CREATE NAMESPACE objectio.analytics")
spark.sql("CREATE TABLE objectio.analytics.events (id BIGINT, data STRING)")

docs.title: Trino
docs.text:
connector.name=iceberg
iceberg.catalog.type=rest
iceberg.rest-catalog.uri=http://gateway:9000/iceberg
iceberg.rest-catalog.warehouse=analytics

docs.title: Error Responses
docs.text:
Iceberg errors follow the Iceberg REST API error format:

{
  "error": {
    "message": "Namespace does not exist: analytics",
    "type": "NoSuchNamespaceException",
    "code": 404
  }
}

docs.title: Error Types
docs.text: Type HTTP Status Description NoSuchNamespaceException 404 Namespace not found NamespaceAlreadyExistsException 409 Namespace already exists NoSuchTableException 404 Table not found AlreadyExistsException 409 Table already exists ForbiddenException 403 Access denied by policy BadRequestException 400 Invalid request

docs.title: Mutual TLS between the services
docs.text:
With mTLS on, every gRPC hop between ObjectIO's components runs over mutual TLS, and each side proves it holds a certificate signed by the cluster's CA:

  • gateway to meta and to the OSDs;
  • OSD to meta;
  • meta to meta, including Raft;
  • meta to the OSDs (liveness, repair, drain);
  • block gateway to meta and to the OSDs;
  • obioctl to the block gateway (volume, snapshot).

A peer without such a certificate is refused when it connects: a plaintext client, a TLS client with no certificate, or one with a certificate from another CA.

TLS for clients (S3, the console, Iceberg) is a separate matter: it's terminated at the ingress or load balancer.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Every component takes the same three settings, as flags or environment variables:

Flag Environment What --tls-cert OBJECTIO_TLS_CERT This node's certificate (PEM). It is presented both as a server and as a client. --tls-key OBJECTIO_TLS_KEY Its private key (PEM) --tls-ca OBJECTIO_TLS_CA The CA (PEM) that signs every node's certificate. It is the only CA trusted.

The three go together. Without them, gRPC is plain, which is fine for development and the all-in-one on a laptop. objectio-aio takes them too: its own internal hops then use mTLS.

The certificate must name every address peers dial the node by: the addresses registered as --advertise-addr (OSDs), --raft-advertise (meta) and the --meta-endpoint targets. Names and IPs both work. One certificate for the whole cluster is simplest, with a wildcard for each headless service.

Enable it at install time. A cluster can't run half on TLS and half off, so turning it on, or off, later means restarting every component at once.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
The chart mounts a Secret holding tls.crt, tls.key and ca.crt (cert-manager's format) into meta, the OSDs, the gateways and the block gateway, and sets the variables above:

tls:
  enabled: true
  # Either name a cert-manager CA issuer, and the chart requests the
  # certificate, with every service and pod name in it:
  certManager:
    issuerRef: {name: objectio-ca, kind: Issuer}
  # or create the Secret yourself:
  # secretName: my-objectio-tls

A CA issuer is what you want here: ca.crt is then the CA that signs each certificate. A minimal one, with cert-manager installed:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Issuer
metadata: {name: objectio-selfsigned}
spec: {selfSigned: {}}
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata: {name: objectio-ca}
spec:
  isCA: true
  commonName: objectio-ca
  secretName: objectio-ca
  issuerRef: {name: objectio-selfsigned, kind: Issuer}
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Issuer
metadata: {name: objectio-ca}
spec: {ca: {secretName: objectio-ca}}

docs.title: Renewal
docs.text:
Components read their certificate when they start. cert-manager renews the Secret 30 days before the certificate expires, and the chart's default lifetime is one year. After a renewal, restart the components one at a time so they pick up the new certificate:

kubectl rollout restart statefulset/<release>-objectio-meta statefulset/<release>-objectio-osd \
  deployment/<release>-objectio-gateway

Picking up a renewed certificate without a restart is planned.

docs.title: How it's tested
docs.text: The end-to-end suite runs with mTLS on: every node of every test cluster gets a test CA's certificate. One test checks that a node refuses a plaintext client, a client with no certificate and one with another CA's certificate, and serves the cluster's own. The rolling-upgrade test starts from the previous release, before TLS existed, so it runs plain. OBJECTIO_E2E_PLAIN=1 runs the whole suite plain; the mTLS test then fails, since it has nothing to test.

docs.title: Public Access
docs.text: How data is made readable without credentials, how that is prevented, and how a policy can depend on where a request comes from.

docs.title: Anonymous requests
docs.text:
A request with no signature is anonymous. It reaches only what a bucket policy grants to everyone ("Principal": "*"). Nothing else ever applies to it: no identity policy, no ownership, no ACL, and nothing outside bucket and object operations (GET /, the admin API and the console all refuse it).

{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{
  "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::assets/*"
}]}

With this policy, curl https://s3.example.com/assets/logo.png works. Listing assets, writing to it, and everything else still need credentials.

docs.title: Block Public Access
docs.text:
Block Public Access stops data being made public by mistake. It works as in S3, at three levels, and a flag set at any level holds:

level set by API bucket whoever may s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock (its owner by default) PUT /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock (S3) tenant the tenant's admin PUT /_admin/public-access-block cluster the system admin PUT /_admin/public-access-block (no tenant)

A bucket can't lift its tenant's block, and a tenant can't lift the cluster's.

flag effect BlockPublicPolicy a bucket policy that would make the bucket public is refused (403 AccessDenied) RestrictPublicBuckets a public grant already in place no longer reaches anonymous callers, or anyone outside the bucket's tenant BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls stored and reported. ACLs are owner-enforced, so no ACL can grant public access and both always hold

New buckets start with all four flags set, as S3's have since 2023. Making a bucket public is therefore a deliberate, two-step act: lift the block, then set the policy.

# A bucket: S3 XML, as aws s3api put-public-access-block sends it
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket assets \
  --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicPolicy=false,RestrictPublicBuckets=false
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket assets
aws s3api delete-public-access-block --bucket assets
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket assets      # IsPublic: true/false

# A tenant (as its admin) or the cluster (as the system admin): JSON
PUT /_admin/public-access-block            {"BlockPublicPolicy": true, "RestrictPublicBuckets": true}
GET /_admin/public-access-block[?tenant=acme]
DELETE /_admin/public-access-block[?tenant=acme]

# The cluster only: whether new buckets start blocked (default true)
PUT /_admin/public-access-block            {"new_buckets_blocked": false}

What counts as public. A policy is public if it allows "*" and no condition limits that to fixed callers. These conditions make it not public: - aws:SourceIp with a network smaller than the whole internet; - aws:SourceVpce; - aws:SourceArn, aws:SourceAccount, aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:userid.

Negative matches and wildcards don't count: "anyone not in 10.0.0.0/8" is still public.

docs.title: Where a request came from
docs.text: Policies can test two facts about a request's origin.

docs.title: aws:SourceVpce: which endpoint it arrived on
docs.text:
Each gateway listener can be given a name. The usual setup is two: - an internal endpoint, the in-cluster Service that pods use; - an external endpoint, which the ingress points at.

objectio-gateway --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 --endpoint-name internal \
                 --data-listen 0.0.0.0:9010=external

--data-listen ADDR=NAME adds a listener that serves S3, Iceberg and Delta Sharing only: no admin API, no console. It can be repeated. A request on an unnamed listener has no aws:SourceVpce, just as an AWS request over the internet has none.

The name is ObjectIO's equivalent of an AWS VPC endpoint ID, so AWS policies written for VPC endpoints carry over.

Readable without keys, from inside the cluster only. Because it's pinned, this policy isn't public. It is accepted with Block Public Access on, and anonymous callers can use it:

{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
 "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::models/*",
 "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:SourceVpce": "internal"}}}

A key that only works from inside. A leaked key is then useless from the internet:

{"Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*",
 "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::payroll", "arn:aws:s3:::payroll/*"],
 "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:SourceVpce": "internal"}}}

docs.title: aws:SourceIp: the client's address
docs.text:
By default this is the address of the connection's peer. Behind a load balancer or ingress controller, the peer is the proxy. List the proxies with --trusted-proxies (CIDRs, comma-separated). For a request from one of them, the client is then the nearest address in X-Forwarded-For that isn't a trusted proxy. X-Forwarded-For from anyone else is ignored, so a client can't claim an address it doesn't have.

objectio-gateway --trusted-proxies 10.244.0.0/16      # e.g. the ingress controller's pod network

The same rule applies to X-Forwarded-Proto, which sets aws:SecureTransport (whether the client used TLS, terminated at the proxy). From an untrusted peer the header is dropped, so a policy that requires TLS can't be passed by claiming it over plain HTTP. If you terminate TLS at an ingress and use aws:SecureTransport, set --trusted-proxies; without it, every request counts as plain HTTP.

{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
 "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::partner-feed/*",
 "Condition": {"IpAddress": {"aws:SourceIp": "203.0.113.0/24"}}}

In Kubernetes, pod addresses change. To mean "inside the cluster", prefer endpoint names; keep IP conditions for fixed networks such as an office range or a partner's servers.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
gateway:
  endpoints:
    internalName: internal        # the gateway Service
    external:
      port: 9010                  # a second port; the ingress targets it
      name: external
  trustedProxies: "10.244.0.0/16"

docs.title: Do I need a private endpoint?
docs.text:
Usually not. If the applications run in the same cluster as ObjectIO, the gateway's ClusterIP Service is already private: traffic stays in the cluster unless you also expose it through an ingress.

Block Public Access is about something else: who may read without credentials, not which network the request uses. Keep it on either way. Endpoint names connect the two when you want "anyone inside the cluster, but no one outside".

docs.title: Bucket replication
docs.text: Copy every new version written to a bucket into a bucket on another ObjectIO cluster, asynchronously, so losing a site loses nothing that had time to replicate.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. On the target cluster: a versioned bucket, and credentials for the source to write with. The admin's work; for least privilege, a user with s3:PutObject, s3:ReplicateObject (and s3:DeleteObject, s3:ReplicateDelete if delete markers replicate) on that bucket.

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket dr-copy --endpoint-url https://site-b:9000
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket dr-copy \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled --endpoint-url https://site-b:9000

2. On the source cluster: the target. Targets belong to a tenant: a bucket's rules can name only its own tenant's targets, so one tenant can never send data into another's remote bucket with the other's credentials. A tenant's admin manages its tenant's targets; the system admin manages the system's (no ?tenant=) and any tenant's (?tenant=).

curl -X POST https://site-a:9000/_admin/replication/targets \
  --aws-sigv4 aws:amz:us-east-1:s3 --user "$AK:$SK" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "site-b", "endpoint": "https://site-b:9000", "bucket": "dr-copy",
       "access_key": "...", "secret_key": "...", "bandwidth": 104857600}'

Or with obioctl (the remote secret from OBIOCTL_REMOTE_SECRET_KEY if not given, which keeps it out of the process list):

obioctl replication target set site-b --remote-endpoint https://site-b:9000 \
  --remote-bucket dr-copy --remote-access-key ... --bandwidth 100M
obioctl replication target list

bandwidth is optional: the bytes a second the whole cluster may send to the target (see Bandwidth); without it, as fast as the link goes.

GET /_admin/replication/targets lists a tenant's targets (the caller's own, for a tenant admin; secrets never shown); DELETE /_admin/replication/targets/{name} removes one. Both take ?tenant= for the system admin. The secret is kept in meta, as users' secret keys are.

A target a tenant's admin sets must be https://, on a host the operator allows tenants (as for tenant audit webhooks); otherwise a tenant could make the gateway send requests to addresses inside the cluster. Until the operator allows some, tenant admins can't set targets, and the system admin sets them with ?tenant=, unrestricted:

curl -X PUT https://site-a:9000/_admin/replication/settings \
  --aws-sigv4 aws:amz:us-east-1:s3 --user "$AK:$SK" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"allowed_tenant_hosts": ["dr.example.com", "*.dr.example.com"]}'

The list is checked again at every send, so removing a host stops tenants' targets on it.

3. On the source bucket: versioning, then the rules (S3's PutBucketReplication), by the bucket's owner or anyone its policy grants s3:PutReplicationConfiguration. The destination names one of the bucket's tenant's targets: arn:obio:replication:::<target>.

<ReplicationConfiguration>
  <Rule>
    <ID>everything</ID>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <Filter><Prefix></Prefix></Filter>
    <DeleteMarkerReplication><Status>Disabled</Status></DeleteMarkerReplication>
    <Destination><Bucket>arn:obio:replication:::site-b</Bucket></Destination>
  </Rule>
</ReplicationConfiguration>

aws s3api put-bucket-replication --bucket photos \
  --replication-configuration file://rules.json --endpoint-url https://site-a:9000

A rule filters by prefix and tags (<And> for both). Both buckets must be versioned; the rules are refused otherwise.

docs.title: What replicates
docs.text:
Change on the source On the target A new version (PUT, multipart upload, copy) The same version: same version id, bytes, ETag, content headers, x-amz-meta-*, tags, Object Lock retention and legal hold, SSE-S3 / SSE-KMS encryption (re-encrypted with the target's keys; an SSE-KMS key id must exist there) A delete marker Only if the rule has DeleteMarkerReplication Enabled A DELETE of a specific version Never: a mistake or an attacker on one site can't destroy the other's copy An SSE-C object Not replicated (its key isn't ours to send), as in S3 Objects written before the rule Only through a resync

The target never replicates a replica onward, so two clusters with rules pointing at each other don't loop.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A version a rule covers is committed with each target marked PENDING, in the same metadata write: no version is ever committed and forgotten.
  • The gateway that took the write sends it at once. One gateway at a time (a lease in meta) also scans every bucket with rules, every --replication-scan-secs (30 s by default), for versions still PENDING or FAILED, and sends them oldest first. That is what makes it reliable: after a crash, or while a target was down, every marked version is found.
  • A failed send is retried with backoff (2 s, doubling, up to 5 min), indefinitely. FAILED is a status to alert on, not a give-up.
  • Objects up to 64 MiB go in one PUT; larger ones as a multipart upload of 16 MiB parts.
  • The target stores a version it already holds (same version id and ETag) once: a send repeated after a crash changes nothing. An older version arriving after a newer one is kept as a version, never made current.

docs.title: Existing objects: resync
docs.text:
A rule sends what is written after it. To send what a bucket already holds (turning replication on for a bucket with data, or bringing a new or rebuilt target up to date), start a resync of the bucket to one of its targets. The bucket's tenant's admin, or the system admin, may:

obioctl replication resync start photos site-b
# or: POST /_admin/replication/resync {"bucket": "photos", "target": "site-b"}

The bucket must have an enabled rule sending to the target. The scanner (one gateway at a time) walks the bucket in key order, a page of 1000 keys at a time: every version a rule sends to the target and that the target hasn't got is marked PENDING and sent. Up to 8 sends run at once, within the target's bandwidth limit. Each pass gives resyncs a minute, then scans for versions not yet sent as usual, so a resync of a big bucket doesn't hold back other buckets' retries.

A version already COMPLETED for the target is left alone, and so is one PENDING or FAILED (the fast path and the scanner send it). To send everything again, for a target that was replaced or lost data, add --again ("again": true): versions already sent are marked and sent too; the target keeps one copy of each.

Watching and stopping it:

obioctl replication resync status photos
# TARGET  STATE    AFTER        SCANNED  MARKED  SENT    FAILED  BYTES     ERROR
# site-b  running  img/0412.jpg 412000   409870  409870  0       88123456  -
obioctl replication resync cancel photos site-b

GET /_admin/replication/resync?bucket= gives each target's resync (running, or the last one, done or cancelled): the last key done (after), the versions looked at (scanned), those a rule sends to the target (covered), marked, sent, failed, the bytes, and the last error. Starting a resync that is running returns it as it is.

A resync survives restarts. Its record in meta moves past a page only once every version in it is marked and sent. If the gateway stops mid-page, the scanner, wherever it runs next, takes the page again (after the scanner's lease runs out, up to a minute or three scan intervals); what that page had marked but not sent is PENDING by then and goes out with the scanner's next pass. Cancelling keeps what was sent and marked; the marked versions still go.

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text:
A target's bandwidth is the cluster's limit for it: the fast path, the scanner and resyncs on every gateway together send it no more than that many bytes a second. Each gateway takes an equal share (the limit divided by the gateways up, as meta last heard from them, refreshed every 30 s) and paces its sends to it, 64 KiB at a time; a quiet spell saves nothing up, so no burst follows it. A gateway can't use another's idle share, so with traffic on one gateway only, the cluster sends below the limit, not above it; and for the seconds before a new gateway first reports, the others still use the old shares.

The limit counts request bodies (the objects' bytes), not headers. A paced send may take longer than the 5-minute send timeout; its timeout grows with what its bytes take at the gateway's share.

docs.title: Watching it
docs.text:
• x-amz-replication-status on HEAD and GET: PENDING, COMPLETED or FAILED on the source, REPLICA on the target.
  • Metrics (gateway /metrics):
  • objectio_replication_backlog{target}: versions not yet replicated, at the last scan;
  • objectio_replication_lag_seconds{target}: the oldest one's age, in effect the RPO;
  • objectio_replication_sent_total{target,result};
  • objectio_replication_bytes_total{target}.

Alert on lag that keeps growing, and on result="error".

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: Two-way replication's conflict tests, and targets that aren't ObjectIO (AWS S3, MinIO), are the next phases.

docs.title: S3 API Operations
docs.text: Supported S3 API operations in ObjectIO.

docs.title: Addressing and signing
docs.text:
• Path-style only. Requests name the bucket in the path (https://s3.example.com/bucket/key). A virtual-hosted-style request (https://bucket.s3.example.com/key) is not recognised: the bucket in the host is ignored and the path is read as bucket and key (objectio#65). Set path style in clients: boto3 Config(s3={"addressing_style": "path"}), the AWS CLI aws configure set default.s3.addressing_style path, the Java and Go SDKs forcePathStyle / UsePathStyle, Iceberg and Spark s3.path-style-access=true.
  • SigV4 only, for requests and presigned URLs; SigV2 is refused with 400. Against a custom endpoint, boto3 without signature_version="s3v4" and AWS CLI v1's aws s3 presign produce SigV2 presigned URLs: set Config(signature_version="s3v4") in boto3, and aws configure set default.s3.signature_version s3v4 for the CLI.

docs.title: ListBuckets
docs.text:
List all buckets owned by the authenticated user.

GET /

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListAllMyBucketsResult>
    <Owner>
        <ID>user-id</ID>
        <DisplayName>User Name</DisplayName>
    </Owner>
    <Buckets>
        <Bucket>
            <Name>my-bucket</Name>
            <CreationDate>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</CreationDate>
        </Bucket>
    </Buckets>
</ListAllMyBucketsResult>

docs.title: CreateBucket
docs.text:
Create a new bucket.

PUT /{bucket}

Headers: - x-amz-acl: only private or bucket-owner-full-control (ACLs are owner-enforced) - x-amz-bucket-object-lock-enabled: true: a lock bucket (versioned) - x-objectio-pool: <pool>: the pool its data goes to (default: the tenant's default pool, else the cluster's default placement). A tenant may use only its default and allowed pools; the pool is fixed for the bucket's life

Response: 200 OK

A new bucket starts with public access blocked, and with no configuration from any earlier bucket of the same name.

docs.title: DeleteBucket
docs.text:
Delete an empty bucket.

DELETE /{bucket}

Response: 204 No Content

Errors: - BucketNotEmpty: the bucket holds objects, or (versioned) noncurrent versions or delete markers

Deleting a bucket also removes its policy, object lock, lifecycle, encryption and public access settings, in the same commit.

docs.title: HeadBucket
docs.text:
Check if a bucket exists and you have access.

HEAD /{bucket}

Response: 200 OK (bucket exists) or 404 Not Found

docs.title: GetBucketLocation
docs.text:
Get the region of a bucket.

GET /{bucket}?location

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<LocationConstraint>us-east-1</LocationConstraint>

docs.title: PutObject
docs.text:
Upload an object.

PUT /{bucket}/{key}

Headers: - Content-Type: MIME type - Content-Length: Object size - x-amz-meta-*: User metadata - Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Expires: kept with the object and served back (and kept by a copy) - If-None-Match: *: write only if no object has the key (412 PreconditionFailed if one does) — a create that can't overwrite - If-Match: <etag>: write only if the current object has this ETag (412, or 404 NoSuchKey if there's none) — compare-and-swap

Conditional writes are checked and applied atomically: of two writers racing with If-None-Match: *, exactly one wins. CompleteMultipartUpload takes the same headers.

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e"

Example:

curl -X PUT \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  -d "Hello World" \
  http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/hello.txt

docs.title: GetObject
docs.text:
Download an object.

GET /{bucket}/{key}

Headers: - Range: Byte range (optional)

Response Headers: - Content-Type: Object MIME type - Content-Length: Object size - ETag: Object hash - Last-Modified: Last modification time

Range Request:

curl -H "Range: bytes=0-99" http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/file.txt

docs.title: HeadObject
docs.text:
Get object metadata without body.

HEAD /{bucket}/{key}

Response Headers: - Content-Type: Object MIME type - Content-Length: Object size - ETag: Object hash - x-amz-meta-*: User metadata

docs.title: DeleteObject
docs.text:
Delete an object.

DELETE /{bucket}/{key}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: CopyObject
docs.text:
Copy an object.

PUT /{bucket}/{key}
x-amz-copy-source: /source-bucket/source-key

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CopyObjectResult>
    <LastModified>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</LastModified>
    <ETag>"d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e"</ETag>
</CopyObjectResult>

docs.title: ListObjectsV2
docs.text:
List objects in a bucket.

GET /{bucket}?list-type=2

Parameters: - prefix: Filter by prefix - delimiter: Group by delimiter - max-keys: Max results (default: 1000) - continuation-token: Pagination token - start-after: Start listing after this key

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListBucketResult>
    <Name>my-bucket</Name>
    <Prefix></Prefix>
    <MaxKeys>1000</MaxKeys>
    <IsTruncated>false</IsTruncated>
    <Contents>
        <Key>file1.txt</Key>
        <LastModified>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</LastModified>
        <ETag>"abc123"</ETag>
        <Size>1024</Size>
        <StorageClass>STANDARD</StorageClass>
    </Contents>
</ListBucketResult>

docs.title: Multipart Upload
docs.text: Multipart upload allows uploading large objects in parts. It is required for objects over 100 MiB: the gateway takes a request body of at most 100 MiB, so a larger single PUT, or a larger part, is refused with 413 (objectio#64).

docs.title: Limits and Behavior
docs.text: Parameter Value Notes Minimum part size 5 MB Except last part Maximum part size 100 MiB S3's is 5 GiB; a larger part gets 413 Maximum single PUT 100 MiB S3's is 5 GiB Maximum parts 10,000 Maximum object size about 976 GiB 10,000 × 100 MiB (S3's is 5 TiB) Default AWS CLI part size 8 MB multipart_chunksize in the CLI's S3 config; keep it at most 100 MiB

docs.title: Multi-Stripe Chunking
docs.text:
ObjectIO uses a 4MB internal block size. When a part exceeds 4MB, it is automatically split into multiple stripes:

8 MB Part Upload:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   8 MB Part Data                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         │
              Split into ~4MB stripes
                         │
         ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
         ▼                               ▼
    ┌─────────┐                     ┌─────────┐
    │ Stripe 0│ (4 MB)              │ Stripe 1│ (4 MB)
    └────┬────┘                     └────┬────┘
         │                               │
    EC Encode (4+2)                 EC Encode (4+2)
         │                               │
    6 shards                        6 shards

Each stripe is independently erasure-coded and distributed across storage nodes.

docs.title: CreateMultipartUpload
docs.text:
Initiate a multipart upload.

POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploads

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<InitiateMultipartUploadResult>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <Key>large-file.zip</Key>
    <UploadId>abc123</UploadId>
</InitiateMultipartUploadResult>

docs.title: UploadPart
docs.text:
Upload a part. Parts can be uploaded in any order and in parallel.

PUT /{bucket}/{key}?partNumber={n}&uploadId={id}

Parameters:

  • partNumber: 1 to 10,000
  • uploadId: From CreateMultipartUpload response

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "part-etag"

Example with curl:

# Upload part 1
curl -X PUT \
  "http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/large-file?partNumber=1&uploadId=abc123" \
  --data-binary @part1.bin

docs.title: CompleteMultipartUpload
docs.text:
Complete the upload by providing the list of parts in order.

POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId={id}

Request Body:

<CompleteMultipartUpload>
    <Part>
        <PartNumber>1</PartNumber>
        <ETag>"part1-etag"</ETag>
    </Part>
    <Part>
        <PartNumber>2</PartNumber>
        <ETag>"part2-etag"</ETag>
    </Part>
</CompleteMultipartUpload>

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<CompleteMultipartUploadResult>
    <Location>http://localhost:9000/my-bucket/large-file</Location>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <Key>large-file</Key>
    <ETag>"abc123-2"</ETag>
</CompleteMultipartUploadResult>

The final ETag format is "<md5-of-part-md5s>-<part-count>".

docs.title: AbortMultipartUpload
docs.text:
Abort an in-progress upload and delete uploaded parts.

DELETE /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId={id}

Response: 204 No Content

docs.title: ListParts
docs.text:
List uploaded parts for an in-progress multipart upload.

GET /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId={id}

Parameters:

  • max-parts: Maximum parts to return (default: 1000)
  • part-number-marker: Start listing after this part number

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListPartsResult>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <Key>large-file</Key>
    <UploadId>abc123</UploadId>
    <MaxParts>1000</MaxParts>
    <IsTruncated>false</IsTruncated>
    <Part>
        <PartNumber>1</PartNumber>
        <LastModified>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</LastModified>
        <ETag>"part1-etag"</ETag>
        <Size>8388608</Size>
    </Part>
</ListPartsResult>

docs.title: ListMultipartUploads
docs.text:
List in-progress multipart uploads for a bucket.

GET /{bucket}?uploads

Parameters:

  • prefix: Filter by key prefix
  • max-uploads: Maximum uploads to return (default: 1000)

Response:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<ListMultipartUploadsResult>
    <Bucket>my-bucket</Bucket>
    <MaxUploads>1000</MaxUploads>
    <IsTruncated>false</IsTruncated>
    <Upload>
        <Key>large-file</Key>
        <UploadId>abc123</UploadId>
        <Initiated>2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z</Initiated>
    </Upload>
</ListMultipartUploadsResult>

docs.title: Example: Upload Large File with AWS CLI
docs.text:
# AWS CLI automatically uses multipart upload for files > 8MB
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp large-file.zip s3://my-bucket/

# Configure part size (minimum 5MB)
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_chunksize 16MB
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp large-file.zip s3://my-bucket/

# Manual multipart upload
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3api create-multipart-upload \
  --bucket my-bucket --key large-file.zip

# Upload parts
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3api upload-part \
  --bucket my-bucket --key large-file.zip \
  --part-number 1 --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID --body part1.bin

# Complete upload
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3api complete-multipart-upload \
  --bucket my-bucket --key large-file.zip \
  --upload-id $UPLOAD_ID \
  --multipart-upload file://parts.json
