docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
PUT    /{bucket}?lifecycle
GET    /{bucket}?lifecycle      → 404 NoSuchLifecycleConfiguration when none
DELETE /{bucket}?lifecycle

<LifecycleConfiguration>
  <Rule>
    <ID>logs</ID>
    <Filter><Prefix>logs/</Prefix></Filter>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <Expiration><Days>30</Days></Expiration>
  </Rule>
  <Rule>
    <ID>old-versions</ID>
    <Filter/>
    <Status>Enabled</Status>
    <NoncurrentVersionExpiration>
      <NoncurrentDays>7</NoncurrentDays>
      <NewerNoncurrentVersions>3</NewerNoncurrentVersions>
    </NoncurrentVersionExpiration>
    <AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload><DaysAfterInitiation>2</DaysAfterInitiation></AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload>
  </Rule>
</LifecycleConfiguration>
action what happens Expiration Days / Date The current version expires. Unversioned: deleted. Versioned or suspended: a delete marker is added, as a DELETE without a version id would — the data stays as a noncurrent version. Expiration ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker A delete marker that is the key's only version is removed. Days does this too in a versioned bucket. A marker with versions behind it is never removed: that would bring the object back. NoncurrentVersionExpiration A noncurrent version is deleted once it has been noncurrent for NoncurrentDays (counted from when the next version was written), keeping the newest NewerNoncurrentVersions noncurrent versions whatever their age. AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload Uploads started more than DaysAfterInitiation days ago are aborted and their parts reclaimed.

Filters: <Prefix>, <Tag>, <ObjectSizeGreaterThan>, <ObjectSizeLessThan>, or several inside <And>; the legacy top-level <Prefix> is accepted. Tag and size filters don't apply to delete markers.

Guarantees. Lifecycle acts through the same delete path as a client, so a version under Object Lock retention or a legal hold is left alone (and counted in objectio_lifecycle_actions_total{action="locked"}), the listing stays right, and space is reclaimed. Every action is an audit event by principal lifecycle:<rule id>.

When. One gateway at a time scans (a lease held in meta); --lifecycle-interval-secs sets how often (default hourly). An object becomes eligible once its age passes the rule's days; it is acted on at the next scan.

Refused: Transition / NoncurrentVersionTransition (InvalidStorageClass — there is one storage class), Days ≤ 0, a Date not at midnight UTC, rules without an action, duplicate IDs, Filter and Prefix together.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
PUT    /{bucket}?cors
GET    /{bucket}?cors      → 404 NoSuchCORSConfiguration when none
DELETE /{bucket}?cors

<CORSConfiguration>
  <CORSRule>
    <ID>web-app</ID>
    <AllowedOrigin>https://app.example.com</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedOrigin>https://*.example.com</AllowedOrigin>
    <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedMethod>PUT</AllowedMethod>
    <AllowedHeader>*</AllowedHeader>
    <ExposeHeader>ETag</ExposeHeader>
    <MaxAgeSeconds>3000</MaxAgeSeconds>
  </CORSRule>
</CORSConfiguration>
  • Preflights (OPTIONS on a bucket or object) are answered without credentials — browsers never sign them — from the configuration alone: the first rule allowing the origin, the method and every requested header. No match (or no configuration): 403 AccessForbidden. A preflight reveals nothing but whether the bucket exists.
  • Actual requests with an Origin that a rule allows get Access-Control-Allow-Origin (the origin itself, with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, unless the rule's origin is exactly *), -Allow-Methods, -Expose-Headers, -Max-Age and Vary: Origin — error responses included, so a browser can read S3's errors. CORS only adds headers: every request is still authenticated and authorized.
  • Up to 100 rules; methods GET PUT POST DELETE HEAD; at most one * in an origin or header pattern.

docs.title: POST Object (browser uploads)
docs.text:
A browser uploads straight into a bucket with an HTML form, signed by your backend — the S3 form-upload API, so boto3's generate_presigned_post and every S3 form library work.

post = s3.generate_presigned_post(
    "uploads", "user-42/${filename}",
    Conditions=[["starts-with", "$key", "user-42/"], ["content-length-range", 1, 10_000_000]],
    ExpiresIn=600)
# hand post["url"] and post["fields"] to the browser's form
  • POST /{bucket} with multipart/form-data; fields key (with ${filename}), policy, x-amz-algorithm (AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 only), x-amz-credential, x-amz-date, x-amz-signature, optional x-amz-security-token, Content-Type, Cache-Control, Content-Disposition, x-amz-meta-*, success_action_status (200, 201, 204), success_action_redirect, and file last.
  • The policy must not have expired, and every form field (except the signature, file, policy and x-ignore-*) must be covered by one of its conditions: exact match, eq, starts-with, content-length-range. The signature and policy are checked before any of the file is read, and the file is read only up to the policy's size limit (and the single-PUT limit, 100 MiB).
  • Authorization is the signer's, exactly as for a PUT: scoped keys, the tenant boundary, policies and Block Public Access all apply. The object is written by the same path a PUT takes (default encryption, Object Lock, versioning, checksums).
  • A form without a signature is anonymous: it needs a bucket policy allowing anonymous s3:PutObject, and public access not blocked.
  • Responses: 204 by default, 200, 201 with a PostResponse document, or 303 to success_action_redirect. Policy violations: 403 AccessDenied ("Invalid according to Policy: …"); a file outside content-length-range: 400 EntityTooLarge / EntityTooSmall.

docs.title: Public Access Block
docs.text:
See Public Access for what the flags do and the tenant- and cluster-wide equivalents.

PUT /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock set the bucket's block (PublicAccessBlockConfiguration XML; absent flags are false) GET /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock the bucket's own block; 404 NoSuchPublicAccessBlockConfiguration if none DELETE /{bucket}?publicAccessBlock remove it (tenant and cluster blocks still apply) GET /{bucket}?policyStatus <PolicyStatus><IsPublic> — whether the bucket policy makes it public

PutBucketPolicy answers 403 AccessDenied for a public policy while BlockPublicPolicy holds at any level.

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text: Buckets are bucket owner enforced. GetBucketAcl / GetObjectAcl answer the owner with FULL_CONTROL; GetBucketOwnershipControls answers BucketOwnerEnforced. An ACL write naming only that is accepted; any other is 400 AccessControlListNotSupported. See ACLs.

docs.title: S3 Select
docs.text:
SelectObjectContent: run SQL over one CSV, JSON or Parquet object and get back only what it selects.

POST /{bucket}/{key}?select&select-type=2

r = s3.select_object_content(
    Bucket="logs", Key="2026/10/app.csv.gz",
    ExpressionType="SQL",
    Expression="SELECT s.ts, s.msg FROM S3Object s WHERE s.level = 'ERROR' LIMIT 100",
    InputSerialization={"CSV": {"FileHeaderInfo": "USE"}, "CompressionType": "GZIP"},
    OutputSerialization={"JSON": {}})
for event in r["Payload"]:
    if "Records" in event:
        print(event["Records"]["Payload"].decode(), end="")
  • Input: CSV (FileHeaderInfo, delimiters, quote and escape, Comments, AllowQuotedRecordDelimiter), JSON (DOCUMENT or LINES), Parquet. CSV and JSON may be GZIP or BZIP2.
  • Output: CSV (delimiters, quoting ASNEEDED/ALWAYS) or JSON.
  • SQL: AWS's subset — SELECT list with aliases, FROM S3Object[*].path alias, WHERE, LIMIT, CAST, string, date and conditional functions, COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX, with AWS's meaning. RGW's additions that AWS would refuse also work (double-quoted strings, INT(x), aliases in WHERE); where RGW gives a valid AWS statement another meaning, ObjectIO follows AWS: in LIKE, [ and ] are themselves (RGW: [a-z] sets), and FROM S3Object[*].arr gives the array as one record (arr[*] reads its elements; RGW reads them in both). See the design.
  • Response: AWS's event stream: Records, Progress when RequestProgress is on, Stats, End; a failure after the stream began is an error event.
  • ScanRange on uncompressed CSV, JSON Lines and Parquet.
  • Permission: s3:GetObject on the key. SSE-C objects need their key headers, as for a GET.
  • Limits: a record or result row at most 1 MB; the expression at most 256 KB. The object is read in ranges, never whole into memory.

docs.title: Not Yet Implemented
docs.text:
A request naming one of these sub-resources is refused with 501 NotImplemented (rather than, say, GET /b?website listing the bucket). Bucket logging (?logging) is supported: see Bucket Logging.

  • Inventory, Analytics, Metrics configuration
  • Website configuration
  • Accelerate configuration, Request Payment
  • SigV2 — refused with 400; use SigV4

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Everything you need to stand up ObjectIO — from a one-binary demo on a laptop to a production Kubernetes install.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Path Walkthrough Best for 🚀 Fastest demo quickstart.md One binary, <60 s to aws s3 ls 🐧 Bare-metal Linux linux.md Production servers, systemd, raw disks 🍏 macOS macos.md Dev laptops (AIO only — not a production target) 🐳 Docker docker.md The container image, CI, single-host appliances ☸ Kubernetes kubernetes.md Helm chart, Kind demo, StatefulSet layout

Platform support: Linux (amd64, arm64), natively and in containers, and macOS for development. Releases publish objectio-aio for Linux amd64 and arm64 and macOS arm64; Intel Macs build from source. ObjectIO is POSIX-only; there is no native Windows build.

docs.title: Deeper references
docs.text:
• hardware-sizing.md — from a capacity and throughput requirement to a bill of quantities, with a calculator.
  • topologies.md — single-node vs rack-aware vs multi-DC; how many disks, nodes, and meta replicas you need for a given EC profile.
  • deployment-options.md — the detailed version: worked scenarios (1, 3, 6+ nodes), EC vs replication, configuration examples, capacity planning.
  • configuration.md — authoritative flag / env / TOML reference for every binary.

docs.title: Minimum requirements
docs.text:
For a production cluster, size from the requirement with Hardware design and sizing and its calculator. To run ObjectIO at all:

Component Minimum Production CPU 2 cores sizing: about one core per drive, plus the gateway's share RAM 4 GB sizing: about 1.5 GB per drive, plus 8 GB Disk 1 × any block device or file NVMe with power-loss protection, one OSD per drive Network 1 Gbps sizing: two ports per host, 25 GbE or faster Linux kernel 4.19+ 5.15+ (io_uring) macOS 12+ — (AIO dev only) Docker 24+ Buildx enabled for multi-arch Kubernetes 1.26+ With a WaitForFirstConsumer StorageClass

docs.title: Cluster sizing at a glance
docs.text:
EC profile Min OSDs Recommended OSDs Meta replicas Survives 4+2 6 7 (+1 spare) 3 2 disk / node failures 8+4 12 14 3 or 5 4 failures LRC 10+2+2 14 15 5 2 failures; more by where they fall; one lost shard repaired from its group replication=3 3 5 3 2 failures (3× overhead)

Meta is a Raft cluster: use 1 pod for dev, 3 for prod, 5 for larger / geo-distributed clusters. Always odd.

docs.title: Default ports (cluster convention)
docs.text:
Port Service Reachable from 9000 Gateway — S3, Iceberg REST, Delta Sharing, /_console/, /_admin/ clients 9100 Meta gRPC + Raft RPC internal 9101 Meta Prometheus /metrics monitoring 9102 Meta admin HTTP (Raft bootstrap / membership) operators 9200 OSD gRPC internal 9201 OSD Prometheus /metrics monitoring 9300 Block gateway gRPC internal 9301 Block gateway Prometheus /metrics monitoring 10809 Block gateway NBD NBD clients

See configuration.md for the code defaults (which differ for meta and OSD) and how to override them.

docs.title: Security checklist (production)
docs.text:
• [ ] TLS terminated in front of the gateway (ingress / LB / reverse-proxy).
  • [ ] Authentication enabled (--no-auth not set).
  • [ ] OIDC configured for the console + Iceberg JWTs, if applicable.
  • [ ] SSE master key present (gateway.sse.enabled: true in Helm).
  • [ ] Firewall / NetworkPolicy restricting 9100/9101/9200/9201 to the internal network, and meta's admin port 9102 (plain HTTP, no authentication: it changes Raft membership) to operators.
  • [ ] Non-root objectio service user with CAP_SYS_RAWIO (not full root) on OSD nodes.
  • [ ] --trusted-proxies set to the ingress / load balancer network if TLS ends there and policies use aws:SecureTransport or aws:SourceIp.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Pick a deployment path above.
  2. Once running, see the Operations tree for monitoring, metrics, and failure recovery.
  3. And Administration for the admin API surface — users, buckets, warehouses, policies.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
ObjectIO binaries are configured with CLI flags, some of which can also be set by an environment variable (shown as [env: …] in each binary's --help). Only objectio-osd reads a TOML file (--config); meta and the gateway take flags only. A flag wins over its environment variable, which wins over the OSD's file, which wins over the built-in default.

This page documents the flag surface for each binary against the current main; <binary> --help is the complete list. Only the env vars listed here are honoured.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Every binary's defaults are the cluster's ports, the ones the Helm chart and these guides use:

Role Port Protocol gateway S3 9000 HTTP meta gRPC (and Raft) 9100 gRPC meta metrics 9101 HTTP meta admin (Raft bootstrap / membership) 9102 HTTP OSD gRPC 9200 gRPC OSD metrics 9201 HTTP block-gateway gRPC 9300 gRPC block-gateway NBD 10809 TCP (NBD)

The clients' defaults follow: the gateway's, the OSD's and the block gateway's --meta-endpoint default to http://localhost:9100. Beyond one host, pass every address. A host running several OSDs gives each its own ports: objectio-install puts OSD i on 9200 + 2i and its metrics on 9201 + 2i.

---|---|---|---| | gateway S3 | 9000 | 9000 | HTTP | | meta gRPC | 9100 | 9001 | gRPC | | meta metrics | 9101 | 9101 | HTTP | | meta admin (Raft bootstrap / membership) | 9102 | 9102 | HTTP | | OSD gRPC | 9200 | none without a config file; 9002 when osd.toml has no listen | gRPC | | OSD metrics | 9201 | 9201 | HTTP | | block-gateway gRPC | 9300 | 9300 | gRPC | | block-gateway NBD | 10809 | 10809 | TCP (NBD) |

The chart's values are what you should document to end users. The code defaults only matter if you run the binaries standalone with no --listen override. The clients' defaults follow the code, not the convention: the gateway's --meta-endpoint defaults to http://localhost:9001, the block gateway's to http://localhost:9100. Pass every address explicitly.

docs.title: objectio-gateway
docs.text: S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing / admin / console.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
objectio-gateway \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100 \
  --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2 \
  --region us-east-1
Flag Default Purpose -l, --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9000 Data plane listen — S3 + Iceberg + Delta Sharing. In single-port mode (no split flags) also serves /_admin/*, /metrics and /_console/*. --admin-listen <addr> empty Optional dedicated listener for /_admin/* + /metrics. Set this and admin moves off --listen entirely (see Listener split). --ops-console-listen <addr> empty Optional dedicated listener for the ops console SPA + /_admin/* (system-admin surface). --tenant-console-listen <addr> empty Optional dedicated listener for the tenant console SPA + /_admin/* (end-user surface). --meta-endpoint <urls> http://localhost:9100 Meta nodes: one address, or every meta node's, comma-separated. Any node serves any call (a follower forwards it to the Raft leader), and one that stops answering is skipped. See Meta high availability. --osd-endpoint <url> http://localhost:9200 Initial OSD peer --ec-k <n> 4 EC data shards --ec-m <n> 2 EC parity shards --protection <kind> ec ec, lrc, or replication --lrc-local-parity <n> 0 LRC local parity count (with --protection=lrc) --lrc-global-parity <n> 0 LRC global parity count --replicas <n> 3 Replica count (with --protection=replication) --no-auth off Disable SigV4 — dev only --prometheus-url <url> empty A Prometheus that scrapes the cluster: the console's long ranges and obioctl metrics query go through it. Without it /_admin/metrics/query answers that none is configured. Env OBJECTIO_PROMETHEUS_URL. --no-reexport-metrics off Leave the OSDs' and meta's metrics out of this gateway's /metrics; set it with more than one gateway (where to scrape). Env OBJECTIO_NO_REEXPORT_METRICS. --no-bucket-metrics off Leave per-bucket objectio_bucket_* series out of /metrics. Env OBJECTIO_NO_BUCKET_METRICS. --inline-max-size <bytes> 4096 Objects up to this size are stored in their metadata record; 0 turns it off --small-shard-max <bytes> 16384 Shards up to this size travel with the object's metadata copies (at most 16384); 0 turns it off --endpoint-name <name> empty Name of the --listen endpoint, seen by policies as aws:SourceVpce (see Public Access). Env OBJECTIO_ENDPOINT_NAME. --data-listen <addr>=<name> — A further data-plane listener (S3, Iceberg, Delta Sharing; no admin, no console) with its own endpoint name. Repeatable. --audit-log <path> unset Append every request's audit event as JSON lines to this file (- for stdout). Env OBJECTIO_AUDIT_LOG. --audit-spool <dir>, --audit-system-bucket <name> unset The audit spool and the system's own audit bucket; the other --audit-* and --bucket-log-* flags are in audit and bucket logging --lifecycle-interval-secs <n> 3600 How often the lifecycle worker scans buckets with rules --pack-interval-secs <n>, --pack-min-age-secs <n> 0 (off), 3600 Small-object packing --heal-interval-secs <n> 10 How often this gateway works its heal queue (0 off) --replication-scan-secs <n> 30 How often the replication scanner looks for unsent versions --trusted-proxies <cidrs> empty Proxies whose X-Forwarded-For / X-Forwarded-Proto are believed for aws:SourceIp / aws:SecureTransport. Env OBJECTIO_TRUSTED_PROXIES. Set it when TLS ends at an ingress. --shutdown-delay-secs <n> 5 On SIGTERM, how long /_ready answers 503 while the gateway still serves, before it stops taking connections. Env OBJECTIO_SHUTDOWN_DELAY_SECS. See how a node stops. --shutdown-drain-secs <n> 20 On shutdown, how long requests in flight are given to finish once the gateway stops taking connections. Env OBJECTIO_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_SECS. --region <name> us-east-1 SigV4 verification region --external-endpoint <url> empty Public URL (Iceberg vended creds, Delta Sharing presign, OIDC callback) --master-key-env <name> OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY Env var name holding the base64 SSE master key --kms-backend <kind> local local or vault --oidc-issuer-url <url> unset Enables OIDC login for console + Iceberg JWTs --oidc-client-id <id> unset OIDC client ID --oidc-client-secret <val> unset OIDC client secret --oidc-audience <val> client id JWT aud expected value --oidc-groups-claim <name> groups Claim mapping to group/role set --oidc-role-claim <name> role Claim mapping to single role --oidc-scopes <scopes> openid profile email Space-separated scope list --oidc-admin-roles <roles> empty Comma-separated list of admin-granting roles --delta-access-key-id <ak> empty Presign AK for Delta Sharing recipient URLs --delta-secret-key <sk> empty Presign SK for Delta Sharing recipient URLs --delta-url-ttl-seconds <n> 0 (3600) Lifetime of Delta Sharing presigned file URLs --host-provider <kind> noop noop (refuses host actions) or k8s — powers /_admin/hosts and /_admin/osds/*/reboot --host-provider-namespace <ns> default Namespace for the k8s provider (from $POD_NAMESPACE) --host-provider-osd-sts <name> objectio-osd OSD StatefulSet name for the k8s provider --topology-region <val> empty Gateway's own topology — drives locality-aware reads --topology-zone <val> empty --topology-datacenter <val> empty --topology-rack <val> empty --topology-host <val> empty --log-level <lvl> info trace, debug, info, warn, error; RUST_LOG, when set, wins --tls-cert, --tls-key, --tls-ca unset mTLS to meta and the OSDs (every binary has these). Env OBJECTIO_TLS_CERT, OBJECTIO_TLS_KEY, OBJECTIO_TLS_CA.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Besides those named in the table above, the clap parser reads these directly:

Env Flag OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_REGION --topology-region OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_ZONE --topology-zone OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_DATACENTER --topology-datacenter OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_RACK --topology-rack OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_HOST --topology-host OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER --host-provider OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER_OSD_STS --host-provider-osd-sts POD_NAMESPACE --host-provider-namespace

Read separately from the flag surface:

Env Purpose OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY 32-byte base64 SSE-S3 master key OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR Directory holding both console bundles, ops/ and tenant/ (default /usr/share/objectio/console): the base for the two below. OBJECTIO_OPS_CONSOLE_DIR Path to the ops SPA bundle. Default: $OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR/ops. Served on --ops-console-listen. OBJECTIO_TENANT_CONSOLE_DIR Path to the tenant SPA bundle. Default: $OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR/tenant. Served on --tenant-console-listen. RUST_LOG Override --log-level; tracing directive syntax

docs.title: Listener split
docs.text:
By default the gateway is a single-port deployment: --listen carries S3, Iceberg, Delta Sharing, /_admin/*, /metrics, and /_console/* all on the same socket. This matches MinIO's default and is fine for small clusters.

For larger or regulated deployments you can split the four planes across separate listeners by setting any combination of --admin-listen, --ops-console-listen, --tenant-console-listen. Each binds independently; you can enable one, two, or all three.

Listener Example Routes mounted Audience data --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 /, /{bucket}*, /iceberg/v1/*, /api/2.1/unity-catalog/*, /delta-sharing/v1/*, /health Public — SDK / CLI / Spark / Trino admin API --admin-listen 127.0.0.1:9001 /_admin/*, /metrics, /health CLI, third-party integrations (Datadog, billing, OTel) ops console --ops-console-listen 127.0.0.1:9002 /_console/* (ops SPA), /_console/api/*, /_admin/*, /health System operators on a mgmt VLAN tenant console --tenant-console-listen 0.0.0.0:9003 /_console/* (tenant SPA), /_console/api/*, /_admin/*, /health End users — safe to expose publicly

Behavior in split mode:

  • /_admin/* is mounted on the admin API listener AND on each console listener (the browser stays same-origin — no CORS). It is removed from the data listener — /_admin/* requests there fall through the S3 wildcard and return SigV4 errors.
  • /metrics lives on the admin API listener only.
  • /_console/* is removed from the data listener; each console listener serves its own SPA bundle from OBJECTIO_OPS_CONSOLE_DIR / OBJECTIO_TENANT_CONSOLE_DIR.
  • The startup log emits a WARN if --admin-listen or --ops-console-listen is bound to 0.0.0.0 — the intent of the split is to firewall the control plane to a mgmt interface.
  • The same /_admin/* handlers run on every listener that mounts them. Per-tenant scope is enforced server-side (see require_tenant_admin_access), so the tenant console listener is not a privilege-elevation path even though it exposes the same surface as the ops console.

Why two consoles, not one with role-gating: see architecture/console-split.

Example — public S3 on the WAN, control plane on a mgmt VLAN:

objectio-gateway \
  --listen                  0.0.0.0:9000 \
  --admin-listen           10.0.5.10:9001 \
  --ops-console-listen     10.0.5.10:9002 \
  --tenant-console-listen   0.0.0.0:9003 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100 \
  --region us-east-1

Omit all three split flags and the gateway serves everything on --listen.

docs.title: objectio-meta
docs.text: Raft metadata cluster.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
objectio-meta \
  --node-id 1 \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9100 \
  --raft-advertise meta1:9100 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/objectio/meta

A meta node starts outside any cluster. The Raft group is formed over the admin port: POST /init on the first node, then on the leader POST /add-learner for each other node ({"node_id": 2, "addr": "meta2:9100"}, the address being the peer's gRPC port, 9100) and POST /change-membership with every voter ({"voters": [1, 2, 3]}). A single node needs only /init. See Linux and meta HA.

Flag Default Purpose --node-id <n> 1 Raft node ID; each node of a group needs its own -l, --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9100 gRPC listen — MetadataService + Raft RPC --peers <list> empty Accepted and not used: membership is set over the admin port --ec-k <n> 4 Default EC data shards --ec-m <n> 2 Default EC parity shards, at least 1. With --ec-k, a profile every loss of m shards decodes (which); meta refuses to start with another, 1+0 too --replication <n> unset Use replication instead of EC: n copies of each object, from 1 (one copy, no redundancy: a one-OSD dev cluster) --data-dir <path> /var/lib/objectio/meta Persistent Raft + redb state --admin-user <name> admin Initial admin username (created on first startup) --metrics-port <n> 9101 Prometheus scrape port (0 none) --admin-port <n> 9102 HTTP admin — Raft bootstrap + membership: /init, /add-learner, /change-membership, /status. Bound on all interfaces, no authentication --raft-advertise <addr> empty Address advertised to Raft peers (defaults to --listen) --repair-interval-secs <n> 3600 Seconds between repair passes (leader); 0 off --drain-interval-secs <n>, --drain-batch <n> 30, 64 Drain sweeps, and shards moved per draining OSD per sweep --raft-snapshot-every <n> 500000 Log entries between snapshots; the log is compacted into each --raft-keep-logs <n> 10000 Entries kept behind the last snapshot --raft-checkpoint-ms <n> 200 How often applied state is made durable --raft-heartbeat-ms <n> 500 Raft heartbeat interval --raft-election-ms <n> 2000 A follower that hears no leader for a random time in [this, 2 × this] stands for election --log-level <lvl> info --tls-cert, --tls-key, --tls-ca unset mTLS

--listen vs --raft-advertise: --listen is what the pod binds to locally; --raft-advertise is what it tells peers to reach it at. In Kubernetes the chart sets advertise to the pod DNS (pod-0.meta-svc.ns.svc.cluster.local).

No --raft-bind flag exists — Raft RPC multiplexes over the same gRPC socket as MetadataService, so a Raft peer address is a node's gRPC port (9100), not its metrics port (9101).

The first Raft leader creates the admin user and every node writes its keys to <data-dir>/admin-creds.env.

docs.title: objectio-osd
docs.text: Object Storage Daemon.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
objectio-osd \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9200 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100 \
  --disks /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc,/dev/sdd
Flag Default Purpose -c, --config <path> /etc/objectio/osd.toml TOML config file, read if it exists; one that doesn't parse stops the OSD -l, --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9200 gRPC listen (the file's listen) --advertise-addr <addr> none How peers reach this OSD (falls back to listen) --disks <list> empty Explicit disk paths (comma-separated); disables discovery --disk-filter <glob> empty Discovery glob(s), e.g. /dev/disk/by-id/wwn-*; repeatable --disk-min-size <bytes> 1 GiB Lower bound for discovered disks --init-blank-disks off Allow discovery to format blank disks (off by default) --meta-endpoint <urls> http://localhost:9100 Meta nodes, comma-separated (the file's meta_endpoint) --data-dir <path> none OSD metadata (WAL, object index); the file's [storage] data_dir, default ./osd-data --metrics-port <n> 9201 Prometheus scrape port (0 none) --scrub-interval-secs <n> 604800 Seconds between scrub passes; 0 off --scrub-rate-mib <n> 50 Scrub read rate cap (MiB/s); 0 unthrottled --full-ratio <r> 0.95 Share of each disk client writes may fill (env OBJECTIO_OSD_FULL_RATIO) --meta-cache-mib <n> 1024 Metadata index page cache (env OBJECTIO_OSD_META_CACHE_MIB) --meta-engine <e> native Metadata index engine: native, or rocksdb in a build with that feature (env OBJECTIO_OSD_META_ENGINE) --log-level <lvl> the file's [logging] level, else info RUST_LOG, when set, wins --tls-cert, --tls-key, --tls-ca unset mTLS

docs.title: TOML
docs.text:
# /etc/objectio/osd.toml
[osd]
listen = "0.0.0.0:9200"
advertise_addr = "http://osd1:9200"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100"

# Only here: no flag sets the failure domain. Unset levels are "default";
# host defaults to the machine's hostname.
[osd.failure_domain]
region = "eu-west-1"
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack1"

[storage]
disks = ["/dev/sdb", "/dev/sdc", "/dev/sdd"]
# block_size: leave unset. A new disk's allocation unit, 4096 by default;
# every shard takes whole blocks, so a larger one wastes space on small
# objects.
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/osd"

[logging]
level = "info"

Disk discovery vs explicit disks. --disks is the production path — list the devices this OSD owns. --disk-filter is for fleets where device names aren't stable (use by-id paths). Without --init-blank-disks, unformatted disks are skipped rather than claimed, as a guard against accidental data loss. A disk named with --disks that can't be claimed (neither blank nor an ObjectIO disk) stops the OSD. The OSD records its disks by the ids in their superblocks: they may be named in any order and under other paths, but an OSD missing one of its disks doesn't start. A disk file that doesn't exist is created only on the OSD's first start; after that, it is a missing disk (runbook).

docs.title: objectio-block-gateway
docs.text:
Block volumes over NBD and gRPC, stored as ObjectIO chunks.

objectio-block-gateway \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9300 \
  --nbd-listen 0.0.0.0:10809 \
  --advertise-host block.internal \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/objectio/block-gw
Flag Default Purpose --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9300 BlockService gRPC listen --nbd-listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:10809 NBD TCP listen --advertise-host <host> empty Hostname used in NBD attachment URLs --meta-endpoint <url> http://localhost:9100 --data-dir <path> ./block-gw-data The write journal (volumes, snapshots and chunk maps are kept in meta) --metrics-listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:9301 Prometheus /metrics; empty serves none --cache-bytes <n> 268435456 Write-cache size (256 MiB) --flush-interval-s <n> 5 Background flush interval --ec-k <n> / --ec-m <n> 4 / 2 EC profile for chunk objects: one with parity that every loss of m shards decodes (which), or the block gateway refuses to start --log-level <lvl> info

docs.title: objectio-aio
docs.text:
Single-process cluster (meta + OSD + gateway). See quickstart.md for the full usage.

Flag Default Purpose --port <n> 9000 Public S3 / Iceberg / Delta / console port --listen-addr <ip> 0.0.0.0 Bind interface --data <dir> tempdir Persistent data root --osds <n> 1 Number of OSDs to spawn in-process --ec-k <n>, --ec-m <n> 0 Erasure-code the pool (needs --osds ≥ k+m); without them it is replication 1, however many OSDs --disk-size <bytes> 0 (10 GiB sparse) Size of each OSD's disk file when created --prometheus-url <url> empty Forwarded to the gateway --external-endpoint <url> empty Forwarded to the gateway --block-port <n> 0 (off) Run the block gateway too (NBD on --nbd-port, 10809) --auth off Enable SigV4 on the gateway (admin AK/SK printed at startup) --admin-port <n> 0 (off) Mirror of objectio-gateway --admin-listen — bind admin API + /metrics to its own port. --ops-console-port <n> 0 (off) Mirror of --ops-console-listen — serve the ops SPA on its own port. --tenant-console-port <n> 0 (off) Mirror of --tenant-console-listen — serve the tenant SPA on its own port. --endpoint-name <name> empty Mirror of the gateway's --endpoint-name, for --port. --data-port <port>=<name> — Mirror of --data-listen on --listen-addr. Repeatable. --trusted-proxies <cidrs> empty Mirror of the gateway's --trusted-proxies. --audit-log <path> unset Mirror of the gateway's --audit-log. --log-level <lvl> info Honoured only if RUST_LOG is unset --strict-port off Fail on --port conflict instead of picking ephemeral

Pass any of --admin-port / --ops-console-port / --tenant-console-port to test split-mode flows locally. The aio binary embeds both SPA bundles (ops + tenant) at compile time, so no separate console build is needed. With --strict-port set, all configured ports are checked for conflicts before launch.

Example — local split-mode test:

objectio-aio \
  --port 9000 \
  --admin-port 9001 \
  --ops-console-port 9002 \
  --tenant-console-port 9003 \
  --auth --strict-port \
  --data /tmp/objectio-aio

Admin AK/SK are written to <data>/meta/admin-creds.env on first start (export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=… and export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=… lines), and printed in the startup banner.

docs.title: objectio-install
docs.text:
Sets a host up to run the services under systemd, and forms meta's Raft group. The Linux guide walks through it.

objectio-install init --role all --node-id 1 --advertise node1.internal \
  --meta-endpoint http://node1.internal:9100,http://node2.internal:9100,http://node3.internal:9100 \
  --disks /dev/disk/by-id/nvme-a,/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-b \
  --ec-profile 4+2 --systemd

objectio-install cluster init node1.internal node2.internal node3.internal

objectio-install disk list [--all]
objectio-install disk check /dev/sdb
objectio-install disk prepare /dev/sdb [--force] [--block-size <bytes>]

objectio-install status

init writes, for the roles it is given:

  • meta: the unit objectio-meta, its data directory /var/lib/objectio/meta;
  • OSD: for each disk i (in the order given), /etc/objectio/osd-<i>.toml, the unit objectio-osd-<i> and the data directory /var/lib/objectio/osd-<i>. One OSD per disk: an OSD holds at most one shard of a stripe;
  • gateway: the unit objectio-gateway, which also reads /etc/objectio/gateway.env when it exists (OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY=… for SSE, the same on every gateway).

The units start meta and the gateway with the flags the Helm chart passes, and each OSD with its file. Meta and the gateway run as the system user objectio, which init creates if it is missing; the OSDs run as root, to open raw devices. init formats no disk: each must be blank, which its OSD formats when it first starts, or an ObjectIO disk; anything else is refused. Run again, it rewrites the files it writes and keeps the data.

init flags:

Flag Default Purpose --role <list> — all, meta, osd, gateway (comma-separated) --disks <list> — The OSDs' disks, one OSD each (osd role) --node-id <n> 1 This host's meta node id; each meta node its own (1, 2, 3 …) --advertise <host> the hostname The name or address the other nodes reach this host at: meta's --raft-advertise, each OSD's advertise_addr --meta-endpoint <urls> this host's meta Every meta node's gRPC address, comma-separated; required on a host without meta --ec-profile <k+m> 4+2 The default pool's erasure code (--ec-k/--ec-m of meta and the gateway) --replication <n> unset n copies instead of an erasure code (--replication of meta, --protection replication --replicas of the gateway) --no-auth off The gateway without authentication (development only) --region <name> us-east-1 The gateway's --region --external-endpoint <url> unset The gateway's --external-endpoint --meta-port, --meta-admin-port, --meta-metrics-port 9100, 9102, 9101 Meta's ports (metrics 0: none) --osd-port, --osd-metrics-port 9200, 9201 OSD i's ports are these + 2i (metrics 0: none) --gateway-port <n> 9000 The gateway's S3 port --systemd off Install the units in /etc/systemd/system (and systemctl daemon-reload); without it, print the services' command lines --bin-dir <dir> /usr/local/bin Where the ObjectIO binaries are --root <dir> / Write everything under this directory instead, naming paths under it: a host's files, staged or tested elsewhere. No user is created and systemd is not reloaded

cluster init <node>… forms the Raft group from meta nodes' admin addresses (host, host:port, port 9102 by default, or a URL), the first being the one the group starts from: /init on it unless a group exists, then, on the leader, /add-learner for every node not yet a voter and /change-membership with all of them. Each node's id and Raft address come from its own /status. Run again, it changes nothing; a voter not named stops it, since dropping one is done by hand (meta HA). It waits up to --wait-secs (120) for every node to answer.

disk prepare formats a disk ahead of its OSD, with the OSD's block size unless --block-size is given; it refuses a disk that isn't blank without --force, which destroys what the disk holds.

docs.title: Configuration precedence
docs.text:
For every setting:

  1. CLI flag
  2. Environment variable (if the flag has one)
  3. The OSD's TOML file (OSD only)
  4. Built-in default

Logging is the exception: RUST_LOG, when set, wins over --log-level (and the file's [logging] level).

The Helm chart passes settings to meta and the gateway as flags in the container's command, and renders osd.toml for each OSD.

docs.title: ObjectIO Deployment Options
docs.text: This guide covers deployment configurations based on your hardware topology, in detail; topologies.md is the overview.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Nodes Disks/Node Recommended Config Efficiency Survives 1 12 EC 4+2 (disk-level) 66% 2 disk failures 3 12 EC 6+3 (node-level) 66% 1 node failure 3 12 Replication 3-way 33% 2 node failures 6+ 6+ LRC 6+2+2 (rack-level) 60% 1 rack + 1 disk 10+ 10+ LRC 10+2+2 (rack-level) 71% 1 rack + 1 disk

docs.title: Failure Domain Hierarchy
docs.text:
Region (geo-redundancy)
└── Datacenter (power/network)
    └── Rack (ToR switch, PDU)
        └── Node (server)
            └── Disk (SSD/HDD)

CRUSH spreads shards across the highest available failure domain to maximize fault tolerance.

docs.title: Topology Configuration
docs.text:
Each OSD reports its failure domain on registration. It is set only in the OSD's /etc/objectio/osd.toml (no flag sets it):

[osd]
listen = "0.0.0.0:9200"
advertise_addr = "http://osd1.internal:9200"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100"

# Failure domain - where this OSD sits in the hierarchy
[osd.failure_domain]
region = "us-east"        # Geographic region
datacenter = "dc1"        # Data center or AZ
rack = "rack-01"          # Physical rack
# host defaults to the machine's hostname

[storage]
disks = ["/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-…"]   # one drive per OSD
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/osd"

How placement uses this:

  1. OSDs register with their failure domain.
  2. A pool names a failure-domain level: host (the default), node (each OSD), rack, datacenter, zone or region.
  3. Each placement group's shards go to distinct domains at that level: one per domain, or, with --spread-domains N --per-domain P, over N domains with at most P in each.
  4. The default pool is made at host level when there are at least k+m hosts, else at node level.

The "Configuration" commands below are obioctl pool create calls (CLI); a bucket goes to a pool with obioctl bucket create <name> --pool <pool> (or the x-objectio-pool header on CreateBucket), fixed for its life.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Single Node (12 Disks)
docs.text:
Hardware: 1 server with 12 disks

Failure Domain: Disk-level only (can't survive node failure)

docs.title: Option 1B: EC 8+4 (Maximum Fault Tolerance)
docs.text:
Configuration (one OSD per drive):
  obioctl pool create p84 --ec-type 0 --ec-k 8 --ec-m 4 --failure-domain node
Metric Value Storage efficiency 66% (8/12) Fault tolerance 4 disk failures Min disks 12 Read performance Parallel from 8 disks Repair cost Read 8 shards, write 1

docs.title: Option 1C: Replication 3-way (Simple, Lower Efficiency)
docs.text:
Configuration (one OSD per drive):
  obioctl pool create r3 --ec-type 2 --replication-count 3 --failure-domain node
Metric Value Storage efficiency 33% (1/3) Fault tolerance 2 disk failures Min disks 3 Read performance Single disk (can load-balance) Repair cost Read 1, write 1

When to use replication: - Small objects (< 1MB) where EC overhead dominates - Random read workloads where single-disk latency matters - Simplest operational model

docs.title: Scenario 2: Three Nodes (12 Disks Each)
docs.text:
Hardware: 3 servers, each with 12 disks (36 total disks)

Failure Domain Options: - Node-level: Survive 1 complete node failure - Disk-level: Survive multiple disk failures across nodes

docs.title: Option 2A: EC 6+3 Node-Level (Recommended)
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Node 0 (12 disks)    │   Node 1 (12 disks)    │   Node 2 (12 disks)  │
│  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐    │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐    │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐  │
│  │ D0 ││ D1 ││ D2 │    │  │ D3 ││ D4 ││ D5 │    │  │ P0 ││ P1 ││ P2 │  │
│  └────┘└────┘└────┘    │  └────┘└────┘└────┘    │  └────┘└────┘└────┘  │
│                        │                        │                      │
│  Each node gets 3      │  Each node gets 3      │  Each node gets 3    │
│  shards per object     │  shards per object     │  shards per object   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration (3 shards on each of 3 hosts):
  obioctl pool create p63 --ec-type 0 --ec-k 6 --ec-m 3 \
    --failure-domain host --spread-domains 3 --per-domain 3
Metric Value Storage efficiency 66% (6/9) Fault tolerance 1 node OR 3 disks Min nodes 3 Shards per node 3 Read performance Parallel from 2+ nodes Repair cost Read 6 shards (cross-node)

Math: With 3 nodes and k=6, m=3: - 9 shards ÷ 3 nodes = 3 shards per node - Node failure loses 3 shards = exactly m - Can reconstruct from remaining 6 shards ✓

docs.title: Option 2B: EC 4+2 Node-Level (Fewer Shards)
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Node 0 (12 disks)    │   Node 1 (12 disks)    │   Node 2 (12 disks)  │
│  ┌────┐┌────┐          │  ┌────┐┌────┐          │  ┌────┐┌────┐        │
│  │ D0 ││ D1 │          │  │ D2 ││ D3 │          │  │ P0 ││ P1 │        │
│  └────┘└────┘          │  └────┘└────┘          │  └────┘└────┘        │
│                        │                        │                      │
│  2 shards per node     │  2 shards per node     │  2 shards per node   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration (2 shards on each of 3 hosts):
  obioctl pool create p42 --ec-type 0 --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2 \
    --failure-domain host --spread-domains 3 --per-domain 2
Metric Value Storage efficiency 66% (4/6) Fault tolerance 1 node OR 2 disks Min nodes 3 Shards per node 2

docs.title: Option 2C: Replication 3-way (Maximum Availability)
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Node 0               │   Node 1               │   Node 2              │
│  ┌────────────────┐    │  ┌────────────────┐    │  ┌────────────────┐   │
│  │   Full Copy    │    │  │   Full Copy    │    │  │   Full Copy    │   │
│  │   (Primary)    │    │  │   (Replica 1)  │    │  │   (Replica 2)  │   │
│  └────────────────┘    │  └────────────────┘    │  └────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration:
  obioctl pool create r3 --ec-type 2 --replication-count 3 --failure-domain host
Metric Value Storage efficiency 33% (1/3) Fault tolerance 2 node failures Read performance Any single node (load-balance) Write performance Must write to all 3 nodes

Use replication when: - Data durability is paramount (financial, medical) - Random read latency is critical - Simple operational model preferred over efficiency

docs.title: Scenario 3: Six+ Nodes (Multi-Rack with LRC)
docs.text:
Hardware: 6+ servers across multiple racks

Failure Domain: Rack-level: each local group in a rack of its own, so a lost shard is repaired inside its rack (a whole rack lost is not survived: see below)

docs.title: Option 3A: LRC 6+2+2 (Recommended for 6+ Nodes)
docs.text:
LRC (Locally Repairable Codes) adds local parity within groups for faster single-failure repair.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              LRC 6+2+2                                   │
│                                                                         │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │        Local Group 0         │  │        Local Group 1         │     │
│  │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐   │  │  ┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐┌────┐   │     │
│  │  │ D0 ││ D1 ││ D2 ││ LP0│   │  │  │ D3 ││ D4 ││ D5 ││ LP1│   │     │
│  │  │Rk0 ││Rk0 ││Rk0 ││Rk0 │   │  │  │Rk1 ││Rk1 ││Rk1 ││Rk1 │   │     │
│  │  └────┘└────┘└────┘└────┘   │  │  └────┘└────┘└────┘└────┘   │     │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                         │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│  │       Global Parity          │                                       │
│  │  ┌────┐┌────┐               │                                       │
│  │  │GP0 ││GP1 │               │  GP = Reed-Solomon over all data      │
│  │  │Rk2 ││Rk2 │               │                                       │
│  │  └────┘└────┘               │                                       │
│  └──────────────────────────────┘                                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuration (each local group in a rack of its own):
  obioctl pool create lrc622 --ec-type 1 --ec-k 6 \
    --ec-local-parity 2 --ec-global-parity 2 \
    --failure-domain rack --lrc-groups-per-domain
  # local group size = k / local parity = 3
Metric Value Storage efficiency 60% (6/10) Total shards 10 (6 data + 2 LP + 2 GP) Fault tolerance Any 2 disks; most losses of 3 (what LRC survives). Not a rack holding a whole group (below) Local repair Read 3 shards (within rack) Global repair Read 6 shards (cross-rack)

LRC Repair Scenarios:

Failure Type Repair Method Network Cost 1 data disk XOR with local parity Read 3 (local) 1 local parity disk XOR with data shards Read 3 (local) 2 disks same group Reed-Solomon global Read 6 (cross-rack) 1 disk + 1 LP (diff) Local + Local Read 6 (2×3 local) Full rack failure Not survived with a group per rack: 3 data shards and the group's local parity lost, more than the 2 global parity rebuild —

docs.title: Option 3B: LRC 10+2+2 (Higher Efficiency)
docs.text:
Configuration:
  obioctl pool create lrc1022 --ec-type 1 --ec-k 10 \
    --ec-local-parity 2 --ec-global-parity 2 \
    --failure-domain rack --lrc-groups-per-domain
Metric Value Storage efficiency 71% (10/14) Total shards 14 (10 data + 2 LP + 2 GP) Min racks 4 (5+1 per local group + GP) Local repair Read 5 shards (within rack)

A pool keeps its losses decodable by the global parity: with each local group in a rack of its own, a rack's loss is survived only when a group has no more data shards than the global parity (meta warns when a pool's rule doesn't survive a whole domain lost). Neither 6+2+2 nor 10+2+2 does; for rack loss, spread an MDS profile over the racks. An LRC that keeps a rack's loss inside the rack is objectio#37.

docs.title: OSDs
docs.text:
Each OSD's osd.toml names its drive and its failure domain; OSDs on one host share a host name (the hostname, by default), and set rack (and datacenter) where a pool spreads over those:

# /etc/objectio/osd.toml (one per OSD; one OSD per drive)
[osd]
listen = "0.0.0.0:9200"
advertise_addr = "http://node1.internal:9200"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100"

[osd.failure_domain]
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack-01"        # a different rack per node, for a rack pool

[storage]
disks = ["/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-…"]
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/osd-0"

Several OSDs on one host each need their own port, data_dir and drive.

docs.title: Pools
docs.text: The default pool's code is meta's --ec-k/--ec-m (or --replication), spread over hosts. Any other layout above is a pool of its own, made with obioctl pool create as shown in each scenario, and buckets are put in it when they are created. The gateway's own --ec-k/--ec-m don't choose where a bucket's data goes.

docs.title: Usable Capacity Formula
docs.text:
Usable = Raw × (k / (k + m))        # For MDS
Usable = Raw × (k / (k + l + g))    # For LRC

docs.title: Example: 3 Nodes × 12 Disks × 10TB
docs.text: Config Raw Capacity Efficiency Usable Capacity Replication 3 360 TB 33% 120 TB EC 4+2 360 TB 66% 240 TB EC 6+3 360 TB 66% 240 TB LRC 6+2+2 360 TB 60% 216 TB

docs.title: IOPS Considerations
docs.text: Config Read IOPS (per object) Write IOPS (per object) Replication 3 1 disk (can load-balance) 3 disks (all replicas) EC 4+2 4 disks (parallel) 6 disks (parallel) EC 6+3 6 disks (parallel) 9 disks (parallel) LRC 6+2+2 6 disks (parallel) 10 disks (parallel)

docs.title: Starting Small, Growing Large
docs.text:
Phase 1: Single node, 6 disks
  └── EC 4+2 (disk-level)
         │
         ▼
Phase 2: 3 nodes, 12 disks each
  └── EC 6+3 (node-level)
         │
         ▼
Phase 3: 6+ nodes across racks
  └── LRC 6+2+2 (rack-level)

Growing: a pool's code and its number of placement groups are fixed when it is made. OSDs added to a pool's failure domains take a share of its placement groups as the balancer and recovery move them. To move to a wider code (4+2 to 6+3, or to LRC), make a new pool and put new buckets in it; existing buckets stay in their pool. Copy a bucket across with any S3 tool if it must move.

docs.title: Summary Recommendations
docs.text: Deployment Size Recommended Config Why Dev/Test Single node, EC 4+2 Simple, efficient, survives disk failures Small Prod 3 nodes, EC 6+3 Survives node failure, good efficiency Medium Prod 6 nodes, LRC 6+2+2 Fast local repair, rack-level tolerance Large Prod 10+ nodes, LRC 10+2+2 Best efficiency (71%), scalable Critical 3-way replication Maximum durability, simple operations

docs.text:
