docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
ObjectIO ships one multi-stage Dockerfile. Its all target is the image that is published and that the Helm chart runs; per-service targets can be built locally.

  • Fastest demo: the objectio-aio binary (it is not in the image)
  • Kubernetes: see kubernetes.md (make kind-up for a local kind cluster)

There is no Compose file for running a cluster: the repository's docker-compose.yml holds development tools (build, test, lint), and deploy/monitoring/ a Prometheus and Grafana.

docs.title: Image targets
docs.text:
Target Binary Ports Role gateway objectio-gateway 9000 S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing / /_console/ meta objectio-meta 9100 (gRPC and Raft), 9101 (metrics), 9102 (admin) Raft metadata osd objectio-osd 9200 (gRPC), 9201 (metrics) Object storage daemon cli obioctl — Admin CLI block-gateway objectio-block-gateway 9300 (gRPC), 10809 (NBD) Block volumes over NBD and gRPC all gateway, meta, osd, obioctl, objectio-install, block-gateway, and the console 9000 + internal One image, any service

Port numbers are the cluster's, used by the Helm chart and every binary's defaults (ports).

One multi-arch image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) is published on GHCR, and it carries every service:

  • ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:<tag> (for example v0.1.0-rc.1), also tagged latest — the all target

It has no entrypoint: name the binary to run, as the Helm chart does. The per-service targets (gateway, meta, osd, cli, block-gateway) are not published; build them locally if you want them. Their default commands pass flags the binaries don't have (--bind, --raft-bind), so always give the arguments yourself:

docker build --target gateway -t objectio-gateway .

Both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 erasure-code with ISA-L and write the same stripes, so a cluster may mix them.

docs.title: The published image
docs.text:
The all target packages the service binaries plus the console SPA. You choose the binary at docker run time:

# The admin CLI against an existing cluster
docker run --rm --network host \
  -e OBJECTIO_ACCESS_KEY -e OBJECTIO_SECRET_KEY \
  ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:v0.1.0-rc.1 \
  obioctl --endpoint http://localhost:9000 user list

# A service: the flags are the binary's own (see configuration.md)
docker run --rm ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:v0.1.0-rc.1 objectio-gateway --help

The image runs as the non-root user objectio, declares /var/lib/objectio as a volume, and has no curl.

docs.title: Running the services in containers
docs.text:
Without Kubernetes, run each service from the image with the flags in Linux: meta with --node-id, --raft-advertise and its data directory on a volume, then the Raft bootstrap calls to its admin port; OSDs with an osd.toml mounted at /etc/objectio/osd.toml; gateways with every meta node's address in --meta-endpoint.

An OSD on raw block devices needs them passed as devices: and the capability to open them with O_DIRECT:

services:
  osd1:
    image: ghcr.io/object-io/objectio:v0.1.0-rc.1
    command: ["objectio-osd", "--config", "/etc/objectio/osd.toml"]
    cap_add: [SYS_RAWIO]
    devices: [/dev/nvme1n1:/dev/nvme1n1]
    volumes:
      - ./osd1.toml:/etc/objectio/osd.toml:ro
      - osd1-state:/var/lib/objectio/osd

docs.title: Building images locally
docs.text:
# Single-arch, native platform
make docker                 # gateway, meta, osd, cli and all
make docker-gateway         # just the gateway
make docker-all             # the published image's target

# Multi-arch (requires docker buildx, pushes to registry)
DOCKER_REGISTRY=ghcr.io/myorg/ DOCKER_TAG=v1.0.0 \
  make docker-multiarch

# Multi-arch local-only (current platform, loads into Docker)
make docker-multiarch-local

Build args exposed by the Dockerfile:

Arg Default Notes RUST_VERSION 1.94 Rust compiler in the builder-base stage (matches rust-toolchain.toml) FEATURES io-uring Cargo features to build with. ISA-L erasure coding is not one: every build has it. TARGETPLATFORM / TARGETARCH from buildx Set automatically by docker buildx

docs.title: Environment variables (containerised services)
docs.text:
Most configuration goes via CLI flags in the container's command. A set of settings is also reachable via env vars (the full list is in configuration.md):

Env var Service Purpose OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_REGION gateway Sets --topology-region OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_ZONE gateway Sets --topology-zone OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_DATACENTER gateway Sets --topology-datacenter OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_RACK gateway Sets --topology-rack OBJECTIO_TOPOLOGY_HOST gateway Sets --topology-host OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER gateway Sets --host-provider (noop | k8s) OBJECTIO_HOST_PROVIDER_OSD_STS gateway OSD StatefulSet name (k8s provider only) POD_NAMESPACE gateway Namespace for host-provider RBAC (k8s only) OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY gateway SSE-S3 master key (base64 32-byte) OBJECTIO_CONSOLE_DIR gateway Override the /_console/ static-asset dir OBJECTIO_TLS_CERT, OBJECTIO_TLS_KEY, OBJECTIO_TLS_CA all mTLS between services RUST_LOG all Overrides --log-level; same syntax as tracing

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
• Gateway: GET /health answers 200 while the process is up; GET /_ready answers 200 once meta and enough OSDs answer (monitoring).
  • Meta and OSDs: GET /health on their metrics ports (9101, 9201).

The all image declares no HEALTHCHECK: use these in your orchestrator. The per-service targets declare one, but the gateway's calls curl, which the image lacks, and the others always succeed.

docs.title: "operation not permitted" on an OSD
docs.text: OSDs need CAP_SYS_RAWIO to open raw block devices with O_DIRECT (cap_add: [SYS_RAWIO], or privileged: true).

docs.title: "falling back to pread" in an OSD's log
docs.text: The image does its disk I/O through io_uring, and docker's default seccomp profile denies the io_uring system calls. The OSD (or aio) then logs storage error: io_uring setup for <device>: Operation not permitted (os error 1); falling back to pread for each device and serves with pread: correct, but slower. A privileged: true container, or a seccomp profile that allows io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter and io_uring_register (--security-opt seccomp=<file>), gets io_uring.

docs.title: Gateway can't reach meta
docs.text: Gateways and OSDs take every meta node's address in one comma-separated --meta-endpoint (for example http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100); any one that answers serves them. Check that the names resolve inside the containers' network and that each meta node's --raft-advertise is an address the others can reach, not 0.0.0.0.

docs.title: Hardware design and sizing
docs.text:
How to go from a requirement (so many terabytes, so many GB/s) to a bill of quantities: how many hosts, which drives, how much CPU, memory and network, and where meta and the gateways run. The calculator at the end does the arithmetic; the sections before it say where each number comes from.

ObjectIO is an early release (0.x) and its multi-host performance numbers are still being measured. Each figure here says whether it was measured (and where) or is an estimate. Size from the estimates with headroom, and check them on your own hardware before you buy at scale.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Work through these in order; each one can only raise the count the previous one gave.

  1. Protection. Choose the erasure code: 4+2 for 7 to 12 hosts, 8+4 from 13. It sets the overhead (1.5× raw for both) and the minimum number of hosts: one per shard plus one to rebuild onto (7 for 4+2, 13 for 8+4).
  2. Capacity. Usable terabytes, with the headroom you want, gives raw terabytes, then drives and hosts.
  3. Throughput. GB/s of writes and of reads gives the drives and hosts the bytes need, and the network every host needs.
  4. Objects. The average object size gives the object count, which sizes the metadata: meta's disks and each drive's metadata partition.
  5. CPU and memory. From drives per host, and from the GB/s the gateways carry.
  6. Placement of services. Meta and the gateways on the storage hosts (converged), or on their own servers.

docs.title: Protection and hosts
docs.text:
Code Raw per usable byte Survives Hosts at least 4+2 1.5 any 2 hosts 7 8+4 1.5 any 4 hosts 13 10+4 1.4 any 4 hosts 15

Placement puts each shard of a stripe on a different host. With fewer hosts than shards it would put two on one host, and losing that host would lose both: the minimum is one host per shard, plus one so a lost host can be rebuilt onto the others.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text:
usable = raw × k/(k+m) × 0.95 − one host's worth
  • 0.95: an OSD refuses client writes past 95% of its drive (--full-ratio) and keeps the rest for repair, drain and backfill.
  • One host's worth: when a host is lost for good, its shards are rebuilt onto the others; keep that much free.
  • Add your own headroom on top: growth, and the "near full" alert at 85%.

Objects of 4 KiB or less are kept whole inside their metadata, on all k + m copies (--inline-max-size): they take metadata space (below), not data space. Small objects in general are packed into shared stripes in the background, so a million 8 KiB objects don't each take a stripe.

docs.title: Drives
docs.text:
• Power-loss protection (PLP). An acknowledgement means the data is on stable storage: every shard and its location are flushed before the client hears back. On a drive without PLP a flush is slow (it empties a volatile cache) and a power cut can still lose what the cache held. Use enterprise NVMe with PLP; otherwise a UPS for every host.
  • One OSD per drive. The shards go on the raw device; the OSD's metadata (its write-ahead log and index) goes on a small partition of the same drive, not the boot disk (see Objects and metadata for its size).
  • Boot: two small drives (M.2, mirrored) for the OS.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
What a write costs, with a k+m code:

Per GB/s of client writes Per GB/s of client reads Bytes written to drives (k+m)/k GB/s (1.5 for 4+2) — Bytes read from drives — 1 GB/s (k shards of the object) Gateway → OSD network (k+m)/k GB/s 1 GB/s (OSD → gateway) Client ↔ gateway network 1 GB/s 1 GB/s

How much one drive sustains under ObjectIO is not yet measured on enterprise NVMe. The calculator assumes 1 GB/s of writes and 2 GB/s of reads per drive, a fraction of what a PCIe 4 drive is rated for; change it to what you measure.

Small objects are bound by operations, not bytes. Measured on one lab host (consumer NVMe without PLP, everything on one machine, 4+2, 32 clients): 1,150–1,300 PUTs/s and 25,900–27,000 GETs/s of 4 KiB objects, 990–1,100 PUTs/s and 17,600–18,200 GETs/s of 64 KiB; the performance page has the details. A drive with PLP makes each flush much cheaper. Treat small- object rates as something to measure on your hardware.

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
Measured per core on an AMD Ryzen 9 7945HX (Zen 4), 4 MiB stripes:

Work GB/s per core Erasure coding, ISA-L, 4+2: encode / decode with 2 shards lost 9.9 / 11.3 Erasure coding, ISA-L, 8+4 8.8 / 9.3 MD5 (every PUT's ETag) 0.80 SHA-256 (clients that sign the payload; CPU with SHA extensions) 2.4 CRC32C (every shard, written and read) 8.4

On arm64 erasure coding is ISA-L's too. One Apple M-series core, in a Linux VM, 4 MiB shards: 4+2 encodes at 23.8 GB/s and decodes with 2 shards lost at 15.6 GB/s; 8+3 at 16.2 and 4.4. A server arm64 core (Graviton, Ampere) is not yet measured.

What a gateway spends per GB/s:

Writes Reads MD5 for the ETag 1.25 cores — SHA-256, if clients sign the payload (most SDKs over HTTPS don't) 0.4 — Erasure coding and checksums 0.3 0.15 Network stack and HTTP (estimate) 1–2 without offload; about 0.3 with TSO/GRO offload or RDMA 1 without; about 0.2 with Total about 3 without offload, 1.6 with about 1.2 without, 0.35 with

The MD5 is computed in the gateway over every byte written, and no NIC can take it: it sets the floor. Offloads take the network stack, and the shard traffic can go over RDMA (behind a flag today). mTLS between services costs about 0.35 cores per GB/s of shard traffic (AES-GCM, estimate).

An OSD's own work is light (checksums, I/O submission, RPC): plan about one core per NVMe drive (estimate), plus a few for the OS.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Plan OSD 1.5 GB per drive: its metadata index cache (--meta-cache-mib, 1 GiB by default), memtables, buffers. Flat however many objects it holds Gateway 4 GB, plus 2 GB per GB/s it carries (buffers for objects in flight) Meta 16 GB; 32 GB above 500 million objects (its database cache) OS 8 GB per host

Measured on the soak cluster (6 hosts, 69,000 objects, before the caches filled): OSD 164 MB, gateway 100 MB, meta 91 MB resident.

docs.title: Objects and metadata
docs.text:
The object count (usable bytes ÷ average object size) sizes the metadata. Measured on the soak cluster:

Where Per object Meta's database, on every meta node about 750 bytes (its listing entry and the rest) An OSD's metadata index, on every OSD holding a copy (k + m of them) about 1.5 KB (the object's metadata copy and its shard's location)

Meta also keeps its Raft log and one snapshot of the database beside it: plan 2.2 × the database on each meta node's disk.

Each drive's metadata partition must hold its share of copies:

index per drive ≈ objects × (k+m) ÷ drives × 1.5 KB

An object whose shards are 16 KiB or less (64 KiB or less with 4+2) keeps them in the index too: add the object's size ÷ k to each copy's 1.5 KB (from format level 8; before it, a shard just past a power of two, such as a 64 KiB object's 16 KiB with 4+2, took twice its size there). At a 1 MiB average object the index is under 1% of the drive; at 64 KiB, where the shards live there, the whole drive's worth of data is in the partition. The calculator gives the partition size.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• Two ports per host, bonded or one per switch, to two top-of-rack switches: losing a switch or a cable must not take a host away.
  • Size for repair too. Rebuilding a lost host moves its whole contents across the network; the calculator doubles the client traffic to leave room for it.
  • Client-facing TLS terminates at the load balancer (or an ingress); between services, mTLS.

docs.title: Drive failures, replacement and hot spares
docs.text:
A failed drive's data is rebuilt at once, onto the free space of every other drive in the cluster: many drives write in parallel, so it takes minutes to hours where rebuilding onto one spare disk, as a RAID array does, is held to one drive's write rate. Replacing the drive afterwards only gives its capacity back. So how fast a vendor replaces drives decides how long capacity is down, not how long data is at risk, as long as there is free space to rebuild into.

  • Spare space, not idle disks. The calculator holds one host's worth of drives free for rebuilds. With the drives' failure rate and the time to replace one (on-site spares, next business day, an OEM's five days), it works out how many drives may be failed and not yet replaced at once (99.9%) and says when that is more than the space held: add hosts or drives, keep hot spares, or shorten the replacement time.
  • Hot spares (drives installed but not in use) make sense where replacement is slow: a remote site, an OEM contract measured in days. One is put in service in minutes, with no site visit, and the capacity is back; restock them at least as fast as drives fail. They don't make data safer: the rebuild has already happened on the other drives.
  • Rebuild times in the calculator are what the drives and the network allow with 30% of them given to repair: a bound. Today's repair is slower than that; raising it is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Where meta and the gateways run
docs.text:
• Meta: three nodes (five to survive two at once), each on its own host, on NVMe with PLP. Up to a few hundred million objects they can share three of the storage hosts; past that, give them servers of their own.
  • Meta gets a drive of its own (not an OSD's drive, not the boot disk), even on a shared host. Every PUT waits for meta's commit, and an OSD's metadata checkpoint writes its index in bursts that hold back other syncs on the same drive. Measured with meta and six OSDs on one NVMe: meta's checkpoints took 0.25–1 s whenever an OSD checkpointed, and every PUT in flight waited (64 KiB PUTs: p99 up to 580 ms against a 38 ms median). With meta on its own drive, none took 0.1 s. A small drive does: meta needs 2.2 × its database (above).
  • Gateways: stateless, behind an L4 load balancer. Converged (one on every storage host) spreads the CPU and network evenly and needs no extra servers; dedicated gateway servers make sense when the storage hosts are small or the GB/s are high.

docs.title: Calculator
docs.text:
Fill in the requirement; the bill of quantities updates as you type. It runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere.

The calculator needs JavaScript.

docs.title: What isn't in the calculator yet
docs.text:
• Repair time as measured. The calculator gives what the hardware allows; repair's own throughput is being raised to meet it (on the roadmap).
  • Small-object operation rates. See Throughput: measure them on your hardware.
  • Multi-site. Replication between clusters doubles the hardware, one cluster per site, plus the link between them.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
ObjectIO's Helm chart (deploy/helm/objectio/ in the source repo, published with each release as oci://ghcr.io/object-io/charts/objectio) installs every component as one release: the gateway (Deployment), meta (StatefulSet with a Raft bootstrap Job), the OSDs (StatefulSet with per-pod volumes), and optionally the block gateway and a Prometheus + Grafana stack.

Its defaults are for production: 4+2 erasure coding over 6 OSDs, 3 metas, 2 gateways, authentication on. A laptop or CI cluster sets its own convenient values (the kind walkthrough does).

Audience Start here Trying it on a laptop Kind walkthrough Production install Install the chart, then a production deployment Tuning an existing release Values reference

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Kubernetes 1.26+ (kubeVersion in Chart.yaml), Helm 3.
  • As many schedulable nodes as failure domains you want: the default 6 OSDs, one per node, survive two nodes lost at once.
  • A StorageClass with ReadWriteOnce volumes, ideally with WaitForFirstConsumer binding (so an OSD schedules on a node whose disk it can bind to); for raw block devices, one that supports volumeMode: Block. Local-path provisioners are for testing only.
  • For ingress: an ingress controller or a Gateway API implementation.
  • RBAC: the chart creates a ServiceAccount and Role for the gateway's host-lifecycle provider, and a ClusterRole reading nodes when OSDs take their failure domains from node labels.

No external dependencies (etcd, ZooKeeper, Redis): meta is a self-contained Raft cluster.

docs.title: Installing the chart
docs.text:
helm install objectio oci://ghcr.io/object-io/charts/objectio \
  --version 0.1.0 \
  --namespace objectio --create-namespace \
  --values my-values.yaml \
  --wait --timeout 15m

The chart's version pins the image to the same release. From a source checkout, use ./deploy/helm/objectio instead of the OCI reference.

--wait returns once every pod is ready (under a minute on a small cluster). The Raft bootstrap Job is created with the rest of the release, not as a post-install hook, so meta and the gateways become ready while Helm waits. A gateway that starts before meta is ready exits and is restarted, so on a first install the gateways show a restart or two.

Check it came up:

kubectl -n objectio get pods
# NAME                              READY   STATUS
# objectio-gateway-<hash>           1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-0                   1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-1                   1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-2                   1/1     Running
# objectio-meta-raft-bootstrap-1-…  0/1     Completed
# objectio-osd-0 … objectio-osd-5   1/1     Running

Workloads are named <release>-objectio-<component>, or <release>-<component> when the release name contains objectio (as above).

The first admin's access key is written by meta, on first boot, to /var/lib/objectio/meta/admin-creds.env in every meta pod (the secret never goes to the logs):

kubectl -n objectio exec objectio-meta-0 -- cat /var/lib/objectio/meta/admin-creds.env
# export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA…
# export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=…

Expose the gateway however your cluster does it (an ingress, type: LoadBalancer), or for a first look:

kubectl -n objectio port-forward svc/objectio-gateway 9000:9000 &
eval "$(kubectl -n objectio exec objectio-meta-0 -- cat /var/lib/objectio/meta/admin-creds.env)"
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 ls

docs.title: What the defaults protect
docs.text:
Default Erasure coding replication: 0, ec.k: 4, ec.m: 2 The default pool survives any two OSDs lost at once OSDs osd.replicas: 6 The chart refuses to render with fewer than ec.k + ec.m (or than replication copies) Meta meta.replicas: 3 Survives one meta pod lost Authentication gateway.noAuth: false Every request is signed (SigV4) or carries an OIDC/STS token Disruption budgets gateway minAvailable: 1; meta and OSD maxUnavailable: 1 A node drain takes one meta and one OSD at a time Grafana (when enabled) a random admin password, in a Secret No well-known password

The chart refuses ec.m: 0: one unprotected copy of each object, for a one-OSD development cluster, is replication: 1, and its notes warn that one lost OSD then loses data. replication: 2 or 3 keeps that many copies instead of erasure coding.

docs.title: A production deployment
docs.text: deploy/helm/objectio/examples/production.yaml is a complete example: gateways behind an ingress, metas and OSDs spread over nodes and zones, OSDs on dedicated storage nodes with raw block volumes and their zone and rack read from node labels, an existing SSE key, NetworkPolicies, mTLS between the services, and the alert rules for a prometheus-operator. Copy it and change what it marks.

docs.title: Where pods run
docs.text:
gateway, meta, osd and blockGateway each take nodeSelector, affinity, tolerations, topologySpreadConstraints, priorityClassName and podAnnotations, as in a pod spec. A spread constraint without a labelSelector gets the component's own pods' labels, so this is enough for one OSD per storage node:

osd:
  nodeSelector:
    objectio.io/storage: "true"
  tolerations:
    - { key: objectio.io/storage, operator: Equal, value: "true", effect: NoSchedule }
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule

global.imagePullSecrets goes to every pod.

docs.title: Failure domains
docs.text:
Placement never puts two shards of a stripe in one failure domain at the level its pool spreads over (topologies). Each OSD registers where it sits:

  • host is always the Kubernetes node the pod runs on, so OSDs on one machine share a host.
  • region, zone, datacenter, rack are the fixed values under osd.failureDomain, the same for every OSD, unless nodeLabels names a node label to read a level from, per pod:
osd:
  failureDomain:
    region: eu-west-1
    datacenter: dc1
    nodeLabels:
      zone: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      rack: topology.objectio.io/rack     # label your nodes with their rack

An init container reads the labels of the pod's node through the API server (the chart creates a ClusterRole allowing get on nodes, and only that container holds the token) and writes them into the OSD's configuration. An OSD on a node without a label it is told to read does not start: its node-topology init container fails, naming the node and the label, rather than place the OSD in a wrong failure domain.

docs.title: OSD storage
docs.text:
Each OSD pod has two volumes: data, its disk, and state, a small volume for its metadata index. osd.persistence.data.volumeMode picks what the disk is:

volumeMode The OSD's disk Filesystem (default) A file, storage.diskFile, on the volume; the OSD creates it on its first start Block The volume itself, a raw block device (local disks through a local-volume provisioner, a SAN), written directly with no filesystem in between

A blank device is formatted on the OSD's first start; a device that carries anything else (a filesystem, another cluster's disk) is refused, and the OSD doesn't start. With a filesystem volume, an OSD whose state volume has run before and whose disk file is missing doesn't start (a disk gone): to replace a data volume, see replacing a disk.

The data volumes' size is the cluster's capacity (hardware sizing).

Disk topology StorageClass Notes Local NVMe through a local-volume provisioner WaitForFirstConsumer, volumeMode: Block One volume per disk; pin OSDs to the nodes that own them Local NVMe through TopoLVM topolvm-provisioner LVM-backed, dynamic Cloud block storage (EBS gp3, PD-SSD) default One volume, one OSD Ceph RBD, NFS or object-backed volumes don't Storage on storage; the engine's durability assumes local block semantics

docs.title: Probes
docs.text:
Every probe asks the service whether it can do its job, not only whether a port is open:

Component Startup Liveness Readiness Gateway GET /health (port 9000) GET /_ready: 503 until meta is reachable and enough OSDs are up for a write to meet quorum, and from the start of a shutdown Meta GET /health on the admin port (9102), up to 5 minutes to open its database GET /health: 503 once its Raft has stopped (a fatal storage error, a panic), so the pod restarts GET /ready: 503 until it is a member of the cluster with a leader known (before the bootstrap Job has added it, during an election) OSD GET /health on the metrics port (9201), up to 10 minutes to open its disk the gRPC port (9200) GET /health: 503 while a disk is unhealthy Block gateway the gRPC port (9300), up to 10 minutes to replay its journal the gRPC port the gRPC port: it opens only once the journal is replayed and the volumes are loaded

A failed disk takes its OSD out of readiness without restarting it. Each probe is a value (meta.readinessProbe and so on) that can be replaced whole.

Meta and the OSDs start their pods in parallel (podManagementPolicy: Parallel): after a full restart a meta pod is ready only with a quorum, so pods started one after another, each waiting for the last to be ready, would never get past the first. Updates still roll one pod at a time, each waiting for readiness.

docs.title: Disruption budgets
docs.text: Default gateway.podDisruptionBudget minAvailable: 1 Raise it with the replica count meta.podDisruptionBudget maxUnavailable: 1 Keeps a Raft majority osd.podDisruptionBudget maxUnavailable: 1 Keep it at or below ec.m

docs.title: NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
networkPolicy.enabled: true renders an ingress policy for meta, the OSDs, the gateway and the block gateway. Pods of the release (the bootstrap Job and the chart's Prometheus included) always reach each other; from outside, only the peers listed:

networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
  gatewayFrom:            # the S3 port; empty: anyone
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx }
  blockGatewayFrom: []    # gRPC and NBD; empty: anyone
  metricsFrom:            # meta's and the OSDs' /metrics
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring }
  adminFrom: []           # meta's admin port; empty: the release only

Egress isn't restricted (the OSDs' node-label lookup reaches the API server, the gateway an OIDC issuer or Vault). Kubelet probes aren't affected on common CNIs.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Secret Values SSE master key gateway.sse.existingSecret (key existingSecretKey, default master-key) Or the chart makes <release>-gateway-sse once OIDC client secret gateway.oidc.existingSecret (key client-secret) Or gateway.oidc.clientSecret Delta Sharing secret key gateway.deltaSharing.existingSecret (key secret-key) Or gateway.deltaSharing.secretKey Grafana admin password monitoring.grafana.existingSecret (key admin-password) Or the chart makes <release>-grafana with a random one Vault token gateway.kms.vault.tokenSecretName (key token) mTLS certificate tls.secretName, or made by cert-manager mTLS

The SSE master key encrypts every object written to a bucket with default encryption; without it they can't be read. Create it yourself, once, and back it up:

kubectl -n objectio create secret generic objectio-sse \
  --from-literal=master-key="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"

gateway:
  sse:
    enabled: true
    existingSecret: objectio-sse

Left to the chart, the key is generated on the first install, read back (lookup) and reused on every helm upgrade, and kept on helm uninstall (helm.sh/resource-policy: keep), as is the Grafana Secret. helm template can't read the cluster, so a tool that deploys by rendering the chart (Argo CD, for one) would make a new key on every render: with those, use existingSecret.

docs.title: Block gateway
docs.text:
blockGateway:
  enabled: true
  advertiseHost: block.example.com   # the host initiators attach to
  cacheBytes: 268435456              # 256 MiB write cache
  persistence:
    size: 5Gi
  service:
    type: LoadBalancer               # NBD is TCP: it must be reachable
    nbdPort: 10809

It runs as a StatefulSet of one pod: its write journal holds every acknowledged write until it reaches the OSDs, and is used by one process at a time. A StatefulSet starts a replacement only once the old pod is gone, and an update stops the old pod first. The journal's volume is kept on helm uninstall.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: The chart's own Prometheus and Grafana (monitoring.enabled: true) are for a quick look. In a cluster with a prometheus-operator, turn on the alert rules as a PrometheusRule (monitoring.prometheusRule.enabled, with labels matching its rule selector) and scrape meta's :9101, the OSDs' :9201 and the gateways' :9000/metrics; the chart has no ServiceMonitor. See monitoring.

docs.title: Values reference
docs.text:
The full defaults, with comments, are in deploy/helm/objectio/values.yaml. The keys an install usually sets:

Key Default replication 0 The default pool's protection: 0 erasure-codes it ec.k+ec.m; n keeps n copies of each object ec.k, ec.m 4, 2 The erasure code (ec.m at least 1); the block gateway codes volumes with it whatever replication is osd.replicas 6 At least ec.k + ec.m (or replication); more lets a stripe be rebuilt elsewhere while an OSD is down osd.persistence.data.size, .storageClass, .volumeMode 50Gi, the cluster's default, Filesystem Each OSD's disk osd.persistence.state.size 5Gi Each OSD's metadata index osd.failureDomain.{region,zone,datacenter,rack} default, empty, default, rack1 Fixed levels, the same for every OSD osd.failureDomain.nodeLabels {} Levels read from each OSD's node labels osd.podDisruptionBudget.maxUnavailable 1 meta.replicas 3 1 (no fault tolerance), 3 or 5; not an even number meta.persistence.size 10Gi gateway.replicas 2 Or gateway.autoscaling (an HPA on CPU) gateway.noAuth false true serves every request unauthenticated, as the admin: development only gateway.externalUrl empty The public URL (Iceberg vended credentials, Delta Sharing, the console's OIDC callback) gateway.ingress off className, hosts, tls, annotations gateway.oidc off issuerUrl, clientId, clientSecret or existingSecret, adminRoles gateway.sse off existingSecret, or a key the chart makes gateway.trustedProxies empty Proxies whose X-Forwarded-For is believed (aws:SourceIp) gateway.endpoints unnamed Named endpoints for aws:SourceVpce; a separate external port for the ingress gateway.topology empty The gateway's own position, for locality-aware reads gateway.audit spool on, bucket objectio-audit, 365 days Audit gateway.hostProvider k8s Lets the admin API add OSD pods and restart them <component>.nodeSelector, .affinity, .tolerations, .topologySpreadConstraints, .priorityClassName, .podAnnotations empty Where pods run <component>.startupProbe, .livenessProbe, .readinessProbe see Probes <component>.resources per component networkPolicy.* off NetworkPolicy tls.enabled false mTLS between the services blockGateway.enabled false Block gateway monitoring.enabled, monitoring.prometheusRule.enabled false Monitoring global.imagePullSecrets [] global.toolsImage curlimages/curl:8.10.1 sh and curl, for the bootstrap Job and the node-label lookup; point it at a mirror when air-gapped

Minimum OSDs for common erasure codes:

Profile OSDs Recommended 4+2 6 7–8 8+4 12 13–14 LRC 10+2+2 14 15

The profiles a pool may have are in data protection.

docs.title: Scaling an existing release
docs.text:
Add OSDs by raising osd.replicas:

helm upgrade objectio oci://ghcr.io/object-io/charts/objectio --version 0.1.0 \
  -n objectio --reuse-values --set osd.replicas=9

New OSDs register with meta and take placement groups; see failure recovery for how data moves.

Meta membership: every install and upgrade runs the Raft bootstrap Job (<release>-meta-raft-bootstrap-<revision>). On the first install it makes the cluster; on an upgrade it adds, through the leader, the pods that aren't voters yet (1 → 3, 3 → 5); with every pod a voter it changes nothing. It doesn't scale meta down: call /change-membership with the smaller voter set first, then lower meta.replicas (meta HA).

docs.title: Losing a meta pod
docs.text: With three metas, any one pod can go (killed, evicted, rescheduled, or rolled by kubectl rollout restart) without losing anything the gateway acknowledged. If it was the leader, the other two elect one in about 5 seconds; writes that arrive meanwhile get 503 ServiceUnavailable, which S3 clients retry, and resume on their own. The pod comes back on its volume, catches up, and is ready again once it knows the leader. Losing two of three at once stops writes until one returns: keep the PodDisruptionBudget (meta.podDisruptionBudget) on.

docs.title: Upgrading from 0.1.0-rc.1
docs.text:
The 0.1.0 chart changes three things an upgrade has to handle:

  • Meta and the OSDs start their pods in parallel, a StatefulSet field an upgrade can't change. Delete the two StatefulSets, leaving their pods running, before the upgrade; it recreates them and rolls the pods one at a time:
kubectl -n objectio delete statefulset objectio-meta objectio-osd --cascade=orphan
  • The block gateway is a StatefulSet, no longer a Deployment. Stop it before the upgrade, so that two pods never use its journal at once: kubectl -n objectio scale deployment objectio-block-gateway --replicas=0.
  • The defaults changed (4+2 over 6 OSDs, authentication on). A release installed with the old defaults (1+0, one OSD, no auth) sets replication: 1, its osd.replicas and, until its clients sign their requests, gateway.noAuth: true when it upgrades (upgrades).

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
helm uninstall objectio -n objectio

Helm leaves the meta and OSD volumes (StatefulSet claims), the block gateway's journal volume, and the SSE and Grafana Secrets the chart made. Reinstalling under the same release name and namespace finds them and uses them again. To remove everything:

kubectl -n objectio delete pvc -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=objectio
kubectl -n objectio delete secret objectio-gateway-sse objectio-grafana --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete namespace objectio

docs.title: Kind (local Kubernetes) walkthrough
docs.text:
deploy/kind/setup.sh stands up a 3-node Kind cluster (1 control-plane + 2 workers), builds every image, loads them into the cluster, installs the chart with deploy/kind/values.yaml, port-forwards the gateway to localhost:9000, and runs a smoke test covering S3, Iceberg and Delta Sharing.

# Prereqs: docker, kind, kubectl, helm
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

make kind-up                                 # build + deploy from source
# OR
make kind-up-registry                        # pull from ghcr.io/object-io (no local build)

If something already listens on port 9000, forward the gateway elsewhere: PF_PORT=19000 make kind-up.

To check meta HA on it, with S3 traffic running from a pod: kill the meta leader's pod, then a follower's, then roll the StatefulSet; every acknowledged write must read back.

deploy/kind/meta-ha-test.sh

When it finishes, the script prints:

Endpoints (via kubectl port-forward):
  S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing  http://localhost:9000
  Grafana                       http://localhost:3000   (admin / objectio)

EC scheme: 4+2  |  Meta: 3 nodes  |  OSDs: 6 nodes

docs.title: Teardown and re-deploy
docs.text:
make kind-down             # delete the whole Kind cluster
make kind-load             # rebuild images + reload into a running cluster
kubectl -n objectio rollout restart statefulset/objectio-osd  # pick up new images

docs.title: What the kind values change
docs.text:
deploy/kind/values.yaml sets, for a throwaway cluster:

  • gateway.noAuth: true: every request is served as the admin, unsigned (the smoke test uses --no-sign-request). Never use these values on a real cluster.
  • Grafana's password objectio, one gateway, and small volumes on Kind's standard (local-path) StorageClass, which is not durable.
  • 4+2 over 6 OSDs on 2 workers: several OSDs share a node, so the cluster doesn't show what losing a node does.

For anything else, start from the chart's defaults or examples/production.yaml.

docs.title: OSD pods stuck Pending
docs.text: Usually a volume that can't bind: kubectl -n objectio describe pvc. The common causes: no default StorageClass, a class without volumeMode: Block support, or WaitForFirstConsumer with a nodeSelector or spread constraint that no node with a free disk satisfies.

docs.title: An OSD stuck in Init:Error or Init:CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text:
Its node-topology init container couldn't read a failure-domain level:

kubectl -n objectio logs objectio-osd-3 -c node-topology
# node worker-7 has no label topology.objectio.io/rack (osd.failureDomain.nodeLabels.rack): …

Label the node (kubectl label node worker-7 topology.objectio.io/rack=r12) and delete the pod.

docs.title: Meta pods Running but not Ready
docs.text:
A meta pod is ready once it is a member of the cluster with a leader known. Its /ready says what is missing:

kubectl -n objectio port-forward pod/objectio-meta-0 9102:9102 &
curl -s localhost:9102/ready; echo
curl -s localhost:9102/status

"not a member of a raft cluster" means the bootstrap Job hasn't added it. Check the Job:

kubectl -n objectio get jobs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=meta-raft-bootstrap
kubectl -n objectio logs job/objectio-meta-raft-bootstrap-<revision>

The Job waits for every meta pod's admin port; a NetworkPolicy of your own that blocks pod-to-pod traffic in the namespace stops it. A failed Job runs again with the next helm upgrade.

docs.title: An OSD Running but not Ready
docs.text: Its /health (metrics port) reports a disk that isn't healthy; the OSD's log says which and why. See failure recovery.

docs.title: kubectl port-forward drops connections
docs.text: Use a Service of type: LoadBalancer (on clouds) or an ingress in production. port-forward is for development only.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Linux is the primary production target. Both amd64 and arm64 are first-class, and both erasure-code with ISA-L (AVX2, AVX-512 and GFNI on amd64; NEON and SVE on arm64). They write the same stripes, so amd64 and arm64 nodes mix in one cluster.

This page covers, in increasing order of commitment:

  1. Release binary — objectio-aio, one process
  2. A cluster under systemd — meta, OSDs and gateways as separate services
  3. From source — Rust toolchain; also how you get the service binaries outside the container image

If you just want a quick local endpoint, use objectio-aio — one binary, no daemons. The Helm chart (Kubernetes) is the tested way to run separate services; this page covers doing it by hand.

docs.title: System requirements
docs.text:
Component Minimum Recommended Kernel 4.19+ 5.15+ (for io_uring) CPU 2 cores 8+ cores RAM 4 GB 16+ GB (OSD), 8 GB (meta), 4 GB (gateway) Disks (OSD) 1 × any block device 4+ dedicated raw disks per OSD node Network 1 Gbps 10+ Gbps (especially between OSDs)

Filesystem: OSDs prefer raw block devices (/dev/sdb, /dev/nvme0n1). File-backed disks (/mnt/.../disk.raw) work but skip the O_DIRECT fast path and lose some durability guarantees. Disks are formatted with ObjectIO's own on-disk layout (superblock + WAL + blocks), not ext4/xfs — mkfs-ing first is not required and is not recommended for production OSDs.

Kernel features used:

  • O_DIRECT on raw block devices (required for OSD disks)
  • ioctl BLKGETSIZE64 for disk sizing
  • io_uring when available (5.15+); falls back to threaded I/O, with a warning in the OSD's log, where the kernel or a seccomp profile denies it

docs.title: 1. Release binary
docs.text:
A release publishes objectio-aio only, for linux-amd64 and linux-arm64 (and darwin-arm64), named with the tag; there is no archive of the service binaries. Those are in the container image (ghcr.io/object-io/objectio, see Docker) or built from source.

TAG=v0.1.0-rc.1
ARCH=$(uname -m | sed 's/x86_64/amd64/;s/aarch64/arm64/')
BASE=https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/download/$TAG
curl -LO $BASE/objectio-aio-$TAG-linux-$ARCH
curl -LO $BASE/objectio-aio-$TAG-linux-$ARCH.sha256
sha256sum -c objectio-aio-$TAG-linux-$ARCH.sha256
sudo install -m 0755 objectio-aio-$TAG-linux-$ARCH /usr/local/bin/objectio-aio
objectio-aio --version

releases/latest/download/… doesn't work for a pre-release such as v0.1.0-rc.1: name the tag.

The release binary needs glibc 2.28 or later and nothing else. It is built on AlmaLinux 8 (glibc 2.28); PCRE2 is linked in, and its TLS is rustls, so it loads no OpenSSL. The only shared libraries it loads are glibc's own, libgcc_s and the dynamic loader. By glibc, that covers (the kernel must meet the system requirements too):

Distribution Release glibc RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux 8 and later 2.28+ Debian 10 and later 2.28+ Ubuntu 20.04 and later 2.31+ Amazon Linux 2023 2.34 Fedora 29 and later 2.28+

Before a release is published, each Linux binary (amd64 and arm64) is checked to need no glibc symbol newer than 2.28 and no other library, and is run on Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Rocky Linux 9 and Amazon Linux 2023. Amazon Linux 2 (glibc 2.26) and CentOS 7 (2.17) are too old: use the container image there.

Outbound HTTPS (to an OIDC provider, for one) trusts Mozilla's root certificates, which are built in, and the system's certificate store, so a private CA added there (update-ca-certificates, update-ca-trust) is trusted too.

v0.1.0-rc.1's binaries are the exception: built on Ubuntu 24.04, they need glibc 2.39, libssl3 and libpcre2-8-0.

docs.title: 2. A cluster under systemd
docs.text:
Every service is configured with flags; only objectio-osd also reads a TOML file (--config), which is where an OSD's failure domain (region, datacenter, rack, host) is set. The ports are the cluster's (ports), every binary's defaults.

objectio-install writes each host's units and OSD files and forms meta's Raft group: below. The same by hand follows it. Either way the binaries come from the image or a build, in /usr/local/bin.

docs.title: With objectio-install
docs.text:
On each host, as root, with its own --node-id (1, 2, 3), the address the other hosts reach it at, every meta node's address, and its disks:

sudo objectio-install init --role all \
  --node-id 1 \
  --advertise node1.internal \
  --meta-endpoint http://node1.internal:9100,http://node2.internal:9100,http://node3.internal:9100 \
  --disks /dev/disk/by-id/nvme-A,/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-B \
  --ec-profile 4+2 \
  --systemd

It writes an OSD per disk (/etc/objectio/osd-0.toml, osd-1.toml, …, the units objectio-osd-0, objectio-osd-1, …), the units objectio-meta and objectio-gateway with their flags, and the data directories under /var/lib/objectio, and creates the system user objectio that meta and the gateway run as. It formats no disk: each must be blank, which its OSD formats when it first starts, or an ObjectIO disk. --ec-profile (or --replication <n>) sets the default pool (profiles allowed): it needs k+m OSDs, on as many hosts where there are that many. A host needn't run everything: --role meta,osd on the others, say, and the gateway on some (behind a load balancer). The flags include each port.

Start meta on every meta host, form the Raft group once, from any host, then start the rest:

sudo systemctl enable --now objectio-meta                  # every meta host
objectio-install cluster init node1.internal node2.internal node3.internal
sudo systemctl enable --now objectio-osd-0 objectio-osd-1 objectio-gateway

cluster init calls each meta node's admin port (9102; plain HTTP, no authentication: keep it to the operators' network), as the by-hand steps do, and is safe to run again. The admin's keys are then in /var/lib/objectio/meta/admin-creds.env on every meta host.

One host is the same with one meta node: --role all, no --meta-endpoint (this host's meta), and an erasure code its disks can hold, one OSD each: three disks, --ec-profile 2+1; one disk, --replication 1. Then objectio-install cluster init 127.0.0.1.

For server-side encryption, put OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY=<base64 of 32 random bytes> in /etc/objectio/gateway.env (mode 0600), the same on every gateway, before starting it. Each OSD's failure domain goes in its file, [osd.failure_domain] (commented out as written); restart the OSD after changing it.

This path is tested end to end: one host, then three, set up by objectio-install, their units' commands run, the group formed by cluster init, then objects written and read through the gateway.

docs.title: Service user and directories
docs.text:
sudo groupadd -r objectio
sudo useradd -r -g objectio -d /var/lib/objectio -s /usr/sbin/nologin objectio
sudo mkdir -p /etc/objectio /var/lib/objectio/meta /var/lib/objectio/osd
sudo chown -R objectio:objectio /var/lib/objectio

docs.title: Meta (three nodes, Raft)
docs.text:
On each meta node, with its own --node-id (1, 2, 3) and the address the others reach it at:

objectio-meta \
  --node-id 1 \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9100 \
  --raft-advertise meta1.internal:9100 \
  --metrics-port 9101 \
  --admin-port 9102 \
  --data-dir /var/lib/objectio/meta \
  --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2

--ec-k/--ec-m set the default pool's erasure code (profiles allowed); it needs at least k+m OSDs, on as many hosts. Once all three run, form the Raft group from node 1, over its admin port (plain HTTP, no authentication: keep 9102 to the operators' network):

curl -X POST http://meta1.internal:9102/init
curl -X POST http://meta1.internal:9102/add-learner \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"node_id": 2, "addr": "meta2.internal:9100"}'
curl -X POST http://meta1.internal:9102/add-learner \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"node_id": 3, "addr": "meta3.internal:9100"}'
curl -X POST http://meta1.internal:9102/change-membership \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"voters": [1, 2, 3]}'
curl -s http://meta1.internal:9102/status    # leader, voters, learners

The first leader creates the admin user once, and every meta node writes its credentials to <data-dir>/admin-creds.env (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY), readable by the service user only.

docs.title: OSDs
docs.text:
One OSD per drive. /etc/objectio/osd.toml:

[osd]
listen = "0.0.0.0:9200"
advertise_addr = "http://osd1.internal:9200"
meta_endpoint = "http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100"

[osd.failure_domain]
datacenter = "dc1"
rack = "rack-a"
# host: the machine's hostname when left out

[storage]
disks = ["/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-…"]
data_dir = "/var/lib/objectio/osd"

objectio-osd --config /etc/objectio/osd.toml --metrics-port 9201

Flags given as well win over the file. A blank disk named in disks is formatted on first start; one that is neither blank nor this OSD's stops it (configuration).

docs.title: Gateways
docs.text:
objectio-gateway \
  --listen 0.0.0.0:9000 \
  --meta-endpoint http://meta1.internal:9100,http://meta2.internal:9100,http://meta3.internal:9100 \
  --external-endpoint https://s3.example.com \
  --region us-east-1

Set OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY (base64 of 32 random bytes, the same on every gateway) for server-side encryption, and run several gateways behind a load balancer that checks /_ready. With more than one gateway, add --no-reexport-metrics and scrape meta and the OSDs directly (metrics).

docs.title: 3. Build from source
docs.text: Needed if you want to track main, run a custom branch, or run the services outside the image. A binary needs the glibc it was built against or newer: to build one that runs where the release's does, build in an almalinux:8 container, with PCRE2_SYS_STATIC=1 to link PCRE2 in (the release workflow, .github/workflows/release.yml, is the recipe).

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
# Rust (1.93+)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustup toolchain install 1.93

# Build deps
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install -y build-essential nasm autoconf automake libtool \
  libclang-dev pkg-config protobuf-compiler libprotobuf-dev cmake

# RHEL / Rocky / Alma 9+
sudo dnf install -y gcc-c++ make nasm autoconf automake libtool \
  clang-devel pkgconf protobuf-compiler protobuf-devel cmake

Every build erasure-codes with ISA-L, which is built from source with autotools (autoconf, automake, libtool) and bound with libclang. NASM is only required on x86_64, for ISA-L's x86 assembly; on ARM64 leave it out.

docs.title: Console (SPA) prerequisites
docs.text:
objectio-aio and the gateway's /_console/ surface embed a pre-built React bundle. If you're only building server binaries and don't need the console, nothing to do. To build the console you need Node 22+:

# Ubuntu — NodeSource 22.x
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs

cd console && npm ci && npm run build   # → console/dist

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

cargo build --workspace --release

Binaries land in target/release/. For a system install:

sudo install -m 0755 target/release/{objectio-aio,objectio-gateway,objectio-meta,objectio-osd,obioctl,objectio-install,objectio-block-gateway} \
  /usr/local/bin/

Then proceed as in section 2.

docs.title: Run the test suite
docs.text:
cargo test --workspace
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
# Or the one-shot:
make ci

docs.title: Disk preparation — production checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Dedicate whole disks to OSDs (no partitioning, no filesystem).
  • [ ] Disable write-cache on SAS/SATA drives with non-battery-backed controllers: hdparm -W 0 /dev/sdX.
  • [ ] For NVMe, confirm the drive supports FUA (Force Unit Access) — check nvme id-ctrl -H <dev> | grep -i fua.
  • [ ] Raise /proc/sys/fs/file-max and ulimit -n (OSD opens one fd per concurrent operation × disk).
  • [ ] Pin CPUs / set tuned-adm profile throughput-performance.
  • [ ] If using io_uring, make sure the kernel is 5.15+ and /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled is 0, and that the OSD's log has no falling back to pread warning.

See topologies.md for how many disks and nodes to size for a given durability target.

docs.title: systemd unit reference
docs.text:
The units objectio-install writes; to write them by hand, keep their shape. An OSD's, one per disk:

# /etc/systemd/system/objectio-osd-0.service
[Unit]
Description=ObjectIO OSD 0 (/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-A)
Documentation=https://object-io.github.io
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
After=objectio-meta.service

[Service]
Type=simple
# Opens raw block devices.
User=root
Group=root
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/objectio-osd --config /etc/objectio/osd-0.toml --metrics-port 9201
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
# Every acknowledged write is already on disk; this is time to finish
# the calls in flight.
TimeoutStopSec=60
LimitNOFILE=1048576
LimitMEMLOCK=infinity
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
SyslogIdentifier=objectio-osd-0

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Meta's and the gateway's run as objectio, with their flags on ExecStart and LimitNOFILE=65536, ProtectSystem=strict, meta's data directory its one writable path (ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/objectio/meta), and the gateway reading EnvironmentFile=-/etc/objectio/gateway.env. The After=objectio-meta.service line is there on a host that runs meta. Every service stops cleanly on SIGTERM (how a node stops); none reloads on SIGHUP, so there is no ExecReload.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
sudo systemctl disable --now objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd-0 objectio-osd-1   # every OSD
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/objectio-*.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/objectio-* /usr/local/bin/obioctl
# Data + config (destructive):
sudo rm -rf /etc/objectio /var/lib/objectio /var/log/objectio
sudo userdel objectio && sudo groupdel objectio

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
macOS is a development-and-test target, not a production target. Use it to build, run objectio-aio, and point Spark / PyIceberg / boto3 at a local S3 endpoint. The split-service OSD binary runs on macOS, but Darwin does not expose the same raw-disk semantics as Linux (O_DIRECT, ioctl BLKGETSIZE64) and the storage engine has no hardened path for APFS-backed OSD disks. Keep macOS deployments to AIO mode, or run the services in a Linux VM.

Releases publish an Apple Silicon (arm64) binary; on Intel (x86_64), build from source. Erasure coding is ISA-L's on both, as on Linux.

docs.title: 1. AIO binary (recommended)
docs.text: This is the fastest path and the one you'll actually want 95% of the time on macOS.

docs.title: Apple Silicon
docs.text:
TAG=v0.1.0-rc.1
BASE=https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/download/$TAG
curl -LO $BASE/objectio-aio-$TAG-darwin-arm64
curl -LO $BASE/objectio-aio-$TAG-darwin-arm64.sha256
shasum -a 256 -c objectio-aio-$TAG-darwin-arm64.sha256
chmod +x objectio-aio-$TAG-darwin-arm64
sudo mv objectio-aio-$TAG-darwin-arm64 /usr/local/bin/objectio-aio

The release binary is named with its tag, and a pre-release such as v0.1.0-rc.1 isn't reachable through releases/latest: name the tag.

docs.title: Intel
docs.text: There is no release binary for Intel Macs: build it (below).

docs.title: Gatekeeper
docs.text:
Unsigned release binaries will be quarantined by Gatekeeper on first run. Either remove the quarantine attribute:

xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /usr/local/bin/objectio-aio

or, on the first launch, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Allow Anyway next to the objectio-aio entry.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio"

The banner prints the admin AK/SK (also in ~/.objectio/meta/admin-creds.env). --data is optional but recommended — without it, every restart wipes the data tempdir. Authentication is off unless you add --auth.

docs.title: 2. Docker Desktop
docs.text: The published image (ghcr.io/object-io/objectio, linux/arm64 and linux/amd64) carries the service binaries and obioctl, not objectio-aio. Use it to run obioctl, or the services in Docker Desktop's Linux VM (docker.md); for a local endpoint, the AIO binary above is simpler.

docs.title: 3. Build from source (contributor path)
docs.text: Only needed if you're hacking on ObjectIO itself.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
# Rust
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
rustup toolchain install 1.93

# Build deps via Homebrew
brew install nasm autoconf automake libtool llvm protobuf cmake
# ISA-L's build runs autoreconf, which wants `libtoolize`; Homebrew
# names it glibtoolize and keeps the plain name here
export PATH="$(brew --prefix libtool)/libexec/gnubin:$PATH"

# Node 22+ for the console SPA (only if you need /_console/)
brew install node@22

Every build erasure-codes with ISA-L, built from source with autotools. nasm is Intel-only (ISA-L's x86 assembly); on Apple Silicon it is installed and not used.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio

cargo build --workspace --release

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
If you want the React /_console/ UI baked into objectio-aio:

cd console && npm ci && npm run build
cd .. && cargo build --release --bin objectio-aio    # rebuild to embed dist

docs.title: Run
docs.text: ./target/release/objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio"

docs.title: What does not work on macOS
docs.text:
• Production OSDs on raw disks. Darwin's /dev/disk* devices don't support the same O_DIRECT / BLKGETSIZE64 interface the storage engine uses. The OSD binary builds and runs against file- backed "disks" (truncate -s 10G disk0.raw), which is fine for unit tests but not for durability-sensitive work.
  • NBD clients. The block gateway serves volumes over NBD (and gRPC); macOS has no NBD client. Use Linux peers for block-storage testing.
  • io_uring performance path. Linux-specific. Not a correctness issue, but macOS performance numbers are not representative.

For any of these, run ObjectIO in a Linux VM (Lima, UTM, Colima, Docker Desktop's Linux VM, or a dedicated machine).

docs.title: Typical dev loop on macOS
docs.text:
# 1. Run AIO in one terminal, persistent data dir
objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio"

# 2. Point your tool at it
source "$HOME/.objectio/meta/admin-creds.env"   # also printed in the banner
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:9000

# 3. Work against S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing
aws s3 ls
obioctl --endpoint http://localhost:9000 warehouse create demo
curl -s 'http://localhost:9000/iceberg/v1/config?warehouse=demo' | jq .

# 4. Console (browser)
open http://localhost:9000/_console/

Shut down with Ctrl-C — AIO drains cleanly. The data directory is reusable across restarts.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
The fastest path to a running ObjectIO is the all-in-one binary (objectio-aio). It runs meta + OSD + gateway as tokio tasks in a single process, shares one log stream, and is shut down with a single Ctrl-C. Same wire protocol as a real cluster — what's different is that there is no HA and, by default, no redundancy and no authentication.

This page covers three paths:

Path Platform Best for AIO release binary Linux (amd64, arm64), macOS (Apple Silicon) Laptop-local S3/Iceberg/Delta endpoint AIO built from source Linux, macOS (Intel too) Tracking main, or a platform with no release binary AIO with several OSDs as above Erasure coding (e.g. 4+2) inside one process

For a cluster of separate processes, use the Helm chart (on kind locally: make kind-up, see Kubernetes) or Linux.

ObjectIO is POSIX-only — no native Windows build. The storage engine uses O_DIRECT, ioctl BLKGETSIZE64, and other unix-only interfaces; there is no meaningful cfg-gate to Windows.

docs.title: 1. AIO release binary (fastest)
docs.text:
Each release publishes objectio-aio for three platforms, named with the release tag: objectio-aio-<tag>-linux-amd64, -linux-arm64 and -darwin-arm64, each with a .sha256, plus SHA256SUMS.txt. There is no Intel macOS binary (build it), and no archive of the other binaries. The current release, v0.1.0-rc.1, is a pre-release, which GitHub's releases/latest link skips: name the tag.

TAG=v0.1.0-rc.1
PLATFORM=linux-amd64     # or linux-arm64, darwin-arm64
BASE=https://github.com/object-io/objectio/releases/download/$TAG
curl -LO $BASE/objectio-aio-$TAG-$PLATFORM
curl -LO $BASE/objectio-aio-$TAG-$PLATFORM.sha256
shasum -a 256 -c objectio-aio-$TAG-$PLATFORM.sha256
chmod +x objectio-aio-$TAG-$PLATFORM
sudo mv objectio-aio-$TAG-$PLATFORM /usr/local/bin/objectio-aio
objectio-aio

On macOS, see Gatekeeper before the first run.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
On start, AIO prints where it listens, the admin access key and secret, and a ready-to-paste aws command:

━━━ ObjectIO ready ━━━
  S3 / Iceberg / Delta Sharing : http://localhost:9000
  Console                       : http://localhost:9000/_console/
  LAN bind                      : 0.0.0.0 — reachable from other hosts on the network
  Data directory                : /tmp/.tmpXXXXXX
  Internals (loopback only)     : meta=:… osd=[…] (monolith — same process)
  Admin access key              : AKIA…
  Admin secret key              : …
  SSE master key                : persisted at /tmp/.tmpXXXXXX/master_key (set OBJECTIO_MASTER_KEY to override)

  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA… AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=… \
    aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 mb s3://test

The credentials are also in <data>/meta/admin-creds.env, readable by its owner only. Authentication is off unless you pass --auth: without it the gateway serves every request, signed or not, so keep aio on a trusted network or bind it to loopback (--listen-addr 127.0.0.1).

Smoke test from another terminal:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...   # from the banner above
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 mb s3://demo
echo 'hello objectio' | aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp - s3://demo/hello.txt
aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:9000 s3 cp s3://demo/hello.txt -

docs.title: Flags you'll actually use
docs.text:
Flag Default Notes --port 9000 Public port. Only port the caller needs to know. --listen-addr 0.0.0.0 Use 127.0.0.1 to restrict to loopback. --data <dir> tempdir Persist data across restarts. Holds meta/ (with admin-creds.env), osd-N/ and master_key. --auth off Turn SigV4 authentication on. --osds <N> 1 OSDs to run. Without --ec-k/--ec-m the pool is replication 1: no redundancy, however many OSDs. --ec-k, --ec-m 0 Erasure code instead, with at least k+m OSDs: --osds 6 --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2. --strict-port off Fail fast on --port conflict instead of picking an ephemeral.

objectio-aio --help has the complete surface; the configuration reference lists more.

docs.title: 2. AIO built from source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/object-io/objectio
cd objectio
cargo build --release --bin objectio-aio
./target/release/objectio-aio

The toolchain and build dependencies are in Linux and macOS. Build the console first (cd console && npm ci && npm run build) if you want /_console/; without it aio serves an empty console.

docs.title: 3. AIO with erasure coding
docs.text:
objectio-aio --data "$HOME/.objectio" --osds 6 --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2

Six OSDs, each on a file-backed disk in the data directory (--disk-size sets its size; 10 GiB, sparse, by default), with a 4+2 pool spread over them. It is still one process on one machine: it survives the loss of two OSDs' disks, not of the machine.
