docs.title: Deployment Topologies
docs.text: ObjectIO supports various deployment configurations. For worked scenarios, configuration examples and capacity planning, see deployment-options.md.

docs.title: Topology 1: Single-Node Multi-Disk
docs.text:
Best for development, edge, and small deployments.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Single Server                      │
│                                                     │
│  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐        │
│  │ Disk 1 │ │ Disk 2 │ │ Disk 3 │ │ Disk 4 │ ...    │
│  │ Shard1 │ │ Shard2 │ │ Shard3 │ │ Shard4 │        │
│  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘        │
│                                                     │
│  EC 4+2: Spread 6 shards across 6+ disks            │
│                                                     │
│  Components:                                        │
│  • objectio-gateway (port 9000)                     │
│  • objectio-meta (embedded, single-node mode)       │
│  • objectio-osd (manages all disks)                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Characteristics: - Survives: Disk failures (up to m disks) - Does NOT survive: Server failure - Storage efficiency: 67% (4+2)

Example: one host, six drives, one OSD per drive, each with its own osd.toml (see Linux), and meta started with --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2. With fewer hosts than shards, the default pool spreads each stripe over OSDs instead of hosts. For a try-out in one process: objectio-aio --osds 6 --ec-k 4 --ec-m 2.

docs.title: Topology 2: Multi-Node Single-DC (Rack Aware)
docs.text:
Production single-datacenter deployment.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          Datacenter                                 │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐      │
│  │     Rack A      │  │     Rack B      │  │     Rack C      │      │
│  │  ┌───────────┐  │  │  ┌───────────┐  │  │  ┌───────────┐  │      │
│  │  │  Node 1   │  │  │  │  Node 3   │  │  │  │  Node 5   │  │      │
│  │  │ D1 D2 D3  │  │  │  │ D1 D2 D3  │  │  │  │ D1 D2 D3  │  │      │
│  │  │ Shards:   │  │  │  │ Shards:   │  │  │  │ Shards:   │  │      │
│  │  │ 1,4,7,10  │  │  │  │ 2,5,8,11  │  │  │  │ 3,6,9,12  │  │      │
│  │  └───────────┘  │  │  └───────────┘  │  │  └───────────┘  │      │
│  │  ┌───────────┐  │  │  ┌───────────┐  │  │  ┌───────────┐  │      │
│  │  │  Node 2   │  │  │  │  Node 4   │  │  │  │  Node 6   │  │      │
│  │  │ D1 D2 D3  │  │  │  │ D1 D2 D3  │  │  │  │ D1 D2 D3  │  │      │
│  │  └───────────┘  │  │  └───────────┘  │  │  └───────────┘  │      │
│  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘      │
│                                                                     │
│  EC 8+4: Shards distributed across racks                            │
│  Metadata: 3-node Raft cluster (one per rack)                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Characteristics: - Survives: Multiple disk, node, and rack failures - Does NOT survive: DC-wide failure - Typical setup: 3+ racks, 6+ nodes

Placement: each OSD names its rack in osd.toml ([osd.failure_domain] rack = "rack-a"; the host defaults to the machine's hostname). The default pool spreads over hosts. For racks, create a pool with a rack failure domain and put buckets in it:

# 8+4 over 3 racks, at most 4 shards of a stripe in one rack
obioctl pool create racked --ec-type 0 --ec-k 8 --ec-m 4 \
  --failure-domain rack --spread-domains 3 --per-domain 4
obioctl bucket create analytics --pool racked

Losing a rack then loses at most 4 shards, which 8+4 survives. Without --spread-domains/--per-domain a pool puts one shard per domain, so 8+4 would need 12 racks. A bucket's pool is fixed when it is created (x-objectio-pool on CreateBucket, or the tenant's default pool).

docs.title: Topology 3: Multi-DC / Multi-AZ
docs.text:
Geo-distributed deployment for disaster recovery.

┌───────────────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────┐
│    Datacenter 1       │    │    Datacenter 2       │    │    Datacenter 3       │
│    (Primary)          │    │    (Secondary)        │    │    (DR)               │
│                       │    │                       │    │                       │
│  ┌─────────────────┐  │    │  ┌─────────────────┐  │    │  ┌─────────────────┐  │
│  │   Full Copy 1   │  │    │  │   Full Copy 2   │  │    │  │   Full Copy 3   │  │
│  │   (EC within)   │◄─┼────┼─►│   (EC within)   │◄─┼────┼─►│   (EC within)   │  │
│  └─────────────────┘  │    │  └─────────────────┘  │    │  └─────────────────┘  │
│         │             │    │         │             │    │         │             │
│    ┌────┴────┐        │    │    ┌────┴────┐        │    │    ┌────┴────┐        │
│    │Racks/   │        │    │    │Racks/   │        │    │    │Racks/   │        │
│    │Nodes    │        │    │    │Nodes    │        │    │    │Nodes    │        │
│    └─────────┘        │    │    └─────────┘        │    │    └─────────┘        │
│                       │    │                       │    │                       │
│  Metadata: Local Raft │    │  Metadata: Local Raft │    │  Metadata: Local Raft │
└───────────────────────┘    └───────────────────────┘    └───────────────────────┘
         │                            │                            │
         └────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                            Async Replication

Each site is a cluster of its own, with its own meta Raft group; nothing is shared between them.

Data flow: 1. A write arrives at a DC1 gateway and is erasure-coded within DC1. 2. Bucket replication sends each new version, asynchronously, to a bucket on the DC2 (and DC3) cluster. 3. Clients read from the cluster they are pointed at.

Characteristics: - Survives: a complete DC/AZ, losing what hadn't replicated yet (objectio_replication_lag_seconds). - Use case: geo-distributed, disaster recovery, compliance

Configuration: per bucket, on the source cluster: a replication target naming the remote cluster's bucket, and the bucket's replication rules (replication).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Topology Failure Tolerance Complexity Use Case Single-node Disk only Low Dev, edge Multi-node Disk, node, rack Medium Production Multi-DC Disk, node, rack, DC High Multi-site production

docs.title: Single-Node Multi-Disk
docs.text: Choose if: - Development or testing - Edge deployment with limited hardware - Cost-sensitive deployments - Acceptable single-node failure risk

docs.title: Multi-Node Single-DC
docs.text: Choose if: - Production workloads - Node and rack fault tolerance required - Single datacenter deployment - No geo-redundancy needs

docs.title: Multi-DC / Multi-AZ
docs.text: Choose if: - Business-critical data - Regulatory compliance (data locality) - Disaster recovery requirements - Global distribution needed

docs.title: Operations Guide
docs.text: Day-to-day operations, monitoring, and maintenance of ObjectIO clusters.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Production - Requirements, sizing, the shipped alert rules, and a runbook for each
  • Failure Recovery - Handling disk, node, and network failures
  • Meta High Availability - Losing and replacing meta nodes; what clients need
  • Upgrades - Rolling upgrades, release by release; finalize
  • Monitoring - Metrics, alerting, and observability
  • Metrics reference - Every metric, its labels, and alerts worth setting

docs.title: Service Management
docs.text:
# Start all services
sudo systemctl start objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd

# Stop all services
sudo systemctl stop objectio-gateway objectio-meta objectio-osd

# Restart a specific service
sudo systemctl restart objectio-gateway

# Check service status
sudo systemctl status objectio-gateway

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
# Gateway: process up, and ready to serve (meta and OSDs reachable)
curl http://localhost:9000/health
curl http://localhost:9000/_ready

# Meta: this node's view of the Raft group (role, leader, term, voters)
curl -s http://meta1:9102/status

# OSDs: status and admin state of each
obioctl node list

# Placement groups not Clean, and every node's release
obioctl pg list --state Degraded
obioctl upgrade status

docs.title: Common Operations
docs.text:
Task Command List buckets obioctl bucket list Check capacity and usage obioctl cluster usage, obioctl node show <osd-id> View cluster map obioctl cluster topology Check data safety curl -s http://<gateway>:9000/metrics \| grep objectio_objects_at_risk, or obioctl metrics query 'max(objectio_objects_at_risk)' with Prometheus (below); each OSD counts at most once a minute, and at once when a node goes up or down Drain OSD obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining, then obioctl cluster drain-status

obioctl metrics query runs PromQL through the gateway, which forwards it to the Prometheus named by its --prometheus-url; without one it answers that none is configured. Reading /metrics (on the admin listener, if split off) needs no Prometheus.

docs.title: Cluster States
docs.text:
No single command prints a cluster state; these signals make it up:

State Signals Healthy Every OSD up and in (obioctl node list); meta has a leader (objectio_meta_raft_has_leader 1); every placement group Clean (objectio_meta_pgs_not_clean 0); objectio_objects_at_risk 0 Degraded An OSD down or PGs Degraded, Recovering or Backfilling: data readable, redundancy being restored. A down OSD's PGs get a stand-in after 120 s (pg/down_out_seconds) and backfill onto it Critical objectio_objects_unreadable above 0, PGs Down or Incomplete, or meta without a leader: bring failed OSDs or meta nodes back (runbooks)

docs.title: Rolling Upgrades
docs.text:
Upgrades has the procedure: back up meta, then the meta nodes (followers first, leader last), then the OSDs one failure domain at a time, then the gateways, then obioctl upgrade finalize. In short:

# 1. Meta, one node at a time: which one leads?
curl -s http://meta1:9102/status
sudo systemctl restart objectio-meta      # on meta2, meta3, then meta1

# 2. OSDs, one host at a time. No drain: a restart doesn't need one.
sudo systemctl restart objectio-osd
obioctl node list                          # up again before the next

# 3. Gateways
sudo systemctl restart objectio-gateway

# 4. Every node on the new release, then finalize
obioctl upgrade status
obioctl upgrade finalize

docs.title: Adding Capacity
docs.text:
Start an OSD on the new host; it registers itself with meta and joins placement. Placement groups rebalance onto it in the background:

obioctl node list                 # the new OSD, "in"
obioctl cluster rebalance status

docs.title: Removing an OSD
docs.text:
obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining     # copies everything off it
obioctl cluster drain-status                # until it is "out"

When the drain finishes the OSD is marked out and wiped. Then stop it and take the hardware away.

docs.title: Metadata Backup
docs.text:
Each meta node keeps its state in <data-dir>/meta.redb and its Raft log beside it. The log is compacted into a snapshot every --raft-snapshot-every entries (default 500,000), keeping the last --raft-keep-logs (10,000), so it doesn't grow without bound (meta HA).

To back up, stop one follower and copy its data directory (or snapshot its volume: on Kubernetes, the meta pod's PVC with your storage class's snapshot mechanism), then start it again. There is no online export command. A fresh install against empty volumes starts a new cluster with no history: restore the volumes first.

docs.title: Object Recovery
docs.text: Repair is continuous: any stripe with at least k readable shards is rebuilt automatically. An object below k shards can't be recovered by any command; objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total counts them.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Quick Reference
docs.text: Symptom Check Solution Slow uploads Network, OSD load Scale gateways, add OSDs High latency Metadata service Check Raft leader via curl meta-N:9102/status, disk I/O Objects missing OSD health objectio_objects_at_risk, objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total Auth failures User credentials Verify access keys Connection refused Service status Restart services

docs.title: Complete Cluster Recovery
docs.text:
If all metadata nodes fail but their PVCs survive:

  1. Restart the meta nodes (on Kubernetes, kubectl rollout restart statefulset/<name>-meta, where <name> is the release name if it contains objectio, else <release>-objectio): each reads its persisted Raft log and state, and the group elects a leader once a majority is up.
  2. OSDs + gateways keep running throughout.

If the PVCs are lost (unrecoverable storage-layer failure):

  1. Restore PVCs from the latest snapshot if you have one.
  2. Otherwise the cluster's metadata is lost: delete the meta StatefulSet and its PVCs, then helm upgrade — the bootstrap Job forms a fresh Raft group. Tenants, users, buckets and the objects' metadata are gone with it.

docs.title: Data Recovery from Raw Disks
docs.text:
Not available: object metadata lives on the OSDs and meta's Raft log, but there is no tool yet to rebuild a cluster's metadata from raw disks. Keep meta's PVCs snapshotted (above).

See Failure Recovery for detailed recovery procedures.

docs.title: Failure Recovery
docs.text: Handling failures in ObjectIO clusters.

docs.title: Failure Domains
docs.text:
ObjectIO is designed to tolerate failures at multiple levels:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Failure Domain Hierarchy                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Datacenter ──┬── Rack ──┬── Host ──┬── Disk                    │
│               │          │          │                           │
│               │          │          └── Single disk failure     │
│               │          │              (most common)           │
│               │          │                                      │
│               │          └── Node failure                       │
│               │              (power, OS, hardware)              │
│               │                                                 │
│               └── Rack failure                                  │
│                   (power, network switch)                       │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
OSDs detect disk failures via: - I/O errors during read/write - Scrubbing (background verification)

SMART readings are exported as metrics (objectio_disk_smart_*, where smartctl is installed) for you to alert on; nothing acts on them.

docs.title: Automatic Recovery
docs.text:
With 4+2 erasure coding, the cluster tolerates 2 disk failures:

Object: photo.jpg (split into 6 shards)

Before failure:
  Disk1: shard1 ✓    Disk4: shard4 ✓
  Disk2: shard2 ✓    Disk5: shard5 ✓
  Disk3: shard3 ✓    Disk6: shard6 ✓

After Disk3 fails:
  Disk1: shard1 ✓    Disk4: shard4 ✓
  Disk2: shard2 ✓    Disk5: shard5 ✓
  Disk3: shard3 ✗    Disk6: shard6 ✓

Recovery: shard3 reconstructed from any 4 remaining shards
          → placed on spare disk (Disk7)

docs.title: Replacing a disk
docs.text:
Lost shards are rebuilt automatically: peering on the meta leader finds what each placement group's members lack, and recovery rebuilds it. Watch it work (obioctl metrics query needs the gateway's --prometheus-url; otherwise read the gateway's /metrics):

obioctl pg list --state Degraded                        # PGs being made whole
obioctl metrics query 'max(objectio_objects_at_risk)'   # objects one more loss from unreadable
obioctl metrics query 'max(objectio_degraded_bytes)'
obioctl metrics query 'rate(objectio_meta_pg_recovered_shards_total[5m])'
obioctl metrics query 'max(objectio_meta_pg_objects_unfound)'

To take an OSD's disk out of service (still readable):

obioctl node list                               # find the OSD's id
obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> draining         # copies everything off it
obioctl cluster drain-status                    # progress; it turns "out" when done

When a drain finishes, the OSD is marked out and wiped (its space is reclaimed, and nothing stale can come back with it). Replace the hardware, start the OSD on the new disk (a blank disk takes the place of the one missing), and set it back in:

obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> in

For a disk or host that is gone for good, set its OSD out straight away:

obioctl osd set-state <osd-id> out
obioctl cluster drain-status        # progress of the evacuation

Everything it held is rebuilt elsewhere, whether or not it still answers: each shard from the rest of its stripe (or copied, if the OSD can still serve it), and each object's metadata copy, inline objects included, on the OSD that takes its place. When nothing refers to it any more it is purged. A drive that comes back, or its replacement, joins as a new OSD, or is set back in once the purge is done; don't put a directly-out OSD back in with old data on it.

An OSD with several disks doesn't start with one of them missing: its log names the disk, and it never runs on the rest, which would look for shards on the wrong disks. Name the disk again (any path, any order), or replace it with a blank one; with no replacement, set the OSD out and, once evacuated, start it afresh on the disks it has left (production runbook).

docs.title: Full disks
docs.text:
Client writes may fill each OSD disk up to its full ratio (--full-ratio, default 0.95, as Ceph's full_ratio). Past that:

  • Writes are refused with 507 StorageFull when a shard's OSD has no room under its ratio and the write can't reach its quorum without it. S3 clients don't retry a 507 blindly, as they would a 503.
  • The rest of the disk is kept for writes that restore redundancy: repair, drain and backfill set use_reserve on their shard writes. A shard lost on a full cluster can still be rebuilt.
  • Nothing acknowledged is lost, and reads and deletes go on.
  • Deleting frees the space, and writes are admitted again.

Watch for it before it happens. Alert when an OSD passes about 85%:

objectio_osd_used_bytes / objectio_osd_capacity_bytes > 0.85

Then add OSDs or a pool, or delete data. Tested by the full_disk e2e suite: a 4+2 cluster on 1 GiB disks is filled with 4 MiB objects until writes are refused. The refusals are StorageFull, no OSD passes about 95%, the acknowledged objects read back intact, and deleting half lets writes in again.

docs.title: Types of OSD Failures
docs.text: Type Detection Impact Process crash Heartbeat timeout Temporary unavailability Network partition Heartbeat timeout Partial cluster access Hardware failure No heartbeat Requires repair

docs.title: Recovery Process
docs.text:
1. Meta probes every OSD every 15 s (every 2 s just after it starts); three misses in a row (about 45 s) mark it Down.
  2. For 120 s after that (config pg/down_out_seconds), its placement groups keep it. Writes go on at k + 1 shards (degraded), and reads decode around it. An OSD back within that time is brought up to date with what was written meanwhile; nothing moves.
  3. After 120 s, each of its placement groups gets a stand-in OSD within the pool's placement rule, and recovery backfills the PG onto it from the rest of each stripe. A PG with no OSD to stand in is Undersized.
  4. Setting it out (obioctl osd set-state <node_id> out: the host or drive is gone for good) evacuates whatever still names it and then purges it, as above; don't put an OSD set out back in with its old data.

See the production runbooks.

docs.title: Manual Recovery
docs.text:
obioctl node list                  # status and admin state of every OSD
obioctl node show <osd-id>         # its disks and capacity
obioctl cluster topology           # where it sits in the failure domains
obioctl metrics query 'objectio_meta_repair_last_pass_timestamp_seconds'

Repair is continuous; there is nothing to start by hand. An OSD that is down long enough to be replaced should be set out (see above).

docs.title: Restarting a Failed OSD
docs.text:
# Check logs for failure reason
journalctl -u objectio-osd -n 100

# Common issues:
# - Disk I/O errors → check disk health
# - Out of memory → increase limits or add RAM
# - Network issues → check connectivity

# Restart OSD
sudo systemctl restart objectio-osd

# Verify reconnection (its node_id or name, from `obioctl node list`)
obioctl node show <osd-id>

docs.title: Raft consensus (openraft 0.9)
docs.text:
The metadata service runs openraft. Every meta pod is a Raft member; cluster size is a deployment decision via meta.replicas in the helm chart:

meta.replicas Semantics Survives 1 Single-voter cluster Pod restart with PVC intact 3 3-voter quorum 1 pod loss 5 5-voter quorum 2 pod losses

Every metadata change (buckets, users, keys, tenants, pools, placement groups, configuration, …) goes through the Raft log, so a new leader has it (what is replicated).

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text:
All endpoints are plain HTTP on the meta admin port (default 9102). They're meta-local and not exposed via the gateway.

# Cluster state (leader id, term, voters, learners, last_log_index)
curl http://meta-0:9102/status | jq

# Add a node to the cluster as a learner (non-voting, catches up
# via log replication); addr is its gRPC port:
curl -X POST http://meta-0:9102/add-learner \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"node_id": 4, "addr": "meta-3.meta-headless:9100"}'

# Promote learners to voters (pass the full voter list, not a delta):
curl -X POST http://meta-0:9102/change-membership \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"voters": [1,2,3,4]}'

docs.title: Single pod failure in a 3-node cluster
docs.text:
The cluster continues with 2 of 3 nodes. A follower forwards every call to the leader, so clients see no difference while a follower is down. When the leader is lost, the followers stand for election after hearing nothing from it for a random 2–4 s (--raft-election-ms, 2000, with heartbeats every --raft-heartbeat-ms, 500); calls in flight fail with 503 to S3 clients, which retry, and writes resume once a new leader is elected. A leader answers only while a majority has confirmed it leads within the last second, so one cut off from the others stops answering rather than serve stale state.

# Watch the others elect a new leader after the leader's pod is killed:
for i in 1 2; do
  curl -s http://<name>-meta-$i.<name>-meta-headless:9102/status
done

A pod that comes back on its volume reads its Raft log, finds the newer term, and rejoins as a follower without operator action. The multi-process end-to-end tests that cover this are listed in meta HA.

Advertise addresses matter. The membership stores each node's --raft-advertise address (the chart sets it to the pod's DNS name on the gRPC port, 9100). A node that advertises 0.0.0.0 is unreachable to its peers.

docs.title: Complete metadata cluster failure
docs.text:
Scenario: all meta pods lose their PVCs simultaneously (rare — typically requires a storage-layer incident).

# If all pods still have their PVCs, just wait — each pod's redb log
# is durable, so restarting the StatefulSet recovers the cluster.
kubectl rollout restart statefulset/<name>-meta -n objectio

# If PVCs are lost, the cluster is lost — there's no quorum to recover
# from. Treat it like a fresh install:
kubectl delete statefulset/<name>-meta pvc -l app.kubernetes.io/component=meta
helm upgrade objectio ./deploy/helm/objectio -f values.yaml
# Helm's post-install Job re-runs /init + /add-learner + /change-membership
# against the new meta-0.

docs.title: Network partitions
docs.text:
Raft's quorum requirement prevents split-brain. In a 3-node cluster partitioned 1 + 2:

  • Minority side (1 pod): can't elect a leader; calls to it fail (UNAVAILABLE, 503 to S3 clients) and clients go to the other nodes.
  • Majority side (2 pods): re-elects a leader if the old one was on the minority side; continues serving writes.

When the partition heals, the minority catches up via AppendEntries and resumes as follower. No manual intervention needed.

docs.title: Stateless Recovery
docs.text:
Gateways are stateless - simply restart:

sudo systemctl restart objectio-gateway

docs.title: Load Balancer Health Checks
docs.text:
Check gateways at GET /_ready: it answers 503 until the gateway can serve, and again while it shuts down, so a load balancer stops sending it requests first. GET /health only says the process is up (health endpoints).

# nginx: passive checks (active /_ready checks need nginx Plus or another LB)
upstream objectio {
    server gateway1:9000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server gateway2:9000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
}

docs.title: Network Partitions
docs.text: Meta-side partition behavior is covered in the Metadata Service Failures section above. Gateway/OSD partitions are handled by client-side retry.

docs.title: Client Retry Logic
docs.text:
Clients should retry on different gateways:

import boto3
from botocore.config import Config

# Configure retries
config = Config(
    retries={
        'max_attempts': 3,
        'mode': 'adaptive'
    }
)

s3 = boto3.client('s3', config=config)

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Online: CRC32C verification on every read
  • Offline: Background scrubbing

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text: A read that finds a shard failing its checksum decodes the object from the other shards and returns correct data; scrub finds the rest, and recovery rebuilds the bad shard. There is no manual step. Watch objectio_osd_corrupt_shards (back to 0 once rebuilt), objectio_meta_repair_unrecoverable_stripes_total and objectio_meta_lost_objects (should stay 0).

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Meta is a Raft group (3+ nodes) and survives the loss of a minority. To protect against losing the whole cluster, replicate buckets to another ObjectIO cluster with bucket replication (asynchronous, per bucket), or copy them with an S3 tool (rclone sync, aws s3 sync) on a schedule.

docs.title: Recovery Time Objectives
docs.text: Failure Type RTO RPO Single disk Automatic 0 (no data loss) Single OSD Automatic 0 (no data loss) Single metadata node Seconds (an election) 0 Loss of a meta majority Until a majority is back 0 (Raft log) Complete cluster loss Fail over to the replica, or restore from your copy Replication lag, or the last copy

docs.title: Failure Simulation
docs.text: Test recovery in a staging cluster by failing things for real: stop an OSD process (systemctl stop objectio-osd), detach a disk, or partition a meta node with a firewall rule. Then check that objectio_objects_at_risk returns to 0 and that a checksum-verified read of a sample of objects (aws s3 cp and compare) succeeds. The end-to-end tests in the source tree (tests/e2e/tests/{repair,drain,pg_recovery}.rs, and meta_ha.rs for meta) do this against real processes.

docs.title: Meta high availability
docs.text: Meta runs as a Raft group, normally three nodes. A group of three keeps serving while any two are up; five, while any three are.

docs.title: What clients need
docs.text:
Give every gateway, OSD and block gateway every meta node's address, comma-separated:

--meta-endpoint http://meta1:9100,http://meta2:9100,http://meta3:9100

In Kubernetes, the chart's meta Service does the same job: point clients at it.

  • Any meta node serves any call. A follower forwards the call to the Raft leader and relays the answer, so clients never see a follower's possibly stale state, and never need to know which node leads.
  • A node that stops answering is skipped. Clients probe each meta address every second, with a one-second timeout, and leave out the ones that don't answer until they do. That covers a node that is down, and one that is frozen or cut off but still accepting connections, and a leader that says it can't serve (below).
  • The leader answers only while a majority confirms it leads. A leader cut off from the other meta nodes still believes it leads, but it stops answering within about 3 seconds (calls fail, 503 to S3 clients) rather than serve state the others may have changed since: a key revoked on the majority's side is not accepted on its side.
  • No call waits forever. A call to meta gives up after 5 seconds. The gateway answers S3 clients 503 when meta can't be reached, which they retry.

docs.title: What happens when a meta node is lost
docs.text: Lost Effect A follower Nothing visible. Calls in flight to it fail and are retried; new calls go to the others. When it returns it catches up from the leader. The leader The others stand for election after hearing nothing from it for 2–4 s (--raft-election-ms, 2000; heartbeats every 500 ms), and elect a new one. Writes resume within a few seconds; calls in flight at the moment of loss fail (503) and are retried. No acknowledged write is lost. The leader, cut off (frozen, partitioned) As above. While cut off it answers nothing from its own state: within about 3 seconds its calls fail (503) and clients go to the others. When it returns it finds a newer term and steps down: it never leads a second cluster. A majority Writes are refused (503) rather than accepted without a quorum. Service resumes as soon as a majority is back, with nothing acknowledged lost.

docs.title: What is replicated
docs.text:
Everything clients rely on lives in the Raft log, so a new leader has it: buckets, users and keys (including the bootstrap admin), policies, tenants, pools, placement groups, the shared-stripe registry, packs, block volumes and chunks, OSD registrations, KMS keys, and multipart uploads in progress.

The bootstrap admin is created once for the cluster, by the first leader; every meta node writes the same admin-creds.env.

docs.title: Log compaction
docs.text: The Raft log doesn't grow without bound. Every --raft-snapshot-every entries (default 500,000), each meta node writes a snapshot of its state and drops the log up to it, keeping the last --raft-keep-logs entries (default 10,000). A node that falls further behind, or a new node, is sent a snapshot of the whole metadata database. It travels in chunks and goes through <data-dir>/raft-snapshots/, so leave free space there of about the size of meta.redb. /status on the admin port shows how far the last snapshot (snapshot) and the purge (purged) reach.

docs.title: Replacing a meta node
docs.text:
Use the Raft admin API on the leader (port 9102 by default):

# 1. Start the new node (empty data dir, a new --node-id), then add it.
curl -X POST meta1:9102/add-learner -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"node_id": 4, "addr": "meta4:9100"}'
# 2. Make the voters the surviving nodes plus the new one.
curl -X POST meta1:9102/change-membership -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"voters": [1, 2, 4]}'
# 3. Stop the old node and remove its data.
curl meta1:9102/status   # voters, leader, and this node's own last applied index

Add the new node's address to clients' --meta-endpoint.

docs.title: How it's tested
docs.text:
tests/e2e/tests/meta_ha.rs runs three meta nodes, six OSDs and two gateways as separate processes, with writers running through both gateways:

  • the leader killed: writes resume within seconds, and every acknowledged write reads back through both gateways;
  • a follower killed and restarted: it catches up, then the leader is killed and the cluster carries on;
  • the leader frozen (SIGSTOP): a new leader is elected, and the old one steps down when it thaws;
  • both followers frozen: the leader, cut off, refuses reads sent to it directly (UNAVAILABLE), and serves again once they thaw;
  • two of three lost: writes refused, then resumed when one returns;
  • a KMS key, the objects encrypted under it, a multipart upload in progress, and the admin's credentials all survive a failover;
  • a meta node replaced by a new, empty one, which then forms part of the majority when another is lost.

docs.title: Metrics reference
docs.text:
Every Prometheus metric ObjectIO exports: where it comes from, what it means, and the alerts worth setting on it. For dashboards, Prometheus setup and the console's views of these metrics, see Monitoring.

All metrics are plain Prometheus text exposition. Names start with objectio_ (and process_ for the standard process family).

docs.title: Where to scrape
docs.text:
Process Endpoint Notes Gateway :9000/metrics Or the --admin-listen address when the admin surface is split off. Meta :9101/metrics --metrics-port; 0 serves none. OSD :9201/metrics --metrics-port; 0 serves none. Block gateway :9301/metrics --metrics-listen; empty serves none.

One gateway (and aio): scrape the gateway alone. By default the gateway polls every OSD and meta node every 30 seconds and re-exports their metrics on its own /metrics. Re-exported OSD series carry an osd_id label, and meta series carry component="meta". The all-in-one binary runs meta, the OSDs and the block gateway in one process with their own ports off, so the gateway's /metrics is the only endpoint and carries everything.

Several gateways (the helm chart): scrape every process directly. Run gateways with --no-reexport-metrics (the chart does, via gateway.reexportMetrics: false). Otherwise each gateway exports a copy of every OSD's and meta's metrics, and every sum multiplies by the number of gateways. The chart's Prometheus scrapes meta on 9101 and the OSDs on 9201 directly.

Do not do both. Scraping a re-exporting gateway and the OSDs and meta directly counts every OSD and meta series twice.

Series the gateway derives from its own poll (objectio_cluster_*, objectio_osd_capacity_bytes, the usage and data-safety families) exist once per gateway. With several gateways, aggregate them with max, not sum.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Latency is a histogram, in seconds, with buckets from 1 ms to 10 s (or wider where noted). Take percentiles with histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(<name>_bucket[5m]))), and keep le in any sum by.
  • Counters reset when a process restarts. Use rate() or increase(), which handle resets.
  • A family can be absent. Counter and histogram families appear once something has been recorded. SMART families need smartctl on the host. Iceberg, Unity, lifecycle and drain families need those features in use. Absent is not the same as zero.
  • Label cardinality is bounded. Operations, methods, codes and reasons come from fixed sets. Per-bucket usage (objectio_bucket_*) is one series per bucket; leave it out with --no-bucket-metrics past tens of thousands of buckets. Per-volume and per-snapshot series are one per volume and snapshot.
  • gRPC status codes use gRPC's names (OK, NOT_FOUND, UNAVAILABLE…). A streaming call that fails part-way counts as OK; its status arrives after the response headers, where it is measured.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: The chart ships the alert rules (deploy/helm/objectio/alerts/objectio-rules.yaml in the code repo). Production lists them, with a runbook for each.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• Gateway to meta calls are measured only on meta's side (objectio_meta_grpc_latency_seconds), which leaves out network time.
  • Lifecycle expiry deletes an object's metadata but not its shards (a known leak); objectio_lifecycle_actions_total{action="expire"} counts the deletes, and the space they leave is not reclaimed yet.
  • The Transfer Engine (RDMA) path reports transfers and fallbacks, but not its own latency.
  • Tracing (OpenTelemetry spans across gateway, meta and OSD) is not implemented.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: How to watch an ObjectIO cluster: where its metrics are, how to have Prometheus collect them, the dashboards and console views built on them, and the health endpoints. Every metric, its labels and the alerts worth setting on it are in the metrics reference.

docs.title: What exports metrics
docs.text:
Process Metrics endpoint Health Gateway :9000/metrics (or --admin-listen) /health, /_ready Meta :9101/metrics (--metrics-port, 0 = off) :9101/health OSD :9201/metrics (--metrics-port, 0 = off) :9201/health Block gateway :9301/metrics (--metrics-listen, empty = off) —

By default the gateway also re-exports the OSDs' and meta's metrics, which it polls every 30 seconds. That way one scrape target covers a small cluster: aio, or a single gateway. With several gateways that duplicates every series, so turn it off with --no-reexport-metrics and scrape each process directly. The metrics reference explains the choice.

docs.title: aio
docs.text:
objectio-aio runs meta, the OSDs, the gateway and (with --block-port) the block gateway in one process. Their own metrics ports are off and everything is on the gateway's /metrics:

curl -s http://localhost:9000/metrics | grep objectio_meta_raft_is_leader

A Prometheus scrape config for it:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: objectio
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9000']

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
The chart runs gateways with --no-reexport-metrics (gateway.reexportMetrics: false). With monitoring.enabled, it deploys a Prometheus that discovers and scrapes the gateway service (:9000), each meta pod (:9101) and each OSD pod (:9201). For a Prometheus of your own, scrape those three the same way: every gateway pod, every meta pod, every OSD pod.

Turn gateway.reexportMetrics on only for a single gateway scraped on its own.

docs.title: Prometheus and the console
docs.text:
The console (/_console/) charts these metrics under Monitoring:

Tab Shows Requests S3 request rate, latency percentiles, errors, Iceberg operations Block storage block operations, latency, throughput and errors by protocol; unflushed data; journal fsync; chunk flushes Metadata Raft leader, term, applied index and replication lag; meta call rate, latency and errors; durable commit time Data protection degraded, at-risk and unreadable objects; when repair and scrub last ran; shards rebuilt; corrupt shards; scrub throughput Disks & OSDs OSDs up, raw capacity used; disk write, sync and read latency; per-OSD shard write latency; WAL fsync; OSD errors

Without Prometheus, the console reads the gateway's /metrics every five seconds. It computes rates and percentiles from what changed between reads, and keeps the last five minutes. With --prometheus-url set on the gateway, the longer windows (1 h to 7 d) come from Prometheus range queries. Under --no-reexport-metrics, the OSD and meta views need Prometheus, since the gateway's /metrics then no longer carries them.

docs.title: Grafana dashboards
docs.text:
deploy/monitoring/grafana/dashboards/ (and the same set in deploy/helm/objectio/dashboards/) has:

Dashboard Covers cluster-overview.json capacity, objects, request rate and latency, disk usage s3-operations.json S3 requests by operation, latency, errors, requests in flight osd-detail.json per-OSD capacity, disk health, gRPC request rate, latency (p99) and errors disk-health.json SMART readings (needs smartctl on the OSD hosts) block-storage.json block volumes, provisioned vs used, block operations, throughput, snapshots

deploy/monitoring/ also has a docker-compose Prometheus and Grafana that load these dashboards.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text:
The chart ships a rule file (deploy/helm/objectio/alerts/objectio-rules.yaml in the code repo); production lists every alert with its runbook. It covers: - data safety: objects unreadable, at risk, unfound or lost, repair not running, scrub stale, corrupt shards; - placement groups: down, incomplete, undersized, not clean for an hour with every OSD up, not scrubbed in two weeks; - metadata: no Raft leader, repeated elections, a follower falling behind, the heal queue failing, a gateway's clock skewed; - capacity and OSDs down; - durability latency; - S3 server errors, and space leaking from failed shard deletes; - audit events dropped, replication lagging; - block journal latency, flushes failing, read errors.

Data-safety alerts come first. objectio_objects_unreadable above zero, or objectio_meta_raft_has_leader at zero, needs someone now.

docs.title: Health endpoints
docs.text:
• GET /health (gateway) answers 200 {"status":"healthy"} while the process is up. It checks nothing else, so use it for liveness.
  • GET /_ready (gateway) answers 503 until meta answers and the OSDs are reachable, then 200 from then on. If some OSDs are still missing after a grace period, it becomes ready as long as enough OSDs for a write quorum are reachable. It is a startup gate for load balancers and readiness probes. It does not drop when OSDs fail later; that is what objectio_cluster_osds_up and the data-safety metrics are for. It answers 503 again ("status": "stopping") once the gateway is shutting down, while it still serves (see how a node stops).
  • GET /health on meta's and the OSDs' metrics ports answers 200 while the process is up.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Every process logs to stderr in plain text. Set the level with --log-level (error, warn, info, debug, trace; default info). Things worth finding in logs that metrics only count: - repair work: repair: rebuilt … and repair: … needs k; - scrub results: scrub pass done: … corrupt; - shard reclaim failures, which leave space allocated; - gateway readiness, including ready without every OSD.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text: Not implemented. Requests are not traced across gateway, meta and OSD; per-phase timing of S3 PUTs and GETs is in objectio_gateway_request_phase_seconds.

docs.title: Running ObjectIO in production
docs.text: What a production cluster needs, how to size it, what to alert on, and what to do when each alert fires. Read it with the failure-recovery, meta HA, metrics and upgrades pages, which go deeper on each subject.

docs.title: Before going live
docs.text:
Every item is a default you have to change, or a requirement the software can't check for you.

Requirement Why Redundancy An erasure code: the chart's default is 4+2 (replication: 0, ec.k/ec.m), and it refuses to render with fewer OSDs than k + m; on hosts, --ec-k/--ec-m. 4+2 for 7–12 hosts, 8+4 from 13; these profiles only. Without parity (or with one copy), one lost disk loses data. Hosts At least k + m OSD hosts, one more to rebuild onto (7 for 4+2). With fewer, placement puts several shards of a stripe on one host, and losing that host can lose data. Placement doesn't refuse it. Meta 3 meta nodes (5 for two failures at once), each on its own host. Raft needs a majority: 3 survive one loss. Authentication On: gateway.noAuth: false, the chart's default. Without it anyone who reaches the gateway can read and write everything. mTLS tls.enabled: true (mTLS). Shards and metadata cross the network between services. Drives NVMe with power-loss protection, or a UPS for the whole host. An acknowledged write is fsynced; on a drive with a volatile write cache and no PLP, a power cut can still lose it. OSD layout Shards on the raw device; each OSD's state directory (--data-dir: metadata WAL and index) on a small partition of the same drive (about 2%), not the boot disk. Every metadata write fsyncs its WAL. With 18 OSDs on a host, a shared boot disk becomes the bottleneck, and its loss takes every OSD. Clocks NTP (chrony) on every host, offset well under 100 ms. A gateway whose clock is more than 500 ms from meta's refuses writes (503) until it is back in step: write order depends on clocks. Monitoring Prometheus scraping the gateways, meta and OSDs, the alert rules loaded, and the alerts routed to someone. Repair is automatic; deciding that a host is gone for good is not. Audit gateway.audit with a system bucket, if you need an audit trail (audit). Events are spooled to disk and delivered later, so a receiver outage loses nothing.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
Hardware design and sizing goes from a capacity and throughput requirement to a bill of quantities, with a calculator: hosts, drives, CPU, memory, network, meta and gateways. In short:

  • Capacity: usable ≈ raw × k/(k+m) × 0.95, less one host's worth for rebuilds.
  • Memory: about 1.5 GB per OSD (one per drive), flat however many objects it holds; 64 GB for a host of 18 drives.
  • Metadata: about 1.5 KB per object copy in each OSD's index, on a partition of the same drive; about 750 bytes per object on each meta node.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
The chart ships the rules in deploy/helm/objectio/alerts/objectio-rules.yaml: - its own Prometheus loads them when monitoring.enabled is set; - monitoring.prometheusRule.enabled also publishes them as a PrometheusRule for a prometheus-operator.

Each alert has a runbook below.

Alert Severity Runbook ObjectIOObjectsUnreadable critical Objects unreadable ObjectIOUnrecoverableStripes critical Objects unreadable ObjectIOObjectsAtRisk warning OSD down ObjectIORepairNotRunning warning Repair not running ObjectIOScrubStale warning Repair not running ObjectIOCorruptShards warning Corrupt shards ObjectIOPgDown critical Placement groups ObjectIOPgIncomplete critical Placement groups ObjectIOObjectsUnfound critical Objects unreadable ObjectIOObjectsLost critical Objects unreadable ObjectIOPgNotCleanWithOsdsUp warning Placement groups ObjectIOPgUndersized warning Placement groups ObjectIOPgScrubStale warning Repair not running ObjectIOMetaNoLeader critical Meta ObjectIOMetaElectionsChurn warning Meta ObjectIOMetaFollowerLagging warning Meta ObjectIOHealQueueFailing warning Meta ObjectIOGatewayClockSkewed critical Clock skew ObjectIOOsdDown warning OSD down ObjectIODiskNearFull warning Disks filling ObjectIODiskFull critical Disks filling ObjectIOClusterFilling warning Disks filling ObjectIOSlowShardSync warning Slow disk ObjectIOS3ServerErrors warning 5xx ObjectIOSpaceLeaking info 5xx ObjectIOAuditEventsDropped warning Audit ObjectIOReplicationLagging warning Replication ObjectIOSlowBlockJournal, ObjectIOBlockFlushFailing, ObjectIOBlockReadErrors Block

Not covered by any alert yet: certificate expiry (no metric; watch cert-manager's own), meta data-dir free space (watch with node_exporter), and the audit spool's size.

docs.title: Runbooks
docs.text: Commands are obioctl (a SigV4 client of the gateway's admin API, bin/cli/README.md in the code repo) and meta's admin port (9102).

docs.title: An OSD is down
docs.text:
What happens on its own. - Meta probes every OSD every 15 s. Three missed probes, about 45 s, mark it Down. - For the first 120 s it is down (config pg/down_out_seconds), its placement groups keep it: writes go on at k + 1 shards (degraded), and reads decode around it. A restart or a reboot moves nothing. - After that, each of its placement groups gets a stand-in OSD (within the pool's placement rule) and backfills onto it: the PG is rebuilt to full redundancy without the down OSD. A position no OSD can take leaves the PG Undersized.

What you do. 1. obioctl node list: which OSD, and since when. 2. If the process died: restart it (systemctl restart objectio-osd, or the pod). Back within 120 s, it rejoins and recovery brings it up to date with what was written while it was gone. 3. If the host or drive is gone for good: obioctl osd set-state <node_id> out, so it is no longer counted as in service. Its PGs already have stand-ins; watch them backfill (obioctl pg list --state Degraded). 4. If it won't start, and its log says its metadata log is damaged ("damage, not a torn append", or records missing): what it holds can't be trusted. Treat it as a failed drive (step 3, then replace the disk with a fresh state directory). A crash alone leaves a torn tail, which the OSD cuts off by itself.

An OSD whose metadata log failed a write or an fsync ("refusing every write until it is reopened" in its log) stays up but refuses every write. Restart it: the restart finds where the log really ends. If it happens again, the drive is failing; replace it.

Done when ObjectIOObjectsAtRisk clears and every placement group is Clean again (objectio_meta_pgs_not_clean 0).

docs.title: Replacing a disk
docs.text:
1. If the disk still reads: obioctl osd set-state <node_id> draining, and wait for obioctl cluster drain-status to show it empty. It turns out by itself.
  2. If it doesn't read: obioctl osd set-state <node_id> out.
  3. Swap the drive and start the OSD on it with the same state directory: it keeps its identity, finds the disk blank, and forgets the shards it held there. On an OSD with several disks, the blank disk takes the place of the one that is missing, whatever its path. A file-backed disk (disk.raw on a volume) is replaced by a blank file the size of the old one, made before the OSD starts (truncate -s <size> /data/disk0/disk.raw): an OSD makes a disk file itself only on its first start.
  4. obioctl osd set-state <node_id> in. Repair rebuilds what it held.

docs.title: An OSD that won't start for a missing disk
docs.text:
An OSD knows its disks by the ids in their superblocks, not by their paths or order. Started without one of them, it doesn't start, and its log says which (this OSD's disk 1 (id …, last at /dev/…) is missing). Running on the rest would look for shards on the wrong disks.

  • The disk is there under another name (a renamed device, a glob that missed it): name it again, at any path, in any order.
  • A disk file does not exist (disk … does not exist, and this OSD has run on its disks): its volume isn't mounted. Mount it; if the disk is lost, put a blank file there as above.
  • The disk is dead: replace it with a blank one, as above.
  • No replacement, and the OSD should run on the disks it has left: that is a new OSD. Set the old one out, wait until obioctl cluster drain-status shows it evacuated, then wipe its state directory and its remaining disks and start it on them: it joins as a new OSD.

It also refuses a disk that is not blank and not one of its own (another OSD's, or one replaced earlier and put back): remove it from the OSD's disks, or wipe it to add it as a new disk. A disk named with --disks that can't be read as an ObjectIO disk stops the OSD, rather than being skipped.

docs.title: Disks filling or full
docs.text:
• Near full (85%). Plan capacity: add OSDs or hosts (the balancer moves data onto them), or delete data. Check obioctl cluster usage.
  • Full (95%). That OSD refuses client writes and clients get 507. The space above 95% is kept for repair. Other OSDs keep taking writes for stripes not placed on the full one.
  • Find which disks: objectio_disk_used_bytes / objectio_disk_capacity_bytes.
  • One full disk among emptier ones is uneven placement: the balancer evens it out (obioctl cluster rebalance status).
  • Everything full: add capacity. Deletes free space within a minute.
  • Don't raise --full-ratio to get writes going: it spends the room repair needs after the next failure.

docs.title: A gateway refuses writes for clock skew
docs.text:
Its clock is more than 500 ms from meta's (objectio_gateway_clock_offset_seconds gives the offset). Writes through it fail with 503 (clients retry, ideally through another gateway). Reads work.

Fix time sync on that host (chronyc tracking, chronyc makestep). Writes resume within a second of the clock coming back in step. Don't restart the gateway: it doesn't help.

docs.title: Meta has no leader, or elects often
docs.text:
• No leader for more than a minute: fewer than a majority of meta nodes are up or can reach each other. Writes fail with 503; reads of object data mostly still work.
  • curl http://<meta>:9102/status on each node shows its role, its term, and who it thinks leads.
  • Bring a majority back. A node lost for good is replaced with POST :9102/add-learner then POST :9102/change-membership (meta HA).
  • No procedure exists yet for a majority lost for good.
  • Elections churn: usually a node that drops off the network intermittently, or a disk too slow for its heartbeats. Compare the nodes' objectio_meta_commit_seconds.
  • A follower lags: it is catching up, or its disk is slow. One far behind is sent a snapshot.
  • Heal queue failing: writes reached a quorum of metadata copies while meta was unreachable; gateways retry queuing them for 10 minutes. Persistent failures mean meta is down: see above.

docs.title: Repair not running
docs.text:
objectio_meta_repair_last_pass_timestamp_seconds hasn't moved in three repair intervals (--repair-interval-secs, an hour by default). Repair runs on the meta leader: - check that there is one (above); - check the leader's log for repair: lines; - a pass that never ends is usually a target OSD that accepts connections but doesn't answer.

Scrub stale: an OSD hasn't finished a scrub pass in 8 days. Check that OSD's log; a pass on a very full disk at 50 MiB/s (--scrub-rate-mib) can take days.

PG scrub stale: a placement group hasn't been scrubbed in two weeks (twice scrub/every_seconds, 7 days). Placement-group scrubs run from the meta leader; check that there is one, and its log. obioctl pg scrub <pg_id> scrubs one now.

docs.title: Corrupt shards
docs.text: Scrub or a read found shards that don't match their checksums. The OSD reports them, and repair rebuilds them from the rest of the stripe. If the count keeps rising on one OSD, its drive is failing: check its SMART metrics (objectio_disk_smart_*) and replace it (above).

docs.title: Placement groups down, incomplete or undersized
docs.text: Peering, on the meta leader, gives each placement group a state. obioctl pg list --pool <pool> --state <state> names the PGs, and obioctl pg get <pg_id> --pool <pool> says why and which members. - Down: fewer members answer than a read needs (k). Its objects can't be read or written. Bring the OSDs back. - Incomplete: fewer than a read quorum of its metadata copies answer, so a newer write may be on those that don't. It serves reads, but nothing is rebuilt. Bring the members back. - Undersized: a position has no usable OSD and none can stand in within the pool's rule (not enough hosts, racks or free space). Add OSDs in the missing domain, or bring the member back. - Not clean for an hour with every OSD up: recovery is stuck or slow. obioctl pg get shows its last error; WaitTooFull means a member to fill is past its full ratio (see disks filling).

docs.title: Objects unreadable or unrecoverable
docs.text: Some stripes have fewer than k good shards: more failures at once than the code tolerates. Peering counts them per placement group as unfound (objectio_meta_pg_objects_unfound) while members may still bring them back; objects recorded lost (objectio_meta_lost_objects) have fewer than k shards anywhere. 1. Bring back every OSD that is down but intact (powered off, network). Their shards make the stripes readable again. 2. Don't set OSDs out or wipe disks until this is resolved. 3. What can't be brought back is lost. obioctl pg get gives the counts per placement group; no tool yet lists the objects.

docs.title: A slow disk
docs.text: p99 shard fsync over 100 ms. Find the OSD from the per-OSD objectio_osd_disk_seconds. A drive getting slower often fails next: check SMART, and drain it (replacing a disk) if it doesn't recover. A drive without power-loss protection is always slow to fsync.

docs.title: S3 requests failing with 5xx
docs.text:
• 503s during a fault are expected: clients retry.
  • Persistent 503s mean meta has no leader, OSDs are unreachable, or a gateway refuses writes for clock skew. See those runbooks.
  • A 500 is a bug: report it with the gateway's log line for the request id.

Space leaking: shard deletes are failing, so freed space stays allocated. Nothing reclaims it later yet (objectio#83). It is usually an OSD that is down. A leak is never a loss.

docs.title: Audit events dropped
docs.text:
Events are spooled on the gateway's disk until delivered. Drops mean: - the spool filled (--audit-spool-max-bytes) because a receiver has been down for long; or - a gateway pod was deleted without a clean shutdown.

Fix the receiver; size the spool for the longest outage you accept (audit).

docs.title: Replication lagging
docs.text: The oldest unreplicated version is over an hour old. That is how much a loss of this site would lose. Check the target's reachability and credentials, and the result="error" count of objectio_replication_sent_total (replication).

docs.title: Block volumes
docs.text:
The block gateway journals writes on its own disk before storing them as chunks. - Slow journal fsync: slows every block write. - Flush failing: chunks aren't being stored; the write cache fills and writes stall. - Read errors: reads that couldn't be served.

The journal is a single copy on the block gateway's disk: losing that disk loses writes not yet flushed (a known gap; see the block design).

  • Journal failed a write or fsync ("refusing every write until it is reopened" in the gateway's log): every block write fails. Restart the gateway; if it happens again, replace its disk.
  • Gateway won't start, journal damaged ("damage, not a torn write"): the entries after the damage are acknowledged writes, possibly not yet stored on the OSDs, and this file is their only copy. Keep the file; moving it aside starts the gateway with those writes lost.

docs.title: Certificates expiring
docs.text: cert-manager renews 30 days before expiry. The services read their certificates only at start, so after a renewal restart them (rolling): kubectl rollout restart statefulset/<name>-meta statefulset/<name>-osd deployment/<name>-gateway, where <name> is the release name if it contains objectio (release objectio: objectio-meta), else <release>-objectio. An expired certificate stops every internal call. There is no expiry metric yet: alert on cert-manager's certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: Follow upgrades: meta first, then OSDs, then gateways, one at a time. Then obioctl upgrade status, and obioctl upgrade finalize once every node runs the new release. Back up a stopped follower's data directory (meta.redb, raft-log) first.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: Move a cluster to the next release one node at a time, under traffic. Design: core/upgrade-path.md.

docs.title: What to know first
docs.text:
• One release at a time. Go from each release to the next; to skip releases, upgrade through each in turn.
  • Format levels. Each release has a format level. During an upgrade, nodes on the new release read what it introduces but keep writing the previous release's formats, so you can still go back. The new formats start only when you finalize.
  • No going back after finalize. Back up meta first (stop a meta follower and copy its data directory, meta.redb and raft-log; an export command is planned).
  • Too-old nodes are refused. After finalize, meta refuses any node or client from an older release, and a node too old for the cluster stops at start-up with a message saying so, instead of running and misreading data.

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. Back up meta.
  2. Meta nodes: the followers one at a time, then the leader. After each, wait until it has rejoined: GET /status on its admin port shows a leader_id, and its own last_applied within a few entries of the leader's (GET /status on the leader). Each node's /status reports only its own indexes.
  3. OSDs, one failure domain at a time. After each, wait until it is registered and healthy (obioctl node list). A restart needs no drain: reads tolerate up to m missing shards meanwhile.
  4. Gateways and block gateways, in any order.
  5. Check that every node runs the new release:
obioctl upgrade status

It lists every node heard from in the last 90 seconds, with its release and format level, and says what blocks finalizing: a meta node or an OSD that hasn't reported (down, or still on a release from before format levels), or a node still on the old release. Gateways are stateless and can't be listed in advance, so check that every gateway you run appears.

  1. Finalize:
obioctl upgrade finalize

It is refused while anything blocks it. It answers once the default pool's placement groups are made, which can take up to 40 s if an OSD is still coming up. Until then, a write to a bucket without a pool of its own is refused with a 503 that S3 clients retry.

To go back before step 6, run the same steps in reverse order with the previous release's binaries.

docs.title: How a node stops
docs.text:
Every service stops cleanly on SIGTERM, which Kubernetes, systemd and docker stop send, or on SIGINT (Ctrl-C), and exits 0:

  • Gateway: /_ready answers 503 at once, while the gateway goes on serving for --shutdown-delay-secs (default 5), so that load balancers and Kubernetes endpoints stop sending it requests first. Then it stops taking connections, gives the requests in flight up to --shutdown-drain-secs (default 20) to finish, and delivers what its audit and bucket-log spools hold, for up to --audit-drain-secs (default 20).
  • Meta: answers the calls in flight, stops Raft, and makes its state durable.
  • OSD: finishes the calls in flight. Every write it acknowledged is already on disk.
  • Block gateway: lets a flush under way finish (up to 10 s) and syncs its journal. Every write it acknowledged is already in the journal.

A second signal exits at once, without waiting for the rest (status 143 for SIGTERM, 130 for SIGINT). objectio-aio stops the same way, its gateway without the delay, and exits after 5 s at most.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Roll the meta and OSD StatefulSets one pod at a time (partition), each gated on readiness, in the order above, then run obioctl upgrade finalize.

A gateway pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds must cover its shutdown: the delay, the request drain and the audit drain. The chart sets it to the audit drain plus 30 s when the audit spool is on; otherwise Kubernetes' default of 30 s covers the delay and the request drain. A pod still running when the grace period ends is killed, and an audit spool on an emptyDir goes with it.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Both calls are system admin only.

Call GET /_admin/upgrade active_level, finalize_to, can_finalize, blockers, and nodes (kind, id, release, format level, address, seconds since last report) POST /_admin/upgrade/finalize Raises the active level. Returns 409 with the blockers when not every node is ready

docs.title: Clusters from before 0.1.0
docs.text:
0.1.0 is the first release: a 0.1.0-rc.1 cluster upgrades to 0.1.0 as above. A cluster on a development build from before 0.1.0 can't be upgraded: install 0.1.0 fresh and copy the data across (with bucket replication, or any S3 tool).

An rc.1 cluster on arm64, or built from source without the isal feature, is not upgraded in place. From 0.1.0 every build erasure-codes with ISA-L; those builds coded MDS stripes with another code (reed-solomon-simd), whose parity 0.1.0 can't decode. A stripe that loses a data shard can't be rebuilt, and while old and new nodes mix, repair of a shard a write never stored rebuilds it in the other code, which reads then serve as data: the rolling-upgrade test, run that way, read objects back wrong. Install 0.1.0 fresh and copy the data across, as above. A cluster on the amd64 rc.1 release binaries or image coded with ISA-L already, and upgrades in place.

An rc.1 cluster installed with the Helm chart's default protection (ec.k: 1, ec.m: 0) sets replication: 1 when it upgrades. 0.1.0's meta refuses to start with a default profile of no parity, and the chart's default is now 4+2 erasure coding over 6 OSDs, which such a cluster's default pool isn't; pass --set replication=1 (one copy) and its osd.replicas (Kubernetes). Its default pool, made 1+0, never took an object over the inline limit (4 KiB) and stays as it was made: install 0.1.0 fresh and copy the objects across, as above.

The first public release of ObjectIO: S3-compatible object storage in Rust, on one storage core (erasure coding, failure-domain-aware placement, repair, metadata on Raft), with data lake catalogs and block volumes on the same core. Apache-2.0, every feature.

Status: release candidate 0.1.0-rc.1, 2026-10-18. What remains before 0.1.0 is final is in the roadmap.

docs.title: An early release
docs.text:
0.1.0 is early, and says so in its number. What that means:

  • Tested for production: S3 and the storage core. The evidence is below: ceph s3-tests, a 48-hour soak under faults, a chaos suite on six machines, and power-cut replay of the OSD's disk writes.
  • Previews: the data lake APIs and block volumes. Built and tested on their own, but not yet with real engines (Spark, Trino, pyiceberg) or under a filesystem and a database. File access is not built.
  • The promise that holds from 0.1.0 on: adjacent releases upgrade one node at a time, under traffic, with every object readable after; a 0.1.0-rc.1 cluster upgrades to 0.1.0 the same way (upgrades). An acknowledgement means the data is on stable storage, in every release.
  • What may change between 0.x releases: the admin API, the CLI and the console. A change to either is in the notes of the release that makes it.

Every feature and how far it has been proven is in features.md.

docs.title: S3
docs.text:
• The S3 API that applications use: buckets, objects, multipart uploads, copies, ranges, conditional requests and writes, checksums, tagging, versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle expiration, CORS, presigned URLs and POST uploads (S3 API).
  • S3 Select: SQL over CSV, JSON and Parquet objects, compressed or not, answered in AWS's event stream; the object is read in ranges and parsed as it arrives, Parquet by the columns the query names, so memory doesn't grow with the object (S3 API).
  • Gateway-side grep: ?grep on an object or a prefix streams matches as NDJSON with byte offsets, so an agent can fetch the context around a match with a range read instead of downloading the file (grep).
  • Audit: one event per request, with the request ID the client got, to webhooks, a file, stdout and each tenant's own webhooks; fsynced to a spool on the gateway before delivery, so a crash or a receiver outage loses nothing; on by default for the system, into an internal bucket (audit).
  • Bucket logging in the S3 access-log format (bucket logging).
  • Bucket replication between ObjectIO clusters: new writes as they happen, a resync of existing objects that resumes where it stopped, and a bandwidth limit (replication).
  • Quotas of bytes and objects per tenant and per bucket.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• Raw-disk OSDs: O_DIRECT, a write-ahead log, io_uring in Linux release builds (pread, with a warning, on a host that denies io_uring, such as a container under docker's default seccomp profile). Each shard is fsynced, then its location record, before a PUT is acknowledged.
  • An OSD's disks are known by the ids in their superblocks, not by their paths or order: an OSD missing one of its disks, or given a disk not its own, doesn't start, and a blank disk replaces a missing one. Every read and scrub checks that the block is the shard its location names.
  • Erasure coding (Reed-Solomon 4+2 by default) with ISA-L on x86_64 and arm64 alike: one code on every build, so amd64 and arm64 nodes mix in one cluster, and a pool takes only the profiles every loss of m shards decodes (data protection). Each shard's checksum is kept with the object and checked on every read and repair, and a data shard a read rebuilds is checked before it is served.
  • A pool's protection scheme is checked when the pool is made or changed, and meta's default scheme when it starts: a profile with no parity (1+0; one unprotected copy is replication of 1), an LRC whose data shards don't split evenly into its groups or that has no local or global parity, a replica count of 0, or more than 255 shards is refused with what is wrong with it (data protection).
  • LRC pools take objects of any length, PUT or multipart, coded as LRC stripes (not yet through the full end-to-end suite or a soak). An LRC stripe survives every loss of its global parity count, more by where they fall: LRC 6+2+2 any 2 shards and 88% of the ways of losing 3 (what LRC survives).
  • Object metadata written at a majority of the object's OSDs and read from a quorum: writes, overwrites and deletes go on with one or two OSDs down.
  • Placement groups across failure domains (host by default; rack, zone and more if declared), each with an epoch committed before any write uses it; recovery, repair, backfill and drain by placement group; a drive lost for good re-protected without an operator.
  • Small objects: their shards travel with their metadata in one round trip, and many are packed into one stripe.
  • Meta on Raft (openraft) on three or more nodes, any node serving, with its own log: a meta node is back within a second of a power cut, and an OSD of 10 M shards serves 17 s after one. The leader answers only while a majority confirms it still leads: one cut off from its followers stops answering, rather than serve what may have changed elsewhere.
  • Rolling upgrades under traffic, new formats gated until every node runs the new release.
  • Bucket listings seek to the continuation marker and past each common prefix, so a page costs the same at the end of a large bucket as at its start.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Users, keys, groups, policies and roles per tenant, through the admin API and the AWS IAM and STS APIs (aws iam, aws sts, boto3, Terraform); a tenant is an account, its admins its root (IAM).
  • STS from an OIDC token, with an identity provider per scope: the operator's for system roles, each tenant's for its own.
  • Anonymous access and Block Public Access at bucket, tenant and cluster level, new buckets blocked; named endpoints and client addresses (aws:SourceVpce, aws:SourceIp, trusted proxies) in policies (public access).
  • SSE-S3, SSE-KMS with the built-in KMS, SSE-C.
  • mTLS on every gRPC hop between services (mTLS).

docs.title: Data lake (preview)
docs.text:
• Iceberg REST Catalog: warehouses, namespaces, tables, commits, policies, vended credentials (Iceberg API).
  • Unity Catalog API at /api/2.1/unity-catalog/*: catalogs, schemas, tables, functions, volumes, models and versions; policies at each level; row filters and column masks bound to SQL functions, which engines read and apply; a backing bucket per catalog that refuses anything but vended credentials, so a permanent key can't bypass a filter; Keycloak groups mapped to IAM groups by name (feature reference).
  • Delta Sharing: shares, recipients, presigned queries over Delta (JSON log) and Iceberg tables (feature reference).

docs.title: Block (preview)
docs.text: • Volumes over NBD and gRPC: thin provisioning, snapshots and clones that share stripes, a write journal fsynced before each acknowledgement, volume metadata in meta, repair of block stripes.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
• objectio-aio, the whole cluster in one process; binaries for Linux x86_64 and arm64 (and macOS for development); a multi-arch image (quickstart).
  • A Helm chart whose defaults protect data and require auth: 4+2 erasure coding over 6 OSDs (it refuses to render with fewer OSDs than the code needs), 3 metas, 2 gateways, disruption budgets for all three. A values file can express a production deployment: placement (node selectors, affinity, tolerations, spread constraints), NetworkPolicies, raw block volumes for OSDs, each OSD's zone and rack read from its node's labels, existing Secrets for the SSE key, OIDC and Delta Sharing (a generated SSE key is kept across upgrades and on uninstall), and probes that ask meta whether its Raft runs and has a leader and the OSDs whether their disks are healthy. The block gateway is a StatefulSet of one pod over its journal; helm install --wait completes. The kind setup sets its own development values (Kubernetes).
  • The Linux binaries need glibc 2.28 or later and no other library: PCRE2 is linked in and TLS loads no OpenSSL. Each is run on Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Rocky Linux 9 and Amazon Linux 2023 before the release is published (Linux).
  • objectio-install sets a Linux host up under systemd: units that start meta and the gateway with the flags the Helm chart passes, an OSD per disk with its own config file and ports, and cluster init, which forms meta's Raft group over the admin ports. Every binary's default ports are the cluster's (meta 9100, OSD 9200); meta and the gateway take flags only. Tested end to end: one host, then three, run from the units the installer wrote, serve S3 (Linux).
  • Every service stops cleanly on SIGTERM: it finishes its work in flight and exits 0, and the gateway leaves the load balancer, drains, and delivers its audit spool first, so a rollout loses no request or audit event (upgrades).
  • The web console (operator and tenant), obioctl, and Go and Python SDKs for the whole admin API (SDKs).
  • Prometheus metrics; a production guide with sizing, alerts and runbooks; a hardware sizing guide with a calculator (production, hardware sizing).

docs.title: How it was tested
docs.text:
All on the release candidate's code.

Test Result Unit and end-to-end tests against real processes, a meta HA test on Kubernetes (kind), a rolling upgrade under traffic, the crash-consistency test, and a performance check, on every change; the data-path end-to-end tests also on binaries built with the release's features (io_uring). A test that can't run where it is run (no root, no previous release, no Mooncake build) fails, never passes untested Pass ceph s3-tests, Linux x86_64 680 of 687 applicable pass; the other 7 are 6 known gaps and 1 test caught by another running beside it (it passes alone). No bugs ceph s3-tests, Linux arm64 679 of 687 applicable pass; the other 8 are the same 6 gaps and 2 tests that fail only beside others (each passes alone). No bugs Soak: 48 hours on a lab host, faults every half hour or so Pass: 84 faults (power cuts, meta leader kills and partitions, disks pulled, drives lost for good), 7.02 M acknowledged operations, 1.50 TB written; every key audited at the end, nothing lost, no space leaked Chaos: six machines, writes through two gateways, six faults Pass: 81,436 acknowledged writes intact after every fault; longest write pause 13.2 s (the meta leader partitioned); afterwards any two OSDs could be stopped with every object readable Crash consistency: the OSD's disk writes recorded and replayed up to random power-cut points Every acknowledged write survives Performance Single host and six cloud VMs, side by side with RustFS and SeaweedFS

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• Meta's memory grows under sustained load: from about 37 MB to 190–340 MB over the 48-hour soak, 498 MB at the peak. It doesn't grow with uptime alone; a heap profile is next.
  • A partitioned meta leader pauses writes longer than before: 13.2 s in the chaos suite, against 5.4 s on 2026-10-04; within the suite's 60 s limit, not yet explained.
  • Repair after a short outage is slow on small machines: on the chaos VMs, every placement group took up to 8 minutes to be clean again after a one-minute outage. Objects stay readable meanwhile, but until repair is done some have less redundancy than their pool's scheme gives.
